claim: Write always-loaded instructions at the 'right altitude': specific enough to guide behavior, but as strong heuristics rather than hardcoded brittle if-else logic, and never vague guidance that assumes shared context.
quote: The right altitude is the Goldilocks zone between two common failure modes. At one extreme, we see engineers hardcoding complex, brittle logic in their prompts to elicit exact agentic behavior.
source: Effective context engineering for AI agents
detail: The other extreme named in the same paragraph is 'vague, high-level guidance that fails to give the LLM concrete signals for desired outputs or falsely assumes shared context.' The target is heuristics the model can apply, not a script it has to execute.

claim: Aim for the smallest set of information that fully specifies the expected behavior. Minimal does not mean short: the agent still needs enough up front to behave correctly.
quote: you should be striving for the minimal set of information that fully outlines your expected behavior. (Note that minimal does not necessarily mean short
source: Effective context engineering for AI agents
detail: The post's guiding principle is to find 'the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome.' This supports the brief's framing that a smaller file is a side effect of a better one, not the goal. Context is a finite 'attention budget' because of context rot.

claim: Start with a minimal prompt on the best available model, then add instructions and examples only for failure modes you actually observe in testing.
quote: start by testing a minimal prompt with the best model available to see how it performs on your task, and then add clear instructions and examples to improve performance based on failure modes found during initial testing.
source: Effective context engineering for AI agents
detail: Every added instruction should trace back to an observed failure, not an anticipated one. The same post's closing advice is 'do the simplest thing that works'.

claim: The source ties this to Claude Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6, not to newer models in general: 'Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 are also more responsive to the system prompt than previous models. If your prompts were designed to reduce undertriggering on tools or skills, these models may now overtrigger.' Its fix is to replace 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...' with 'Use this tool when...' and to drop 'If in doubt, use [tool]'. The same page says a technique that names a model is measured on that model, so re-check it on current models before treating it as general advice.
quote: If your prompts were designed to reduce undertriggering on tools or skills, these models may now overtrigger. The fix is to dial back any aggressive language.
source: Prompting best practices (Claude docs)
published: living doc, undated; covers Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5 and earlier; read 2026-09-25
original_claim: Remove emphatic language (CRITICAL, MUST, 'If in doubt, use X') that was written to stop older models undertriggering. Newer models now overtrigger on it, so use plain conditional phrasing ('Use this tool when...').
detail: The page gives this rewrite: 'CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...' becomes 'Use this tool when...'. It also says 'Instructions like "If in doubt, use [tool]" will cause overtriggering.' It recommends replacing blanket defaults ('Default to using [tool]') with conditions ('Use [tool] when it would enhance your understanding of the problem'). Migration step 6 says to dial back anti-laziness and thoroughness prompting. One nuance: the Claude Code best-practices doc still allows 'IMPORTANT' on the single line Claude keeps skipping, and warns that 'If you emphasize many lines, none of them stands out.'

claim: This comes from the Claude Fable 5 / Mythos 5 guide and is scoped to that model: its instruction-following has improved enough that you can steer most behaviors with a brief instruction rather than naming each one. The guide's examples are a brevity instruction and a checkpoint instruction. It makes no claim that current models in general generalize this way.
quote: Instruction-following is improved enough that you can steer most behaviors with a brief instruction rather than enumerating each behavior by name.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5
published: living doc, undated (Claude Fable 5 / Mythos 5 generation); read 2026-09-25
original_claim: Steer behavior with one brief, general instruction rather than listing every undesired behavior by name. Current models generalize from it.
detail: The same page applies this to checkpoints: 'To have Claude Fable 5 stop only where it genuinely needs you, there is no need to enumerate every case.' It also says capability jumps are 'a good prompt to re-evaluate which instructions, tools, and guardrails are still needed.' Counterpoint: the Sonnet 5 guide says Sonnet 5 reads instructions literally and 'does not silently generalize an instruction from one item to another', so scope should be stated explicitly for that model.

claim: Scope note: the source is about Claude Fable 5 ('often too prescriptive for Claude Fable 5'), and it says to 'consider removing' older instructions if default performance is better. It does not say 'always remove'.
quote: Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive for Claude Fable 5 and can degrade output quality. Review and consider removing older instructions if default performance is better.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5
original_claim: Re-examine skills and prompts written for earlier models when migrating, and remove prescriptive instructions whenever default model behavior is better. Old prescriptiveness can reduce quality.
detail: This is listed under 'Recommended scaffolding changes'. For an audit it means the test for each instruction is whether it beats the model's default behavior, not whether it is correct. Prescriptiveness is a defect in itself.

claim: Scope note: this is one engineer's design rationale for a planner agent in an experimental harness ('It seemed smarter...'). The cascade was a concern ('if the planner... got something wrong, the errors in the spec would cascade'), not a measured result.
quote: It seemed smarter to constrain the agents on the deliverables to be produced and let them figure out the path as they worked.
source: Harness design for long-running application development
original_claim: Constrain agents on the deliverables and let them work out the path. Specifying granular implementation details up front makes any errors cascade downstream.
detail: The planner was told to stay on product context and high-level design 'due to the concern that if the planner tried to specify granular technical details upfront and got something wrong, the errors in the spec would cascade into the downstream implementation.' Before each chunk of work, the generator and evaluator agreed a contract saying what 'done' meant and how it would be tested. This is outcome plus completion bar without a fixed path. The prompting best-practices doc says the same about reasoning: 'A prompt like "think thoroughly" often produces better reasoning than a hand-written step-by-step plan.'

claim: Treat every harness or instruction component as an assumption about what the model cannot do on its own. Re-test those assumptions when each new model ships, removing one component at a time to find which ones still carry weight.
quote: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing
source: Harness design for long-running application development
detail: A radical cut-back failed and made it 'difficult to tell which pieces of the harness design were actually load-bearing', so the author switched to 'removing one component at a time and reviewing what impact it had on the final result.' The sprint construct and per-sprint QA were dropped for Opus 4.6. Context resets, which Sonnet 4.5 needed because of 'context anxiety', were unnecessary on Opus 4.5; the Managed Agents post (2026-04-08) says 'The resets had become dead weight.' The evaluator is 'worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo.'

claim: Precision note: Anthropic's commitment covers Claude Code's system prompt. It runs a broad per-model eval suite on every change and is 'continuing ablations' to learn each line's impact; it does not gate every change on per-line ablation. The '≤25 words / ≤100 words' length line passed weeks of testing on the narrower eval set. Broader ablations then showed a 3% drop on one evaluation for Opus 4.6 and 4.7, and together with other prompt changes the line hurt coding quality.
quote: We will run a broad suite of per-model evals for every system prompt change to Claude Code, continuing ablations to understand the impact of each line
source: An update on recent Claude Code quality reports
original_claim: Gate every always-loaded prompt change behind line-by-line ablations and a broad, per-model eval suite. One plausible line (a hard numeric length limit) lowered coding quality even though a narrower eval suite showed no regression.
detail: The offending line was 'Length limits: keep text between tool calls to ≤25 words. Keep final responses to ≤100 words unless the task requires more detail.' It shipped after 'multiple weeks of internal testing and no regressions in the set of evaluations we ran'. Later ablations on broader evals 'showed a 3% drop for both Opus 4.6 and 4.7' and the line was reverted. Anthropic also added CLAUDE.md guidance 'to ensure model-specific changes are gated to the specific model they're targeting.' This is evidence against hard word-count caps in always-loaded prompts.

claim: Treat model-specific prompting advice as measured on that one model, and re-check it on your own evals before applying it to another model. A portable instruction set should not bake in one model's quirks.
quote: Where a technique names a specific model, treat it as measured on that model and re-check it against your own evals before applying it to another.
source: Prompting best practices (Claude docs)
detail: Model behaviors differ in opposite directions. Opus 5 is verbose and narrates heavily, while Fable 5.1 writes fewer updates and less formatting. The Fable 5.1 guide says its standard anti-markdown block 'can suppress structure the content needs'. Sonnet 5 follows instructions literally. Guidance that fixes one model can harm another.

claim: Give the reason behind an instruction (its purpose or constraint), not just the bare rule. The model generalizes from the explanation to related cases.
quote: Providing context or motivation behind your instructions, such as explaining to Claude why such behavior is important, can help Claude better understand your goals and deliver more targeted responses.
source: Prompting best practices (Claude docs)
detail: Example given: 'NEVER use ellipses' is weaker than explaining that a text-to-speech engine cannot pronounce them. 'Claude is smart enough to generalize from the explanation.' The Fable 5 guide agrees ('Give the reason, not only the request'), and so does the claude.com 'Steering Claude Code' post ('explaining the why behind constraints'). See the contested Claude Code skills-doc finding for the opposite view on skill bodies.

claim: Keep a skill's body concise because it stays in context for every later turn once loaded. State what to do rather than narrating how or why, and write guidance that applies for the whole task as standing instructions.
quote: Keep the body itself concise. Once a skill loads, its content stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost. State what to do rather than narrating how or why
source: Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code docs)
detail: This conflicts on its face with the prompting docs and the Fable 5 guide, which recommend explaining why. One way to reconcile them: give the reason in a clause where it changes the model's decisions, and cut narrative rationale that does not. The same doc says Claude Code does not re-read a skill on later turns ('write guidance that should apply throughout a task as standing instructions rather than one-time steps'). After compaction, only the first 5,000 tokens of each re-attached skill are kept, within a 25,000-token shared budget.

claim: The cited post supports this: don't stuff a laundry list of edge cases into a prompt; curate diverse, canonical examples of the expected behavior instead. The clause 'prefer showing what to do over saying what not to do' is not in that post. The nearest text is in the platform prompting best-practices doc ('Tell Claude what to do instead of what not to do'), where it appears as an output-formatting technique. Drop the clause or cite that doc for it separately.
quote: teams will often stuff a laundry list of edge cases into a prompt in an attempt to articulate every possible rule the LLM should follow for a particular task. We do not recommend this.
source: Effective context engineering for AI agents
original_claim: Do not pack prompts with a long list of edge-case rules. Use a small set of diverse, canonical examples of the expected behavior instead, and prefer showing what to do over saying what not to do.
detail: The recommended alternative: 'curate a set of diverse, canonical examples that effectively portray the expected behavior'. The Opus 5 guide adds: 'Positive examples of the communication style you want tend to be more effective than instructions about what not to do.' The sources disagree on how many examples to use: the docs say 3–5, while the claude.com prompting blog says start with one and add more only if needed. That blog also warns that Claude 4.x-and-later models 'pay very close attention to details in examples.'

claim: Prune always-loaded instruction files line by line. Cut any line whose removal would not cause mistakes, and anything Claude can infer from the code. Bloat makes Claude ignore the rules that matter.
quote: For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!
source: Best practices for Claude Code
published: living doc, undated (the 2025-04-18 engineering post now redirects here); read 2026-09-25
detail: The page's Exclude column lists: anything Claude can work out by reading the code, standard language conventions, detailed API docs, information that changes often, long tutorials, file-by-file codebase descriptions, and 'Self-evident practices like "write clean code"'. Its diagnostic: 'If Claude keeps doing something you don't want despite having a rule against it, the file is probably too long and the rule is getting lost.' It also says 'CLAUDE.md is loaded every session, so only include things that apply broadly', with sometimes-relevant workflows moved to skills. Its failure-pattern fix for an over-specified file: 'If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it or convert it to a hook.' This works directly as an audit rubric.

claim: Keep each always-loaded instruction file under about 200 lines, write rules concrete enough to verify, and remove contradictions, because Claude may follow either of two conflicting rules arbitrarily.
quote: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.
source: How Claude remembers your project (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md, Claude Code docs)
detail: Same section, Specificity: 'write instructions that are concrete enough to verify' (e.g. 'Run `npm test` before committing' rather than 'Test your changes'). Consistency: 'if two rules contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily.' The page also says memory files are 'context, not enforced configuration'. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md natively from v2.1.277, but reads CLAUDE.md only when both exist, unless CLAUDE.md imports AGENTS.md. The 200-line target also appears in the claude.com 'Steering Claude Code' post (2026-06-18).

claim: Do not put 'never do X' or 'every time X, always do Y' rules in prose instruction files when they must hold. Enforce them deterministically with hooks, permissions or managed settings, because prompted rules fail under pressure, in long sessions, or under prompt injection.
quote: A real guardrail needs to be deterministic, and the enforcement methods are hooks and permissions.
source: Steering Claude Code: when to use CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, and subagents
detail: Preceding text: 'When there's something that absolutely must not happen, an instruction is the wrong tool. Claude will follow the instruction most of the time, but when under pressure, in a long session or an ambiguous situation, or due to a prompt injection ... the model can fail to follow a prompted rule.' The post lists seven instruction channels, each trading context cost against authority. It also says: 'A 30-line procedure in CLAUDE.md. Procedures belong in skills.' The Claude Code best-practices doc agrees: 'Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.'

claim: Limit agent risk mainly through containment (sandboxes, filesystem boundaries, egress controls, keeping credentials out of reach), not per-action human approval, which decays into rubber-stamping. Model-layer defenses are probabilistic and cannot stand alone.
quote: Our telemetry showed users approved roughly 93% of permission prompts. The more approvals a user sees, the less attention they pay to each, becoming over time much less diligent in their supervision.
source: How we contain Claude across products
detail: On the model layer (system prompts, classifiers): 'Because models are probabilistic, these shape only what the agent tends to do, not what it is theoretically capable of doing.' Claude Code auto mode catches about 83% of overeager behaviors. 'A tight perimeter also means you can relax oversight.' More capable models are 'better at finding unexpected paths to a goal, often by routing around restrictions nobody thought to write down' (e.g. escaping a sandbox, reading git history to find test answers).

claim: Match an instruction's degree of freedom to how fragile the task is. Use exact scripts with no variation for fragile, sequence-critical operations; use heuristics where many approaches are valid; and prefer bundled scripts over model-generated code for deterministic operations.
quote: Match the level of specificity to the task's fragility and variability.
source: Skill authoring best practices (Claude docs)
detail: The page's analogy: a 'narrow bridge with cliffs on both sides' needs exact instructions and low freedom (e.g. 'Run exactly this script ... Do not modify the command'), while an 'open field with no hazards' needs only general direction. Same page: 'Prefer scripts for deterministic operations', 'Solve, don't defer' (scripts should handle errors themselves), no 'voodoo constants', and make clear whether Claude should run a script or read it. Also: keep SKILL.md under 500 lines, keep references one level deep, write descriptions in the third person covering both what the skill does and when to use it, and 'Default assumption: Claude is already very smart.' The Agent Skills engineering post (2025-10-16) adds: 'many applications require the deterministic reliability that only code can provide.'

claim: Build evaluations before writing guidance. Measure the model on representative tasks without the skill, then write only enough instruction to close the observed gaps, and iterate against that baseline.
quote: Create evaluations BEFORE writing extensive documentation. This ensures your Skill solves real problems rather than documenting imagined ones.
source: Skill authoring best practices (Claude docs)
detail: Steps given: identify gaps, create three scenarios, establish a baseline without the skill, write minimal instructions, iterate. Also suggested: pair one Claude that refines the skill with another that uses it on real tasks, and watch for unexpected exploration paths, missed references and content that is never read. Note the page's own heading uses emphatic capitals ('BEFORE'), which differs from the prompting guide's advice to dial back emphasis, though here it is aimed at human authors, not the model.

claim: Give the agent a runnable check that returns pass or fail (tests, build exit code, linter, a diff against a fixture) and decide how hard it gates stopping. Options are an in-prompt loop, a session goal, a Stop hook, or a fresh-context reviewer.
quote: Give Claude something that produces a pass or fail, and the loop closes on its own.
source: Best practices for Claude Code
detail: 'Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available.' Also: 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success.' On adversarial review, same page: 'A reviewer prompted to find gaps will usually report some, even when the work is sound ... Chasing every finding leads to over-engineering'. It advises telling the reviewer to flag only gaps affecting correctness or the stated requirements. Another failure pattern it names: 'If you can't verify it, don't ship it.'

claim: Scope note: the measured result ('nearly eliminated fabricated status reports') is from Anthropic's testing of Claude Fable 5.
quote: On long autonomous runs, instruct Claude Fable 5 to audit progress against actual tool results. In Anthropic's testing, this nearly eliminated fabricated status reports even on tasks designed to elicit them
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5
original_claim: On long runs, have the agent check every progress claim against a tool result from the session, report only what it has evidence for, and state explicitly what is not yet verified.
detail: The sample instruction reads: 'Before reporting progress, audit each claim against a tool result from this session. Only report work you can point to evidence for; if something is not yet verified, say so explicitly. Report outcomes faithfully...' This closely matches OutcomeBound's PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED reporting rule and is one of the few measured results in this sweep.

claim: This is guidance for Claude Opus 5 specifically. Because that model verifies its own work without being asked, remove explicit verification instructions from its prompts, such as 'include a final verification step for any non-trivial task' and 'use a subagent to verify', along with legacy verification scaffolding. Anthropic reports this cuts wasted tokens with no loss in quality. The source does not extend this to 'models that already self-verify' in general, and its examples are those two instructions, not generic 'double-check' wording. The conflict with the Fable 5 guide's advice to use fresh-context verifier subagents is real.
quote: If your prompt contains explicit verification instructions ("include a final verification step for any non-trivial task," "use a subagent to verify"), remove them: instructions like these cause over-verification on Claude Opus 5
source: Prompting Claude Opus 5
original_claim: Remove generic 'verify your work' or 'double-check' instructions for models that already self-verify, because they cause over-verification. This conflicts with other Anthropic guidance recommending fresh-context verifier or reviewer subagents.
detail: The Opus 5 guide also says 'do not use subagents to verify or double-check your own work', and the main best-practices page says to 'remove these instructions rather than rewriting them' on Opus 5. Anthropic sources disagree here. The Claude Code best-practices doc recommends 'have a subagent review the diff in a fresh context'. The Fable 5 guide says 'Separate, fresh-context verifier subagents tend to outperform self-critique'. The harness-design post found generator self-evaluation lenient. A plausible reconciliation for a portable contract: tie verification to the risk of the change and to deterministic checks, not to a blanket 'always verify' instruction.

claim: Separate the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it, and tune the judge to be skeptical against concrete, gradable criteria. Agents confidently praise their own mediocre work.
quote: tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical turns out to be far more tractable than making a generator critical of its own work
source: Harness design for long-running application development
detail: 'When asked to evaluate work they've produced, agents tend to respond by confidently praising the work.' Out of the box, 'Claude is a poor QA agent': it found real issues, 'then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal'. The evaluator was calibrated with few-shot score breakdowns, and each criterion had a hard threshold. The criteria's wording shaped outputs too: phrases like 'museum quality' pushed designs toward one style.

claim: Scope note: this was measured on Claude Fable 5.1.
quote: It responds well to explicit instructions about what to leave out. With the following instruction, unrequested additions and committed test code drop substantially with no measurable change in task success
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5.1
original_claim: Tell the agent explicitly what to leave out of a change: pre-existing bugs, unrequested extensions and extra permanent tests are follow-ups to report, not changes to make. Keep full completion of what was actually requested.
detail: The instruction includes: 'report it as a follow-up in your summary', 'implement the reading its wording and the surrounding code most directly support, state that assumption', commit tests only 'where the task asks for them or this repository already keeps tests for this kind of change', and 'implement every behavior the task asks for, completely.' The same page's 'Delivering work' block says: 'The user's request ... sets the scope, and the scope is the deliverable: don't quietly narrow, widen, or swap it.' This is close to OutcomeBound's 'smallest complete, not least work'.

claim: Define checkpoints briefly by class, not by listing cases: pause only for destructive or irreversible actions, real scope changes, or input only the user can provide. Otherwise proceed on stated assumptions.
quote: Pause for the user only when the work genuinely requires them: a destructive or irreversible action, a real scope change, or input that only they can provide.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5
detail: This mirrors the OutcomeBound kernel line 'Stop only before expanding authority or crossing an ungranted irreversible edge.' Related guidance: the main best-practices page has a reversibility-based safety block ('take local, reversible actions ... for actions that are hard to reverse, affect shared systems, or could be destructive, ask the user'), with the warning 'don't bypass safety checks (e.g. --no-verify)'. The Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 guides add that autonomous agents should not end a turn on a promise, since 'A step you have decided on is something to run, not to announce.' The Opus 5.5 guide says to treat a text-only end of turn as a report, not proof of completion, and to cap automatic continuations at two or three.

claim: Specify larger tasks as self-contained specs up front: name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works.
quote: The most useful specs are self-contained: they name the files and interfaces involved, state what is out of scope, and end with an end-to-end verification step that proves the feature works.
source: Best practices for Claude Code
detail: This maps directly onto the four OutcomeBound inputs: outcome, context (files and interfaces), bounds (out of scope), completion bar (end-to-end verification). The Sonnet 5 guide agrees: 'specify the task, intent, and relevant constraints upfront in the first human turn', whereas 'ambiguous or underspecified prompts conveyed progressively over multiple user turns tend to relatively reduce token efficiency and sometimes performance.' The Opus 5 guide says it 'performs best when given the complete task specification up front and left to run.'

claim: Design check and CLI output for an agent reader. Print a few summary lines, write detail to a log file, put ERROR and the reason on the same line so grep finds it, precompute summary statistics, and offer a fast deterministic subsample mode.
quote: The test harness should not print thousands of useless bytes. At most, it should print a few lines of output and log all important information to a file so Claude can find it when needed.
source: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes
detail: Same section: 'if there are errors, Claude should write ERROR and put the reason on the same line so grep will find it.' It also names 'Time blindness': a default --fast option runs a deterministic 1–10% sample. And: 'it's important that the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem.' 'Writing effective tools for agents' (2025-09-11) agrees: return high-signal fields and 'prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks.' Evidence comes from one large project.

claim: Build eval sets with cases where the behavior should occur and cases where it should not, so you tune against both undertriggering and overtriggering. Grade the outcome, not the path taken.
quote: Test both the cases where a behavior should occur and where it shouldn't. One-sided evals create one-sided optimization.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Same post: it is 'often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took', because checking the exact sequence of steps was 'too rigid'. Also: start with '20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures'; a good task is one where 'two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict'; 0% pass@100 'is most often a signal of a broken task'; prefer deterministic graders; calibrate LLM judges against humans and give them an 'Unknown' option; 'we do not take eval scores at face value until someone digs into the details of the eval and reads some transcripts.' The balanced-set lesson came from search over- and undertriggering in claude.ai, which is the same problem as skill and instruction triggering.

claim: Contested: whether to structure prompts with XML tags and role prompting. The docs still recommend XML for mixed-content prompts, while a claude.com prompting guide and the context-engineering post say formatting and XML matter less as models improve.
quote: Don't rely on outdated techniques: XML tags and heavy role prompting are less necessary with modern models. Start with explicit, clear instructions.
source: Best practices for prompt engineering for 2026
published: 2025-11-10 (page text refers to Claude 5 generation, so apparently updated since)
detail: The docs' prompting best-practices page says 'XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously, especially when your prompt mixes instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs.' The context-engineering post says 'the exact formatting of prompts is likely becoming less important as models become more capable.' The same blog also says 'prompting is converging with context engineering for Claude 5 generation models — less scaffolding, more curation.' Caution: the blog still recommends assistant prefill, but the docs say prefill on the last assistant turn returns a 400 error from Claude 4.6 onward, so parts of it are stale. The docs also note that prompt style carries into output ('removing markdown from your prompt can reduce the volume of markdown in the output').

claim: The cited Fable 5 guide says only that prompts telling the model to echo, transcribe or explain its internal reasoning can trigger the reasoning_extraction refusal on Claude Fable 5; read structured thinking blocks instead. The Opus 5.5 guide says the same for Opus 5.5, and calls the category new for users coming from Opus 5, so it does not apply to 'current models' across the board. The advice to remove 'think carefully' lines is not on the cited page. It comes from the Opus 5.5 guide, is scoped to chat applications on Opus 5.5 ('consider removing them'), and rests on Anthropic's testing in a chat product.
quote: Prompts, skills, or harness instructions that tell the model to echo, transcribe, or explain its internal reasoning as response text can trigger the reasoning_extraction refusal category on Claude Fable 5
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5
original_claim: Do not tell the model to echo, transcribe or explain its internal reasoning in the response. On current models this can trigger a reasoning-extraction refusal. Read structured thinking blocks instead, and remove 'think carefully' lines where effort already controls depth.
detail: The Fable 5 guide says to 'Audit existing skills and system prompts for reflection or show-your-thinking instructions when migrating'. The Opus 5.5 guide repeats this, adding that in chat products, removing 'think carefully before answering' lines 'made replies start sooner, with no clear decline in the quality of the reply'. On Opus 5 with thinking disabled, rules telling the model not to think increase internal-tag leakage. This is a concrete lint rule for auditing adopters' instruction files.

claim: Quote is verbatim in the GPT-5.5 guide (API availability 2026-04-24). It is scoped to GPT-5.5 ('GPT-5.5 is better at working from a clear goal...').
quote: Describe the expected outcome, success criteria, allowed side effects, evidence rules, and output shape. Avoid step-by-step process guidance unless the exact path matters.
source: Using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI API prompt guidance)
original_claim: Prompt for the outcome, not the process: state the expected outcome, success criteria, allowed side effects, evidence rules and output shape, and leave the path to the model unless the exact path matters.
detail: Listed under 'What's new: Stronger task execution with outcome-first prompts'. The same guide's migration checklist says to reduce or remove detailed step-by-step guidance. This maps closely onto OutcomeBound's Outcome, Bounds and Completion-bar inputs.

claim: OpenAI's GPT-5.5 guide says legacy prompts often over-specify the process because earlier models needed more help, and that with GPT-5.5 this CAN add noise, narrow the search space, OR produce overly mechanical answers. It advises a fresh baseline instead of carrying over every old instruction. It does not say this happens with every model or every time.
quote: Legacy prompts often over-specify the process because earlier models needed more help staying on track. With GPT-5.5, that can add noise, narrow the model's search space, or lead to overly mechanical answers.
source: Using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI API prompt guidance)
original_claim: Treat instructions carried over from older models as suspect: process over-specification that older models needed now adds noise, narrows the search space and makes answers mechanical.
detail: An earlier instance appears in the GPT-5 guide (2025-08-07). Cursor's 'Be THOROUGH when gathering information... maximize_context_understanding' block worked on older models but was counterproductive with GPT-5, causing repeated searches. Softening it fixed the problem.

claim: Verbatim. The skeleton is offered 'as a starting point for complex prompts' in the GPT-5.5 guide.
quote: Use this structure as a starting point for complex prompts. Keep each section short. Add detail only where it changes behavior.
source: Using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI API prompt guidance)
original_claim: Keep each prompt section short and add detail only where it changes behavior; a suggested skeleton is Role, Personality, Goal, Success criteria, Constraints, Output, Stop rules.
detail: This works as an audit test: a sentence that changes no behavior is a candidate for removal. It lines up with OutcomeBound's 'anything that changes no decision and reduces no risk' definition of overengineering.

claim: Reserve absolute words (ALWAYS, NEVER, must, only) for true invariants, and express judgment calls such as when to search, ask, use a tool or keep going as decision rules.
quote: Use those words for true invariants, such as safety rules, required output fields, or actions that should never happen. For judgment calls, such as when to search, ask for clarification, use a tool, or keep iterating, prefer decision rules instead.
source: Using GPT-5.5 (OpenAI API prompt guidance)
detail: Appears under the heading 'Avoid unnecessary absolute rules'. The guide also says GPT-5.5 reads prompts 'in a literal and thorough manner', which makes absolutes more binding than their authors may intend. An audit can flag each absolute and check that it guards a true invariant.

claim: Verbatim in the GPT-5.4 guide. Its 'Migrate prompts to GPT-5.4 one change at a time' section supports the one-change-at-a-time clause.
quote: These patterns are observed defaults, not guarantees. Start with the smallest prompt that passes your evals, and add blocks only when they fix a measured failure mode.
source: Using GPT-5.4 (OpenAI API latest-model guide)
original_claim: Start from the smallest prompt that passes your evals and add an instruction block only when it fixes a measured failure mode; change one thing at a time when migrating models.
detail: The GPT-5.2 guide (2025-12-11) prescribes the same eval-first discipline for migration: 'Switch models, don't change prompts yet... Make one change at a time', then re-run evals after each small change. The GPT-5.5 guide adds: start migration from 'a fresh baseline instead of carrying over every instruction from an older prompt stack'.

claim: The GPT-5 guide (2025-08-07) says contradictory or vague prompts can be more damaging to GPT-5 than to other models, because it spends reasoning tokens trying to reconcile them. It also says OpenAI has 'seen multiple early users' find ambiguities and contradictions in their prompt libraries, and that removing them 'drastically streamlined and improved their GPT-5 performance'. That is an anecdotal report, not a measured result, and it is about GPT-5 specifically.
quote: poorly-constructed prompts containing contradictory or vague instructions can be more damaging to GPT-5 than to other models, as it expends reasoning tokens searching for a way to reconcile the contradictions
source: GPT-5 prompting guide (OpenAI Cookbook; canonical https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt-5/gpt-5_prompting_guide)
original_claim: Remove contradictory or vague instructions: a precise instruction-follower spends reasoning trying to reconcile them, and reviewing prompt libraries for contradictions measurably improved results for early users.
detail: The guide's worked example contains hidden conflicts such as 'always look up the patient first' against 'escalate emergencies immediately'. It reports that early users who reviewed their prompt libraries and removed ambiguities and contradictions 'drastically streamlined and improved their GPT-5 performance'. GPT-5.5 adds that conflicting instructions combined with high reasoning effort can cause overthinking.

claim: Audit a prompt with the model itself: give it the prompt and grouped failure traces, have it quote the lines that cause each failure, then ask for surgical edits rather than a rewrite.
quote: Prefer small, explicit edits: clarify conflicting rules, remove redundant or contradictory lines, tighten vague guidance.
source: GPT-5.1 prompting guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
detail: The method has two steps: diagnose (quote or paraphrase the lines causing each failure mode, including contradictions), then patch with minimal edits and patch notes. Failure modes should be grouped, because too many at once makes the diagnosis worse. Afterwards, re-run the queries to check for regressions. The Codex prompting guide (2026-02-25) recommends the same metaprompting approach and warns that suggested fixes can be too specific, so generate several and keep the common elements.

claim: The GPT-6 guide says GPT-6 Astra 'can be more sensitive' to instructions in skills and files such as AGENTS.md, and it strongly recommends auditing skills and other files the model can read. It makes this claim about GPT-6 Astra, not about stronger instruction-followers in general, and it says 'can be', not 'are'.
quote: It can be more sensitive to instructions contained in skills and other files, such as `AGENTS.md`. We strongly recommend auditing skills and other files accessible to your model for instructions that could influence its behavior.
source: Using GPT-6 (OpenAI API latest-model guide, GPT-6 Astra/Sol/Luna)
original_claim: Audit every skill and AGENTS.md file the model can read, because stronger instruction-followers are more sensitive to guidance in those files.
detail: The guide also warns that 'unclear or conflicting guidance in a skill file may cause the model to pause and block work early'. It recommends stating the priority explicitly: user instructions take precedence over a skill's. This is OpenAI's most direct official endorsement of auditing instruction files. The publication date is inferred from the GPT-6 Astra launch; the page itself is undated.

claim: The prompt is GPT-6 Astra guidance. It asks the model to name and link the exact SKILL.md, quote the instruction, and keep explicit skill requirements apart from its own interpretation. The guide says to use it 'to find silent and conflicting guidance' when many skills and instruction files such as AGENTS.md are loaded.
quote: Use this prompt to find silent and conflicting guidance when your application loads many skills and instruction files such as `AGENTS.md`.
source: Using GPT-6 (OpenAI API latest-model guide)
original_claim: When auditing a large instruction set, have the model name and quote the exact skill or instruction file that made it pause, ask for approval, or diverge, keeping explicit requirements apart from its own interpretation.
detail: The diagnostic prompt reads: if a skill causes you to pause, leave work unfinished or diverge, name and link the exact SKILL.md, quote the relevant instruction, briefly explain how it applies, and distinguish explicit skill requirements from your interpretation of guidelines. An instruction-file audit could use this as a runtime probe.

claim: The blog (2026-09-11) says previous models needed encouragement to run tests and check their work, that GPT-6 Astra does this on its own, and so the same instructions CAN lead to unnecessary testing. 'Size verification to the change instead' is not in the source; it is an added recommendation.
quote: Previous models needed encouragement to run tests and check their work. GPT-6 Astra does that on its own, so the same instructions can lead to unnecessary testing.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
original_claim: Remove standing 'run tests / check your work' exhortations written for older models: GPT-6 Astra verifies on its own, so they cause unnecessary testing. Size verification to the change instead.
detail: The GPT-6 guide suggests replacement wording: 'Run tests appropriate to the change and complete required checks. Once those pass, broaden or repeat testing only when new changes, failures, or unresolved concerns justify it', and says not to write tests for reversible, low-impact changes that mirror the implementation. This contrasts with GPT-5.5's recommendation to ask coding agents for concrete validation commands. Which one applies depends on the model generation.

claim: In AGENTS.md, point to docs by condition ('X for schema changes') instead of requiring the model to read a stack of docs or a repo map before every edit.
quote: Prompting the model to read files before every edit is a great way to burn context and slow work down. Pointing to some docs can still be helpful, however, so long as it is contextual.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
detail: Bad example: 'Before every edit, read architecture.md, database.md, and deployment.md.' Good example: 'Use architecture.md for service boundaries, database.md for schema changes, and deployment.md when preparing a deployment.' The post also says to revisit each AGENTS.md instruction often and ask whether it is still needed.

claim: The source is about switching to GPT-6 Astra. The pre-authorization advice ('give it permission for a specific workflow you know is safe') appears in the AGENTS.md section as a remedy for Astra's tentativeness.
quote: consider updating that language: Astra could take it too seriously and may stop work where you'd actually be happy for it to continue.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
original_claim: Recalibrate boundary and ask-first language written to restrain earlier models, since a better-aligned model may take it too literally and stop early. Pre-authorize specific safe workflows explicitly instead.
detail: Example grant from the same post: 'The local tests use disposable fixtures and have no production access. Run them, fix failures caused by the requested change, and rerun affected tests without asking for approval at each step.' The ChatGPT/Codex Prompting doc makes a similar point: 'Focus on the one or two boundaries that matter most. You don't need to control every step.' This bears directly on OutcomeBound's Bounds wording and its 'stop only before expanding authority' rule.

claim: Define completion before starting, and question any standing 'stop for review after the first implementation' rule, because it pulls the model toward an early stop.
quote: A requirement to stop for review after the first implementation will pull the model toward an earlier stopping point, so check whether that's a decision you actually need to make.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
detail: The same section says: 'This is where it helps to define completion before starting.' If the task includes running, inspecting and fixing, the request should say so. If further exploration is wanted, say what to explore and where to stop.

claim: The truncation is Codex-specific: 'Codex starts shortening their descriptions to fit' when too many skills are added.
quote: skill descriptions should be as short as possible while making it clear when the model should use them
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
original_claim: Keep skill descriptions as short as possible while making the trigger condition specific. Over-broad or overlong descriptions over-trigger, contradict each other, and get truncated when many skills are installed.
detail: Bad: '...Use when working with databases, queries, models, or persistence.' Good: '...Use when adding or changing a migration, or reviewing its rollout.' The Codex Build-skills doc (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills.md, undated living doc) says the initial skills list is capped at 2% of the context window (8,000 characters when the size is unknown) and descriptions are shortened first, so 'front-load the key use case and trigger words'.

claim: Don't write skills as step-by-step itineraries: highly specific recipes that once helped now hinder capable models. Also consider which models will read the guidance, since what helps a smaller model can overconstrain a stronger one.
quote: many skills were written as elaborate itineraries or recipes. Models have gotten much better at understanding nuance and ambiguity, so overly specific guidance can now hinder results where it previously helped.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers blog)
detail: The same post: 'Guidance that helps Sol or Luna may overconstrain GPT-6 Astra, so consider which models will use the instructions you leave behind.' It also recommends that multi-workflow skills use a minimal root document that routes to supporting docs and scripts. This is in tension with the Codex Build-skills doc's older advice to 'Write imperative steps with explicit inputs and outputs'. For a portable contract read by several models, the multi-model caveat is the key constraint.

claim: This is a suggested prompt in the GPT-6 Astra guide, not a general rule.
quote: Before asking the user clarifying questions, you should complete the work that is already authorized from context and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result.
source: Using GPT-6 (OpenAI API latest-model guide)
original_claim: Before asking for approval, finish all the work already authorized so that the person approves a concrete, reviewable result. Reversible, read-only, or already-authorized work needs no permission.
detail: The prompt continues: 'You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or strongly implied', and 'Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.' The guide says GPT-6 Astra asks for clarification more often than earlier models and can stop where users expect it to continue.

claim: This is an example default_follow_through_policy in the GPT-5.4 guide. Its item (c) also covers missing sensitive information.
quote: Ask permission only if the next step is: (a) irreversible, (b) has external side effects (for example sending, purchasing, deleting, or writing to production), or (c) requires missing sensitive information or a choice that would materially change the outcome.
source: Using GPT-5.4 (OpenAI API latest-model guide)
original_claim: Give a default follow-through policy: proceed when intent is clear and the step is reversible and low-risk, and ask only for irreversible steps, external side effects, or choices that would materially change the outcome.
detail: The guide pairs this with an explicit instruction-priority block (newer user instructions override earlier ones; non-conflicting earlier instructions persist; safety and permission constraints do not yield). It also adds a lightweight verification step before irreversible actions. The GPT-5 guide (2025-08-07) made the same point with per-tool uncertainty thresholds: a delete-file tool should have a much lower threshold than grep.

claim: Verbatim in the Model Spec version dated August 18, 2026. That page now says a newer version exists and that this one is kept for historical reference.
quote: autonomy must be bounded by a clear, mutually understood scope of autonomy shared between the assistant and the user.
source: OpenAI Model Spec (2026-08-18), 'Act within an agreed-upon scope of autonomy'
original_claim: Bound autonomy with an explicit, mutually understood scope (sub-goals, acceptable side effects, when to pause) that has an ending condition and passes unchanged to every sub-agent.
detail: Root-level rules: 'Every scope must include an ending condition'. Scopes should be semi-structured (allowed_tools, latest_time, max_cost...) so they can be validated and audited. A scope should not be so narrow that trivial confirmations habituate users to approve everything. 'If the assistant delegates work, it must ensure that all sub-agents... operate under the same scope and respect any subsequent changes, including stop-work requests.' A companion section asks the model to prefer reversible actions and to mitigate irreversible ones with backups and dry runs. This lines up with OutcomeBound's goal envelope and its rule that delegates receive the same bounds.

claim: The spec's wording is 'In some cases, users may implicitly delegate authority to tool outputs', and it gives the coding example.
quote: when a user asks a coding assistant to implement a feature, the expected behavior is to act in line with instructions in AGENTS or README files as well as relevant code comments.
source: OpenAI Model Spec (2026-08-18), 'Ignore untrusted data by default'
original_claim: By default, instructions in tool outputs and files have no authority, but a coding user implicitly delegates authority to AGENTS/README files and relevant code comments. Other embedded instructions are triaged by relevance and risk.
detail: Triage rule for tool-output instructions: ignore clearly unrelated ones; follow clearly intended low-risk ones; ask when an instruction might be intended but could cause serious side effects; otherwise make a best guess and call out the assumption. The authority order is Root > System > Developer > User > Guideline > No Authority (tool outputs and quoted text). A later instruction at the same level supersedes an earlier one. In Codex, AGENTS.md files are injected as user-role messages that the model 'has been trained to closely adhere to' (Codex Prompting Guide, 2026-02-25).

claim: Verbatim. The post is dated Feb 11, 2026, by Ryan Lopopolo, and it describes one internal project, so the 'anecdote' label is correct.
quote: Too much guidance becomes non-guidance. When everything is “important,” nothing is. Agents end up pattern-matching locally instead of navigating intentionally.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI)
original_claim: Treat AGENTS.md as a short map (roughly 100 lines) pointing into a versioned, structured docs directory. One monolithic instruction file crowds out the task, turns into non-guidance, rots, and can't be checked mechanically.
detail: From one internal team's five-month build of about 1M lines of code. The four stated failure modes of 'one big AGENTS.md' are: context is scarce, too much guidance becomes non-guidance, it rots instantly, and it's hard to verify. Their fix: 'we treat it as the table of contents', with progressive disclosure, dedicated linters and CI jobs that check the knowledge base is current and cross-linked, and a recurring doc-gardening agent. Also: 'anything it can't access in-context while running effectively doesn't exist.'

claim: Verbatim. The page also has 'When documentation falls short, we promote the rule into code' and 'enforcing invariants, not micromanaging implementations'.
quote: Because the lints are custom, we write the error messages to inject remediation instructions into agent context.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI)
original_claim: Enforce invariants mechanically with custom linters and structural tests whose error messages tell the agent how to fix the problem, and promote a rule from docs into code when documentation falls short. Enforce invariants, not implementations.
detail: The same post: 'By enforcing invariants, not micromanaging implementations, we let agents ship fast without undermining the foundation.' Also: 'enforce boundaries centrally, allow autonomy locally'. On taste: 'When documentation falls short, we promote the rule into code.' Recurring background agents scan for deviations and open small refactor PRs ('garbage collection'). Their failure diagnostic is to ask what capability is missing and how to make it legible and enforceable for the agent, rather than telling it to 'try harder'.

claim: Verbatim, dated Aug 13, 2026. The source frames it as using the programmatic tool calling API feature.
quote: Move deterministic work into code: using programmatic tool calling to filter, aggregate, and orchestrate tool outputs outside the model’s context window, reserving model tokens for judgment and reducing cost, latency, and context rot.
source: The builder's guide to GPT-5.6 (OpenAI Applied AI)
original_claim: Move deterministic work (filtering, aggregating, orchestrating tool outputs) out of the model's context and into code, and reserve model tokens for judgment.
detail: Reported numbers: a customer (Rogo) matched its rubric quality with 21% fewer input tokens using programmatic tool calling. Keeping the harness fixed except for retained reasoning and compaction raised GPT-5.6 Sol on ARC-AGI-3 from 13.3% to 38.3% with about 6x fewer output tokens ('No changes to the model'). Both support the view that harness and deterministic scaffolding matter as much as prompt wording.

claim: The cookbook registry date is 2026-05-09. The source lists these Goal components: outcome, verification surface, constraints, boundaries, iteration policy, and blocked stop condition.
quote: A Goal gives Codex a completion condition: what should be true, how success should be checked, and what constraints must stay intact.
source: Using Goals in Codex: Persistent Objectives for Long-Running Work (OpenAI Cookbook)
original_claim: For long-running work, state the goal as a completion contract: the outcome, a verification surface, constraints that must not regress, boundaries, an iteration policy, and a blocked-stop condition.
detail: The template: '/goal <desired end state> verified by <specific evidence> while preserving <constraints>. Use <allowed inputs, tools, or boundaries>. Between iterations, <...>. If blocked..., <what to report and what would unlock progress>.' A goal should be 'narrow enough to audit but broad enough to let Codex choose the next action'. Its elements map closely onto OutcomeBound's Outcome, Bounds and Completion-bar inputs and its goal envelope.

claim: The confirmed/approximate/blocked/uncertain reporting comes from the notebook's research-Goal examples.
quote: A Goal should not be marked complete because the model believes it is probably done. It should be complete only after the objective is checked against the relevant files, tests, logs, benchmark output, generated artifacts, or other concrete evidence.
source: Using Goals in Codex: Persistent Objectives for Long-Running Work (OpenAI Cookbook)
original_claim: Mark work complete only on concrete evidence, never on the model's belief that it is probably done. Keep reaching a budget limit distinct from completion, and report outcomes at their actual level of support (confirmed, approximate, blocked, uncertain).
detail: Also: 'Reaching a budget limit is not the same as completing the objective.' The model may mark a goal complete only when evidence supports it; pause, resume, clear and budget transitions stay with the user or system. The research example ends in a ledger separating confirmed, approximate, blocked and uncertain claims. This is close to OutcomeBound's PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED rule.

claim: The source (Jul 20, 2026) is about Codex Code Review rules kept in AGENTS.md, not every AGENTS.md rule. It says to START with a consequential, non-obvious invariant (not 'only when'), scope rules to the code they govern, state the invariant and a safe path, describe outcomes rather than function names, and narrow or remove guidance that repeatedly produces noise. The measured result is that rule-guided review recovered 98% of required custom findings against a 58.3% baseline. The writing tips draw on that eval plus internal use, so 'measured' fits only in part.
quote: Start with a consequential, non-obvious invariant. Encode a check reviewers repeatedly explain, such as a compatibility requirement or data boundary. If removing a rule would not change the review, leave it out.
source: Custom Code Review rules for Codex (OpenAI Developers blog)
original_claim: Add a rule to AGENTS.md only when it is consequential and non-obvious, scope it to the code it governs, state the invariant together with a safe path, describe outcomes rather than volatile names, and delete rules that only add noise.
detail: Measured on OpenAI's eval suite of known violations and safe counterexamples: rule-guided variants recovered 98% of the required findings, against 58.3% for the baseline control. 'broad instructions could easily create noise'. 'Keep formatting and other mechanical checks in CI' and 'Tests and linters work well for checks you can express deterministically; repository rules help capture the judgment that is harder to encode.' Suggested acceptance test for each rule: one triggering change, one safe counterexample, one unrelated change.

claim: Dated Jan 22, 2026. It recommends 10–20 prompts, a CSV that grows over time, should_trigger=false negative controls, deterministic checks on JSONL traces, and a rubric pass 'where rules fall short'.
quote: Before writing the skill itself, write down what “success” means in terms you can actually measure.
source: Testing Agent Skills Systematically with Evals (OpenAI Developers blog)
original_claim: Evaluate skills like any prompt: define measurable success first, keep a small growing prompt set (10–20) that includes should-not-trigger negative controls, grade captured traces with deterministic checks, and add model-graded rubrics only where rules fall short.
detail: Checks fall into outcome, process, style and efficiency goals. 'For a single skill, a small set of 10–20 prompts is enough to surface regressions'. The suite covers explicit, implicit and contextual invocation plus negative controls. Use `codex exec --json` traces for deterministic checks and `--output-schema` for structured rubric grading. 'begin with fast checks that explain behavior, then add slower, heavier checks only when they reduce risk.' Every manual fix becomes a new eval row.

claim: Keep AGENTS.md short and accurate, and add a rule only after observing a repeated mistake. Move durable rules out of prompts into AGENTS.md or skills, and point to task-specific docs when the file grows.
quote: Keep it practical. A short, accurate AGENTS.md is more useful than a long file full of vague rules. Start with the basics, then add new rules only after you notice repeated mistakes.
source: Codex Best practices (ChatGPT Learn / Codex docs)
published: 2026-09 (undated living doc; references GPT-6 models; retrieved 2026-09-25)
detail: A good AGENTS.md covers repo layout, how to run the project, build/test/lint commands, conventions, constraints and do-not rules, and 'What done means and how to verify work'. Tip: 'When Codex makes the same mistake twice, ask it for a retrospective and update AGENTS.md.' Codex caps the combined AGENTS.md chain at 32 KiB by default (project_doc_max_bytes) and truncates the rest, per https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/agents-md.md.

claim: The page gives the four parts as 'a good default' to include in a prompt.
quote: Done when: What should be true before the task is complete, such as tests passing, behavior changing, or a bug no longer reproducing?
source: Codex Best practices (ChatGPT Learn / Codex docs)
original_claim: Frame each task with four parts: Goal, Context, Constraints, and Done when (what must be true before completion, and how to verify it).
detail: The four parts are Goal, Context, Constraints and Done when, which 'helps Codex stay scoped, make fewer assumptions, and produce work that's easier to review.' The ChatGPT/Codex Prompting doc (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/prompting.md) uses Goal/Context/Output/Boundaries and adds 'Use only the parts that help.' This is independent lab support for OutcomeBound's Outcome/Context/Bounds/Completion-bar framing.

claim: The general Prompt-engineering guide still says GPT models like gpt-6-astra 'benefit from precise instructions that explicitly provide the logic and data', and its agentic example includes a 'plan extensively' / 'keep going' block. The same section defers to the latest-model guide. The GPT-5.5 guide does advise against step-by-step process guidance. But the model-specific guides do NOT say to cut persistence scaffolding. The GPT-6 guide recommends a 'persist until the user's intended goal is complete' prompt, the Astra blog says Astra may need a push to keep going, and GPT-5.4 recommends an autonomy_and_persistence block. The tension is about process specificity only.
quote: GPT models like `gpt-6-astra` benefit from precise instructions that explicitly provide the logic and data required to complete the task in the prompt.
source: Prompt engineering (OpenAI API docs, evergreen guide)
published: undated living doc (model name updated to gpt-6-astra; retrieved 2026-09-25)
original_claim: CONTESTED within OpenAI's docs: the general Prompt-engineering guide still says the latest GPT models need precise, logic-explicit instructions and 'plan extensively' persistence blocks, while the model-specific guides say to cut process guidance and persistence scaffolding.
detail: The same evergreen page carries GPT-4.1-era agent boilerplate ('You must plan extensively... reflect extensively') and 'require thorough testing', now labelled for gpt-6-astra. That contradicts the GPT-5.5 guide (avoid step-by-step process) and the GPT-6 guide and blog (unneeded testing prompts; over-specific guidance hinders). The model-specific guides are newer and dated, so they should take precedence. When citing OpenAI, cite the model-specific guide, not the evergreen page. The older Reasoning best practices page (2025, o-series) also says reasoning models 'perform best with straightforward prompts' and that 'think step by step' 'can sometimes hinder' them.

claim: Verbatim; the cookbook registry date is 2026-02-25. The source says such prompting 'can cause' early stopping, not that it did. The same guide says that from gpt-5.3-codex, updates are promptable (with phase handling), so the guide is internally inconsistent rather than contradicting the GPT-5 guide.
quote: You should also remove all prompting for the model to communicate an upfront plan, preambles, or other status updates during the rollout, as this can cause the model to stop abruptly before the rollout is complete.
source: Codex Prompting Guide (OpenAI Cookbook)
original_claim: CONTESTED: OpenAI recommends prompted tool preambles and progress updates for GPT-5-family agents, but told Codex-model harnesses to remove all prompting for upfront plans and status updates because it caused early stopping (from gpt-5.3-codex, updates are promptable again with the `phase` field).
detail: By contrast, the GPT-5 guide (2025-08-07) says preambles 'can drastically improve the user's ability to follow along', and the GPT-5.5 guide recommends a 1–2 sentence preamble before tool calls. The Codex guide itself says that for gpt-5.3-codex and later, updates can be prompted if the harness preserves assistant `phase` ('commentary' vs 'final_answer'); dropping it causes 'significant performance degradation'. The takeaway: instructions that make the agent report mid-run interact with the harness and model version, and can end runs early.

claim: For current reasoning models (Gemini 3.x), write short, direct instructions and drop the verbose prompt-engineering techniques and forced chain-of-thought that older models needed.
quote: Be concise. Gemini 3.x responds best to direct, clear instructions. Verbose or complex prompt engineering techniques designed for older models may cause the model to over-analyze.
source: What's new in Gemini 3.5 Flash (Gemini API docs)
by: Google DeepMind / Google AI for Developers
detail: The same page's migration checklist says: "Simplify prompts. If you used chain-of-thought prompt engineering to force reasoning, try thinking_level: "medium" or "high" with simpler prompts instead." The general prompt-design page (updated 2026-09-17) adds that it is "generally not necessary to have the model outline, plan, or detail reasoning steps in the returned response itself." Other practices this guide lists as no longer recommended for Gemini 3.x: tuning temperature/top_p/top_k (remove them; use a system instruction with explicit rules for determinism) and the numeric thinking_budget (replaced by thinking_level). Google contradicts itself here: the same prompt-design page ships a template ending "Remember to think step-by-step before answering." It also ships a long agentic system instruction full of MUST, which it says "has been evaluated by researchers to improve performance on agentic benchmarks where the model must adhere to a complex rulebook and interact with a user."

claim: In an agent's instructions, say when it may proceed on assumptions and when it must stop to ask for clarification or permission, and have it treat low-risk reads differently from high-risk writes.
quote: Ambiguity and permission handling: Defines when the model is permitted to make assumptions versus when it must pause execution to ask the user for clarification or permission.
source: Prompt design strategies — Agentic workflows (Gemini API docs)
by: Google DeepMind / Google AI for Developers
detail: Google lists the behaviours you can steer in an agent: logical decomposition, problem diagnosis, information exhaustiveness, adaptability, persistence and recovery, risk assessment ("Explicitly distinguishes between low-risk exploratory actions (reads) and high-risk state changes (writes)"), ambiguity/permission handling, verbosity, and precision. Google's evaluated agentic template says a missing optional parameter is LOW risk for exploratory tasks and to "Prefer calling the tool with the available information over asking the user, unless" a later step needs that information. It also says to retry transient errors only up to an explicit retry limit and otherwise change strategy, and warns that an action once taken cannot be taken back. Philipp Schmid's Gemini 3 template (philschmid.de/gemini-3-prompt-practices, 2025-11-19) says the same in one line: "Ask clarifying questions ONLY if critical info is missing; otherwise, make reasonable assumptions and state them."

claim: Start with general instructions that describe the desired outcome, watch how the model reasons, and add explicit step-by-step guidance only where the first attempt goes wrong.
quote: Begin with general instructions that describe the preferred outcome. Start with a low-complexity prompt and observe the model's initial thoughts on how to respond.
source: Thinking prompting guide (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI)
published: 2026-09-24 (page last updated; its examples use gemini-2.5-pro, so the content dates from 2025)
detail: The guide suggests explicit step-by-step instructions only 'If the initial attempt does not yield the expected result'. It also recommends adding verification steps ("ask Gemini to verify its sources, review its reasoning, identify potential errors, and check its final answer") and reading the model's thoughts to find which instruction it misunderstood. This matches Schmid's 'Describe what you want, not the path' and Agent Skills' 'Match specificity to fragility'.

claim: In GEMINI.md, state specific negative constraints ('do not X') instead of vague positive instructions, keep the file focused, and regularly remove outdated rules.
quote: Use negative constraints: Explicitly telling the agent what not to do (for example, "Do not use class components") is often more effective than vague positive instructions.
source: Gemini CLI — Manage context and memory (tutorial)
detail: The same best-practices list says: "Keep it focused: Avoid adding excessive content to GEMINI.md. Keep instructions actionable and relevant to code generation." and "Review often: Periodically check your GEMINI.md files to remove outdated rules." `/memory show` prints the exact concatenated context the model receives, which helps with auditing. Why contested: the page compares specific negatives against *vague* positives and cites no evidence. Agent Skills' evaluation guide says reasoning-based instructions beat rigid 'ALWAYS do X, NEVER do Y' directives. Antigravity and Schmid use short negative invariants ('Never push directly to main') but pair them with reasons elsewhere. Mechanics: Gemini CLI concatenates a global file, workspace files, and 'just-in-time' GEMINI.md files found when a tool touches a directory, and `context.fileName` can be set to AGENTS.md.

claim: Keep always-on constraints and invariants in rule files (AGENTS.md/GEMINI.md), and package multi-step procedures as on-demand skills.
quote: Write a rule for constraints and invariants (for example, “Always use zod for validation” or “Never import internal/ across packages”). Write a skill for multi-step workflows (for example, “How to run database migrations”).
source: Rules | Google Antigravity Docs
detail: Rules have activation modes: always_on (full text on every turn; AGENTS.md/GEMINI.md are always_on for their directory scope), model_decision (only the path and description are injected up front; this is progressive disclosure for rules), glob, and manual (@-mention only; the docs suggest this for 'release checklists or audit rubrics'). Vercel's evals point the same way: broad knowledge works best loaded passively, while vertical workflows suit skills.

claim: Give the agent a local verification mechanism (tests, build, formatters) and have it run and iterate on it, and split complex changes into explore, plan, then execute.
quote: The single most effective way to ensure reliable, correct modifications from an autonomous agent is to provide the agent with a local verification mechanism (such as unit tests, build commands, or formatting scripts).
source: Best practices for Antigravity CLI
detail: The page also recommends 'Explore, plan, then execute' with an implementation-plan artifact approved before edits. Safety comes from harness permission tiers (request-review, proceed-in-sandbox, strict), not from prompt text. The agents.md FAQ agrees: listed checks get run and failures fixed. Schmid's 'Inner Loop vs Outer Loop' (2026-02-20) says the choice to verify comes "Today, mostly from the system prompt ("always run tests after code changes"). Increasingly, from post-training". That suggests prompts will need to push verification less as models internalise it.

claim: The page describes one harness only, Antigravity. It truncates any single rule file over 24,000 bytes, and all always-on and global rules share a 20,000-token budget. Past that budget, Antigravity turns the largest rule files into on-demand pointers. So in Antigravity, keeping always-loaded rule files small avoids truncation and demotion. The page does not say that harnesses in general do this, and it does not compare how different tools load or prioritise instruction files. It covers only Antigravity's own scope precedence.
quote: If the total exceeds 20,000 tokens, Antigravity automatically demotes the largest rule files from inline text to lightweight pointers (- <path>: <description>), allowing the agent to read them on demand.
source: Rules | Google Antigravity Docs
original_claim: Keep always-loaded rule files small, because harnesses budget, truncate or demote them, and each tool loads and prioritises instruction files differently.
detail: Antigravity truncates any single rule file over 24,000 bytes, and silently discards .agents/rules/*.md files that lack a valid trigger in their frontmatter. How other tools differ: xAI Grok loads rule files "in full, with no size cap" and reads AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .grok/rules. Meta Muse Code loads only the first file present at each directory level (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .agents/AGENTS.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md); project rules beat user rules, the deeper file wins, and project rules load only after the workspace is trusted. agents.md: "The closest AGENTS.md to the edited file wins; explicit user chat prompts override everything." Gemini CLI concatenates everything it finds. Audit implication (analyst note): the same file can be fully applied, truncated or ignored depending on the harness, so an audit should check size and each harness's load path.

claim: Package repeatable procedures as Agent Skills (SKILL.md directories that load progressively and bundle scripts), not as monolithic workflow prompts loaded in full.
quote: In May 2026, Antigravity adopted the open industry standard for Agent Skills.
source: Workflows to Skills Migration | Google Antigravity Docs
published: undated (describes the May 2026 adoption; workflows retire 2026-11-01)
detail: Rationale given: "Skills load only essential metadata (name and description) into the agent’s context upfront. Full instructions and reference materials are loaded on demand, preventing prompt bloat." Legacy workflows had a 12,000-character limit and loaded the entire file. The standard is spreading across labs: Mistral Vibe "follows the Agent Skills specification" and reads ./.agents/skills/; Meta Muse Code reads <repo>/.agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md and also scans .codex/skills and .claude/skills; Antigravity CLI moved workspace skills from .gemini/skills to .agents/skills. xAI Grok reads SKILL.md but from .grok/skills, and says allowed-tools 'Does not grant or restrict tools'. So support for optional fields varies.

claim: Use a skill that points agents to the docs as the source of truth to close model knowledge gaps (such as SDK changes), measure it against a no-skill baseline, expect the gain mainly on strong reasoning models, and plan how skills get updated.
quote: The latest Gemini 3 series of models achieve excellent results with the addition of the gemini-api-dev skill, notably coming from a low baseline without it (6.8% for both 3.0 Pro and Flash, 28% for 3.1 Pro).
source: Closing the knowledge gap with agent skills (Google Developers Blog)
detail: The eval harness had 117 prompts, each run 'vanilla' and with the skill (Gemini CLI system instruction plus activate_skill and fetch_url tools); a prompt failed if the code used an old SDK. Headline: "Skills work, but they need reasoning"; the 2.5 models gained 'nowhere near as much'. The authors add two caveats: "we know from Vercel's work that direct instruction through AGENTS.md can be more effective than using skills", and "right now there isn't a great skill update story, other than requiring users to update manually. In the long term this could leave old skill information in user's workspaces, doing more harm than good." Stale installed guidance is a lifecycle problem, which deterministic update and drift tooling addresses.

claim: Give every model call and sub-agent only the minimum context it needs by default, and let it pull more through tools; keep large data behind handles and stable instructions in a cache-friendly prefix.
quote: Scope by default: Every model call and sub-agent sees the minimum context required. Agents must reach for more information explicitly via tools, rather than being flooded by default.
source: Architecting efficient context-aware multi-agent framework for production (Google ADK)
detail: The post's main idea is that context should be a 'compiled view' produced by explicit processors that can be observed and tested, not ad-hoc string concatenation. It warns that irrelevant logs and stale tool outputs "can distract the model, causing it to fixate on past patterns rather than the immediate instruction." Its recommendations: keep large artifacts behind handles and load them only for one call; make memory searchable rather than pinned; scope sub-agent handoffs (include_contents 'none'); rewrite prior agents' messages as narrative so the new agent does not claim their actions; keep stable instructions at the front ('static instruction') and dynamic content at the end. The last point supports a small, stable always-loaded kernel and minimal, explicit delegation briefs.

claim: Treat agent-facing files (AGENTS.md, SKILL.md, agent settings, hooks) as a security surface: limit which ones a repo may contain, require automated review before merge, and give agents least-privilege access.
