quote: Organizations can formalize this approach by implementing repository-level security policies that strictly define permitted agent-facing files and ideally mandate that they undergo automated peer reviews before being merged.
source: Beyond source code: The files AI coding agents trust — and attackers exploit (Google Cloud Blog)
detail: The post groups the attack surface into four kinds: what executes, what instructs, what connects, and what extends. It reports a steady rise since early 2026 in Skill.md files with risky or malicious instructions. Examples include a skill telling the model to exfiltrate API keys and not to mention it to the user, and settings.json files that override ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to route an agent through a proxy. Other sources agree: the Agent Skills client guide says to gate project-level skills on a trust check; Mistral Vibe and Meta Muse Code load project AGENTS.md and skills only after the workspace is trusted. Muse Code warns that committed memory loads even in untrusted workspaces: "Treat a repo's MEMORY.md as a prompt-injection surface, and review it on checkouts you don't control." Implication: an audit of adopters' instruction files should cover intent and safety, not only quality.

claim: Keep AGENTS.md short and limited to what the agent cannot discover (stack, purpose, build/test/verify commands, non-obvious tooling). Leave out directory overviews, task-specific rules and style rules, and enforce style with linters and formatters instead.
quote: Code style guidelines. Use linters and formatters instead—they're faster, cheaper, and deterministic. LLMs are in-context learners and will follow existing patterns in your code.
source: Writing a Good AGENTS.md
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
detail: Schmid bases this on the ETH Zurich study and on HumanLayer's practice. Figures as he reports them: human-written files give only about +4% success at up to +19% cost; overviews do not speed up navigation; unnecessary requirements raise reasoning tokens by 14–22%; "Tools mentioned in AGENTS.md get used 160x more often than unmentioned ones." His guidance: "Keep it short. General consensus is <300 lines; HumanLayer keeps theirs under 60 lines." Use progressive disclosure (list agent_docs/*.md with descriptions), "Prefer pointers over copies", and leave out non-universal instructions because they 'dilute focus'. One claim is unsourced: "Frontier models can reliably follow ~150–200 instructions; the agent harness already uses ~50 of those." The agents.md site disagrees on content: its sample includes a 'Code style' section.

claim: Write AGENTS.md deliberately by hand, rather than generating it with /init or letting the agent write it.
quote: Auto-generated content. Don't use /init or let the agent write its own AGENTS.md. The data shows this hurts more than it helps.
source: Writing a Good AGENTS.md
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
detail: The supporting evidence is ETH Zurich's finding that LLM-generated context files cost about −3% success and +20% inference cost. Schmid also reports that with all other documentation removed, generated files improved results by 2.7%, meaning they hurt when they duplicate what the agent can already discover. Sources that disagree: the agents.md site ("Most coding agents can even scaffold one for you if you ask nicely") and Meta Muse Code, whose `muse init` seeds an AGENTS.md. Gemini CLI's experimental Auto Memory drafts memory and skill patches from transcripts but never applies them without human approval, which is a middle ground.

claim: Tell the agent what to achieve and which constraints hold, not the step-by-step path; when exact steps matter, put them in a script.
quote: When you dictate every step, you take away their ability to adapt, recover from errors, or find better approaches. Describe what you want, not the path to get there.
source: 8 Tips for Writing Agent Skills
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
detail: He contrasts 'Provide constraints, not procedures' ('Always run tests before opening a PR. Never push directly to main.') with 'If exact steps matter, write a script'; a fragile sequence is 'not a skill problem, it's a scripting problem'. He also claims, as an anecdote, "I have seen 50% improvements just by improving the description." This agrees with Agent Skills' 'Match specificity to fragility', Gemini CLI's 'degrees of freedom' (low freedom, meaning scripts, when a specific sequence MUST be followed), and the Google Cloud thinking guide's outcome-first advice. Agent Skills' 'Favor procedures over declarations' is about reusable methods versus one-off answers, not step-by-step micromanagement.

claim: The practice matches the post, but it is one practitioner's guidance, not a measured result. The post says to grade outcomes rather than paths and to use deterministic checks first, with an LLM judge used selectively for qualitative criteria. It also says to run 3 to 5 isolated trials per prompt and to include negative cases. The only measured result is one skill going from 66.7% to 100% over about 20 tests. That gain came from rewriting the description and using explicit directives, and it did not test outcome-versus-path grading. Evidence should be practitioner guidance, not measured.
quote: Grade outcomes, not paths. Agents find creative solutions, and you don't want to penalize an unexpected route to the right answer.
source: Practical Guide to Evaluating and Testing Agent Skills
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
original_claim: Evaluate instructions by grading observable outcomes, not the path taken: use deterministic checks first, an LLM judge only for qualitative criteria, several isolated trials per prompt, and negative cases.
detail: Measured on one skill: the Gemini Interactions API skill went from 66.7% to 100% over about 20 cases, and "The description change alone fixed 5 of 7 failures." The three things he grades are outcome, style/instruction-following, and efficiency (tokens, retries), which he calls 'the most undervalued dimension'. Other advice: 10–20 prompts, 3–5 trials each, isolated runs, testing across harnesses, and 'graduating' capability evals into regression evals. He also says "Use directives, not information. Models follow instructions better than they infer implications." That sits in tension with Agent Skills' advice to explain the why rather than use rigid ALWAYS/NEVER directives.

claim: The source covers skills, not instructions in general. As models improve, run your evals with the skill unloaded, and retire the skill if they still pass. The post says this applies especially to capability skills. It calls preference skills, which encode your own workflow, durable, needing only to stay in sync with your process. This is one practitioner's advice.
quote: Run evals without the skill. If they pass, the model has absorbed the skill's value and the skill is no longer necessary. Retire it.
source: 8 Tips for Writing Agent Skills
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
original_claim: Re-run evals with the skill (or instruction) removed after model upgrades, and retire it once the model passes without it.
detail: He separates 'capability skills', which 'may become unnecessary as models improve, evals will tell you when', from 'preference skills', which encode your own workflow and are durable but must stay in sync with it. This agrees with the Agent Skills eval guide's with/without baseline, with Latent Space's AIEWF 2026 report ('re-visit and re-implement your skills' at each model release), and with Schmid's 'Build to Delete'.

claim: Keep the harness and control flow minimal: provide robust atomic tools, let the model plan, add guardrails, retries and verification, and build so that logic can be removed when models improve.
quote: Start Simple: Do not build massive control flows. Provide robust atomic tools. Let the model make the plan. Implement guardrails, retries and verifications.
source: The importance of Agent Harness in 2026
by: Google DeepMind DevRel (Philipp Schmid, personal blog)
detail: The same post says: "If you over-engineer the control flow, the next model update will break your system" and "Capabilities that required complex, hand-coded pipelines in 2024 are now handled by a single context-window prompt in 2026." His 'Context Engineering for AI Agents: Part 2' (2025-12-04, drawing on Manus) adds: "If your harness is getting more complex while models improve, you are likely over-engineering" and context engineering "is about finding the minimal effective context required for the next step." It also prefers computationally verifiable, binary success metrics over LLM-as-judge.

claim: The agents.md FAQ says that if you list testing commands, the agent will attempt to run the relevant checks and fix failures before finishing. That is the format site's own claim, with no measurement behind it. It does not guarantee that every agent reading AGENTS.md runs the checks. The site recommends listing build and test commands, but the behaviour is an attempt, not an assured outcome.
quote: Yes—if you list them. The agent will attempt to execute relevant programmatic checks and fix failures before finishing the task.
source: AGENTS.md (open format site, FAQ)
by: AGENTS.md (OpenAI Codex, Amp, Google Jules, Cursor, Factory; Agentic AI Foundation)
published: undated site; repository last updated 2026-09-10; stewarded by the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation)
original_claim: List the project's build, test and lint commands in AGENTS.md; agents that follow the format run the relevant checks and fix failures before finishing.
detail: The format has no required fields: "AGENTS.md is just standard Markdown. Use any headings you like". Suggested sections: project overview, build and test commands, code style, testing, security. Monorepos use nested files, where the closest file wins and chat prompts override. The site says "Treat AGENTS.md as living documentation." Google Jules reads a root AGENTS.md ("Keep AGENTS.md up to date") and uses agents.md or README hints to set up its VM. The site's sample includes "Add or update tests for the code you change, even if nobody asked."

claim: Include only what the agent would get wrong without being told, and cut the rest; exhaustive coverage hurts because agents follow instructions that don't apply.
quote: Ask yourself about each piece of content: "Would the agent get this wrong without this instruction?" If the answer is no, cut it.
source: Best practices for skill creators (Agent Skills open standard)
by: Agent Skills (originated at Anthropic; open standard)
detail: The page also says: "Overly comprehensive skills can hurt more than they help — the agent struggles to extract what's relevant and may pursue unproductive paths triggered by instructions that don't apply to the current task." Give defaults, not menus. Read execution traces: wasted steps come from vague instructions, instructions that don't apply but are followed anyway, or too many options with no default. The same criterion appears in Meta Muse Code ("Facts the agent could get wrong from general knowledge alone are the ones worth recording") and in the ETH finding that unnecessary requirements make tasks harder. It works as a per-line audit test.

claim: Prioritise a 'gotchas' list of environment-specific facts that defy reasonable assumptions, keep it where the agent reads it before hitting the situation, and add every correction you have to make.
quote: The highest-value content in many skills is a list of gotchas — environment-specific facts that defy reasonable assumptions.
source: Best practices for skill creators (Agent Skills open standard)
detail: Gotchas belong in SKILL.md rather than a reference file, because the agent may not recognise when to load it. If a reference file is used, say exactly when to read it ('Read references/api-errors.md if the API returns a non-200 status code', not 'see references/'). Other patterns on the page: output templates are more reliable than prose descriptions; checklists for multi-step work; validation loops; and plan-validate-execute with a validator script checked against the source of truth.

claim: Run each eval case both with and without the instruction or skill (or against its previous version), record token and time cost, and pass an assertion only on concrete evidence.
quote: The core pattern is to run each test case twice: once with the skill and once without it (or with a previous version).
source: Evaluating skill output quality (Agent Skills open standard)
detail: Grading principle: "Require concrete evidence for a PASS. Don't give the benefit of the doubt." Use scripts for mechanical checks and an LLM for the rest. Drop assertions that pass in both configurations, investigate those that fail in both, and give each run a clean context. Weigh the cost delta: "A skill that adds 13 seconds but improves pass rate by 50 percentage points is probably worth it." Blind A/B comparison and human review complement assertions. This matches a PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED reporting discipline.

claim: Explain why an instruction matters rather than issuing rigid ALWAYS/NEVER directives; keep instructions few, and if adding rules stops helping, try removing some.
quote: Explain the why. Reasoning-based instructions ("Do X because Y tends to cause Z") work better than rigid directives ("ALWAYS do X, NEVER do Y"). Models follow instructions more reliably when they understand the purpose.
source: Evaluating skill output quality — Iterating on the skill (Agent Skills open standard)
detail: The same section: "Keep the skill lean. Fewer, better instructions often outperform exhaustive rules... If pass rates plateau despite adding more rules, the skill may be over-constrained — try removing instructions and see if results hold or improve." It also advises generalising from feedback rather than patching individual cases. Why contested: Gemini CLI favours explicit negative constraints, Schmid says 'Use directives, not information', and Google's evaluated agentic template relies on MUST and upper-case emphasis. Vercel measured the risk of forceful wording: "You MUST invoke the skill" made the agent anchor on the docs and miss project context, while 'Explore project first, then invoke skill' did better.

claim: Design scripts that agents run to be non-interactive and self-documenting (--help), with actionable errors, structured stdout kept separate from stderr diagnostics, idempotent behaviour, dry-run, meaningful exit codes and bounded output.
quote: When an agent gets an error, the message directly shapes its next attempt. An opaque "Error: invalid input" wastes a turn.
source: Using scripts in skills (Agent Skills open standard)
detail: Avoiding interactive prompts is "a hard requirement of the agent execution environment". Other points: "Reject ambiguous input with a clear error rather than guessing"; harnesses truncate output at roughly 10–30K characters, so default to a summary, support --offset, or require --output; pin versions for one-off commands; turn complex commands into tested scripts. Gemini CLI's skills guide agrees: "Ensure scripts output LLM-friendly stdout. Suppress verbose tracebacks and provide clear, concise success/failure messages." Gemini 3.5 docs: instructions attached to tool results should be appended to the function-response text, because separate parts "can lead to unexpected model behavior (e.g. thought leakage)".

claim: The guide firmly recommends that clients exempt activated skill content from context compaction or pruning. It frames the other two points only as options: consider tracking which skills are activated so a skill already in context is not re-injected, and consider loading project-level skills only after the user has trusted the workspace.
quote: Skill instructions are durable behavioral guidance — losing them mid-conversation silently degrades the agent's performance without any visible error.
source: Adding skills support (Agent Skills client implementation guide)
original_claim: Harnesses should protect activated skill instructions from context compaction, avoid re-injecting a skill that is already loaded, and load project-level skills only after a workspace trust check.
detail: Wrap skill content in structured tags so compaction can recognise and keep it. On trust: "Consider gating project-level skill loading on a trust check — only load them if the user has marked the project folder as trusted." Mistral Vibe (AGENTS.md and .agents/ count as 'trustable content'; "treat its .vibe/ configuration the same way you would treat any other code") and Meta Muse Code do this. Whether guidance survives a long session depends on the harness, not only on the prompt.

claim: Keep project rule files short and specific, because short instructions are followed more reliably than long ones.
quote: Files are loaded in full, with no size cap; short, specific instructions are followed more reliably than long ones.
source: AGENTS.md — Grok Build features (xAI docs)
detail: Grok loads global ~/.grok rules plus every directory from the repo root down; deeper files win. It reads AGENTS.md, AGENT.md, CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, .grok/rules/*.md and, for compatibility, .claude/rules and .cursor/rules, and skips gitignored files. `grok inspect` lists each file with its token count. Change within xAI's own guidance: the 2025 'Prompt Engineering for Grok Code Fast 1' page (now 404; read via the Wayback snapshot of 2025-11-18) told API builders "Be thorough and give many details in your system prompt" and said the model is "accustomed to seeing a lot of context in the initial user prompt". That guide also recommended native tool calling over XML tool-call outputs and not rewriting prompt history, to keep cache hits.

claim: Check long system prompts for contradictions and resolve overlapping conditions with an explicit ordered decision tree; write for a reader with no prior context, replace vague words with objective measures, and pass in computed values (such as counts) instead of asking the model to compute them.
quote: As your system prompt gets long, slight contradictions may appear.
source: Prompting (Mistral AI docs)
detail: Rule of thumb: "imagine you're writing for someone with no prior context—they should be able to understand and execute the task solely by reading the prompt." "Avoid blurry quantitative adjectives" ('too long', 'many') and words like 'better'; use objective measures instead. 'Do Not Make LLMs Count Words': "Instead, provide character counts as input". This is a clear case for deterministic support: compute facts in code and give them to the model. The guide also warns that "different models from different labs, and even a simple update, can change the model behaviour", so prompts should be re-evaluated. Google's Gemini 3 guidance similarly says 'Define parameters: Explicitly explain any ambiguous terms or parameters.' Schmid's Context Engineering Part 2 calls system instructions that 'clash in itself' a cause of 'Context Confusion'.

claim: In committed memory or instructions, record only durable, project-specific facts the agent could get wrong from general knowledge; load an index and read topic files on demand; treat repo-committed memory as a prompt-injection surface.
quote: Facts the agent could get wrong from general knowledge alone are the ones worth recording.
source: Configuration and context — Muse Code (Meta Model API docs)
detail: Muse Code injects only an index of memory (MEMORY.md plus up to 48 file paths, not their contents) and reads files on demand. Project AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md load only after the workspace is trusted, but committed memory loads even in untrusted workspaces, hence "Treat a repo's MEMORY.md as a prompt-injection surface, and review it on checkouts you don't control." The harness has guardrail defaults built in: it will not commit, amend or push unless asked in the session, and "The end of a task is not a request to commit." `muse init` seeds an AGENTS.md, which conflicts with Schmid's advice against generated files. Meta publishes no dedicated prompting guide for Muse Spark agents; the Llama prompt-engineering guide is generic and older.

claim: Treat repository context files as a cost that must earn its place: specify non-standard practices the agent must follow, leave out repository overviews, and evaluate any content added to improve performance before deploying it.
quote: we find that providing context files does not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (ETH Zurich)
by: ETH Zurich SRI Lab (Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev)
detail: The abstract says the result holds across LLMs, agents, and both LLM-generated and developer-committed files. Instructions "are well followed", but "repository overviews, although popular and recommended by model providers, are not helpful". Its conclusion: context files "are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices". Counter-evidence: Lulla et al. (arXiv 2601.20404, 2026-01-28; 10 repositories, 124 PRs) found AGENTS.md associated with lower median runtime (−28.64%) and fewer output tokens (−16.58%) at comparable task completion. The two studies disagree on the direction of cost, using different setups (SWE-bench with generated files versus real PRs). Vercel's +47 pp shows large gains when the file carries knowledge not in the training data. Analyst synthesis: the files help when they carry non-discoverable, non-standard information and hurt when they are redundant.

claim: For knowledge the agent needs on most tasks (such as version-specific framework APIs), put a compact index in the always-loaded AGENTS.md that points to retrievable docs rather than relying on the agent to invoke a skill; keep skills for vertical, user-triggered workflows.
quote: A compressed 8KB docs index embedded directly in AGENTS.md achieved a 100% pass rate, while skills maxed out at 79% even with explicit instructions telling the agent to use them.
source: AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals (Vercel)
detail: "In 56% of eval cases, the skill was never invoked." A default skill scored the same as the no-docs baseline (53%); explicit trigger instructions raised it to 79%; the AGENTS.md index reached 100% on build, lint and test. The index was compressed from 40KB to 8KB with no loss, and included "Prefer retrieval-led reasoning over pre-training-led reasoning". Their explanation: no decision point, the content is always available, and there are no ordering issues. Instruction wording was fragile: MUST-invoke versus explore-first changed the outcomes. Caveat: "The gap may close as models get better at tool use." This conflicts with the design premise of Agent Skills and with Google's gains from its skill; the Google authors themselves cite this result. Agent Skills' descriptions guide adds that agents 'typically only consult skills for tasks that require knowledge or capabilities beyond what they can handle alone'.

claim: Latent Space's AIEWF 2026 recap (Richard MacManus, 2026-07-14) quotes one attendee, Tyler Brown, from X. His takeaway was to revisit and re-implement your skills with each new model release, to get the benefit of the new model. Separately, the recap reports Matt Pocock's advice to write fewer and smaller skills. Neither source mentions harness guidance beyond skills. Both are individual opinions, not a measured or consensus practice.
quote: Each time there’s a new model release, it’s as if you have a kid that grows from middle school to high school. You have to change the curriculum for them to get the benefits of the new model.
source: 5 Trends That Defined AI Engineering at World’s Fair 2026 (Latent Space)
by: Latent Space (Richard MacManus, quoting attendee Tyler Brown)
original_claim: Revisit and rewrite skills and harness guidance at each new model release, and prefer fewer, smaller skills.
detail: Trend 5 of the report is 'Every agent platform is building around skills'. It reports that Matt Pocock advises "writing fewer and smaller skills, and putting more thought into structure" and warns of 'skills hell'. Philipp Schmid (Google DeepMind) said on the main stage: "Agents are just files. We write markdown files to extend capabilities." On 'loop engineering', Addy Osmani said "agents can run much more of the inner execution loop, but that outer loop is still engineering"; Dex Horthy noted that Kubernetes control loops work "but they’re deterministic loops"; Tyler Brown: "autonomy without structure creates as much slop as leverage."

claim: Quote is swyx's intro summarising OpenAI's harness-engineering experiment, not Ryan Lopopolo speaking. Date 2026-04-07 confirmed.
quote: when the agent failed, instead of prompting it better or to “try harder,” the team would look at “what capability, context, or structure is missing?”
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires: 1M LOC, 1B toks/day, 0% human code, 0% human review — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
by: Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier (interviewed by swyx and Vibhu); framing from the Latent Space show notes
original_claim: When an agent fails, don't prompt it harder. Ask what capability, context or structure is missing, and add that to the environment.
detail: This comes from a 5-month, >1M LOC internal product built with zero human-written code. Each failure is treated as a missing building block to decompose and build. Notion's Sarah Sachs says something similar in https://www.latent.space/p/notion (2026-04-15): 'quickly realizing if you’re just pressing against model capabilities versus not exposing the model to the right information'. For auditing, this gives a diagnostic: sort each failure into missing capability, missing context or missing structure before rewording anything.

claim: Verbatim from Ryan Lopopolo (about 00:24). The same passage says agent mistakes are code 'misaligned with some as yet not written down, non-functional requirement'.
quote: ways to put all the non-functional requirements of building high scale, high quality, reliable software into a space that prompt injects the agent.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
original_claim: Write the team's non-functional requirements and taste into repo docs, tests and review agents. Treat each agent mistake as a requirement nobody wrote down, and record the fix durably, not just in the moment.
detail: Example: after a page caused by a missing timeout, he fixes it and has Codex update the reliability doc to require timeouts on all network calls: 'So I have not only made a point in time fix, but also like durably encoded this process knowledge around what good looks like.' Review agents and tests are pointed at the same docs. Error messages link to the right way to do things. swyx pushes back: a rule persisted 'for all time across everything' misses exceptions and may need rolling back. Lopopolo answers that agents are prompted so they can push back.

claim: Minor hedge lost: the source says such a scaffold 'would be prone to being scrapped', not that it 'gets scrapped'. Better wording: 'a separate restrictive scaffold is, in Lopopolo's view, prone to being scrapped as models advance'.
quote: If we were building an entire separate rust scaffold around Codex to restrict its output, that I think would be like additional harness that would be prone to being scrapped.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
original_claim: Build guardrails that live in the code the agent already produces (tests, lints, CI), not a separate restrictive scaffold around the model. That kind of scaffold gets scrapped as models improve.
detail: His success criterion: none of the harness 'actively degrade[s]' agent performance, because it mostly runs tests, which is 'just good engineering'. swyx calls this an 'on policy harness' that stays within the model's distribution. This backs deterministic support that uses project-native checks rather than engine-imposed restrictions.

claim: With reasoning models, predefined state-machine scaffolds are outdated. Let the harness be the box and give the model options plus enough context to choose how to proceed.
quote: Whereas here we have the model, the harness be the whole box. And give it a bunch of options for how to proceed with enough context for it to make intelligent choices.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
detail: He contrasts this with the 4o era, when models 'could not think so you had to put them in boxes with a predefined set of state transitions'. The team inverts setup: Codex is the entry point and chooses, via skills and scripts, whether to boot the local observability stack. Co-host Vibhu adds that reasoning models are 'seeming to perform better when you don’t have a scaffold'. Swyx pushes back on 'don't put the agent in a box' by saying the box should hold everything the agent needs.

claim: The page backs every part: prettier --silent, a wrapper script that prints only the failing tests, and a one-minute inner build loop ('one minute was just a nice round number').
quote: the CLI are nice ‘cause they’re super token efficient and they can be made more token efficient really easily.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
original_claim: Make tool and CLI output token-efficient for agents: quiet passing output, report only failures, and keep the inner build/test loop fast (under about a minute).
detail: The team wrapped the recursive test runner so it prints only failing tests, and passes a silent flag to the formatter. When Codex 5.3 got background shells it became 'less patient', so they rebuilt the build system to finish in under a minute ('want the inner loop to be as fast as possible'). Counterpoint from Amp's Thorsten Ball (https://www.latent.space/p/amp-the-emperor-has-no-clothes, 2025-09-25): summarizing or hiding verbose output takes you into territory where 'what you see is what you get is not true anymore', and tools are adapting to agents anyway.

claim: The '100 line table of contents' line is the host (Vibhu) paraphrasing the article. Lopopolo supplies the rest: 'we have, I think, six skills. That's it', and new process goes first into 'one of the existing setup skills'.
quote: one 100 line overall table of contents and then you have little skills, right?
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires — Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier & Symphony
by: Co-host Vibhu Sapra summarizing Ryan Lopopolo's (OpenAI) harness-engineering essay; Lopopolo confirms
original_claim: Keep the always-loaded AGENTS.md short, like a table of contents of about 100 lines. Point it at docs and a small set of skills, and route new process knowledge into existing skills instead of adding more.
detail: Lopopolo: 'in our code base, we have, I think, six skills. That’s it.' Any uncovered part of the loop goes first into an existing skill, because changing agent behavior that way is cheaper than changing human behavior. core-beliefs.md carries team, product, customers and the 12-month vision. Contrast with May 2025 Codex team guidance (https://www.latent.space/p/codex): 'Groom your Agents.md: the new hierarchical Agents.md is designed to capture all your instructions to the model and grow as model intelligence grows.'

claim: The source describes Claude Code's memory design as read from the leaked source. It does not recommend a tested practice, so the practice is an inference from one product's architecture.
quote: Claude Code’s Memory has a 3 layer design with 1) a MEMORY.md that is just an index to other knowledge, 2) topic files loaded on demand, and 3) full session transcripts that can be searched.
source: [AINews] The Claude Code Source Leak
by: AINews / Latent Space, summarizing analyses (e.g. Sebastian Raschka) of Anthropic's leaked Claude Code source
original_claim: Use the always-loaded memory file only as an index. Load topic files on demand and keep full session transcripts searchable, rather than putting everything into the always-on file.
detail: This describes what Anthropic's shipped harness does, reverse-engineered from leaked source. It is not official guidance. Other observations in the same issue: fewer than 20 tools are on by default (60+ total), repo state goes into context, and an 'autoDream' mode merges, dedupes and prunes memories and removes contradictions. Earlier (https://www.latent.space/p/claude-code, 2025-05-07) Boris Cherny described CLAUDE.md as 'the simplest thing... a file that has some stuff. And it's auto-read into context.'

claim: Replace few-shot example prompts with goal-driven descriptions of each tool and goal. Few-shot examples are sensitive to ordering, and one shared example string doesn't scale across teams.
quote: When we went away from few shots to describing the goal of the tool in like goal-driven, basically moving from a DAG to like a, a true system with feedback
source: Notion’s Token Town: 5 Rebuilds, 100+ Tools, MCP vs CLIs and the Software Factory Future — Simon Last & Sarah Sachs of Notion
by: Sarah Sachs and Simon Last, Notion
detail: In the few-shot era, 'everyone truly editing one string' competed for position ('The higher up it is in your examples, like the more the model listens'), and only 5–6 people could approve changes. Goal-driven tool definitions let each team own its tools, backed by evals. Simon Last on the arc: 'you gradually strip away everything.'

claim: Tool search and progressive disclosure are Simon Last at about 00:52. The CLI help-commands point comes from his separate MCP-vs-CLI answer at about 00:39.
quote: We’re fighting to keep the prompt as short as possible now
source: Notion’s Token Town — Simon Last & Sarah Sachs of Notion
by: Simon Last and Sarah Sachs, Notion
original_claim: Keep the system prompt as short as possible. As tools multiply, disclose them progressively (tool search, CLI help) instead of loading every tool into every turn.
detail: With 100+ tools, one engineer's niche tool could 'Nerf the overall model by... causing it to call the tool too much', and saying hello cost thousands of tokens. On CLIs: 'it has a progressive disclosure inherently. Uh, so, you know, you don’t see all the tools at once.' They disagree on MCP versus CLI: Last still likes MCP for narrow, tightly permissioned agents ('MCP is just like the dumb simple thing that works'). Sachs: 'We don’t think our system prompt is our secret sauce.'

claim: This is Notion's own eval structure (Sarah Sachs). 'You should have a coding agent write the eval' comes with 'there's a lot of supervision in that still'.
quote: then what we have what we call frontier or headroom evals, where we actively wanna be at 30% pass rate.
source: Notion’s Token Town — Simon Last & Sarah Sachs of Notion
original_claim: Tier evals by purpose: regression evals in CI with a tolerated stochastic error rate, a launch report card of user journeys, and 'headroom' evals deliberately held near a 30% pass rate. Have coding agents write and iterate on evals.
detail: They built headroom evals because their evals saturated and could only say 'it wasn’t worse'. The eval system is treated as an agent harness, so an agent can download data, run the eval, debug and fix end to end with a human watching the outer loop. Sachs: 'the same way that you would’ve a coding agent write the unit test. You should have a coding agent write the eval.' The launch bar is 80–90% of user journeys.

claim: The quote is in the episode transcript (the page's Transcript tab, auto-transcribed as 'element of text' for llms.txt), not in the show notes. The setup was an llms.txt plus a simple file-search tool.
quote: The only catch is I found that the descriptions in your element of text matter a lot because the LM actually has to use the descriptions to know what to read.
source: Context Engineering for Agents - Lance Martin, LangChain
original_claim: For on-demand docs, give the agent an index with a good description of each document plus a simple fetch tool. The descriptions decide what it chooses to read, so write them for recall.
detail: 'element of text' is the machine transcript's rendering of llms.txt. In his 20-question LangGraph test, llms.txt plus a file-loader tool beat both a vector store and stuffing all ~3M tokens of docs, and LLM-written descriptions helped. He also says the instructions for using an MCP server belong in the server itself. Claude Code's team reports the same preference for agentic search over RAG indexing (https://www.latent.space/p/claude-code). This bears directly on skill and reference descriptions.

claim: The quote is swyx's show-note tip. Only one part is measured: Chroma's linked Context Rot report, that LLM performance is not invariant to token count. The claim that clearly present instructions were ignored in multi-turn runs is Jeff Huber's informal observation that led to that research. The phrase 'attention budget' is not on the page.
quote: Respect context rot: tight, structured contexts beat maximal windows.
source: "RAG is Dead, Context Engineering is King" — with Jeff Huber of Chroma
by: Jeff Huber, Chroma (Context Rot technical report); tip list in Latent Space show notes
original_claim: Treat context as a finite attention budget. Performance drops as tokens accumulate, and clearly present instructions get ignored in long multi-turn contexts, so keep contexts tight and structured.
detail: Huber says that in multi-turn agent runs 'instructions that were clearly in there, like, were being ignored'. He would rather have a 60k window used perfectly than a 5M one used poorly, and says needle-in-a-haystack marketing overstates usable context. Lance Martin (2025-09-11) adds that caching lowers cost and latency but does not fix context rot.

claim: Verbatim in the episode transcript (Transcript tab). The 'desired outcome' part is also there: 'you have to know what the desired outcome is'.
quote: what helps LLMs is not tricks and phrasing your prompt in a certain way. It's fundamentally information that you have in your head that you can bring into the prompt.
source: Amp: The Emperor Has No Clothes
by: Quinn Slack and Thorsten Ball, Sourcegraph / Amp
original_claim: Don't rely on prompt 'enhancers' or clever phrasing. What improves results is information only the human holds, together with the human knowing the desired outcome.
detail: Thorsten Ball names the core failure as 'outsourcing the thinking, but not the typing', and says it should be the reverse. Amp also declined custom subagents (hard to debug, not what models are trained for) and large MCP tool sets ('50 tools exposed that often are too low-level granularity'). It warns that custom tools the model wasn't trained on often go unused ('it never calls the tools'), so build 'with the grain of the model'. Related: Codex team (https://www.latent.space/p/gpt5-codex-max-training-agents-with, 2025-12-26) says naming a tool 'rg' instead of 'grep' measurably improves Codex's tool calls.

claim: Guest essay by Dan McAteer. The 80% deletion claim is his secondhand report of Thariq Shihipar, and 'measure by how much you can delete' is the author's own view.
quote: Thariq Shihipar from Anthropic said that the team recently deleted 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness
by: Dan McAteer (guest essay on Latent Space), reporting Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic
original_claim: As models absorb harness capabilities, delete the matching scaffolding and prompt text. Measure harness progress by how much you can delete while keeping capability.
detail: The essay describes a 'train -> absorb -> shed -> repeat' loop, citing GPT-5.1-Codex-Max as natively trained for compaction, and says: 'The measure of the pace of agent harness evolution is how much of the harness you get to delete, while retaining the same capability level.' It also reports Harness-Bench: the same model on the same 106 tasks scored 52.4–76.2 across harnesses, so the harness still matters. Related: an AIEWF 2026 attendee (https://www.latent.space/p/aiewf26trends) advises re-visiting and re-implementing skills with each model release.

claim: Noam Brown's quote is opinion. The measured parts are the cited METR, Scale SWE-Atlas and harness-only ('Only the Harness Changed') results. The post is marked Paid, but this section is visible.
quote: Like you just give the reasoning model the same question without any sort of scaffolding and it just does it.
source: [AINews] Is Harness Engineering real?
by: AINews / swyx, quoting Noam Brown (OpenAI), Boris Cherny (Anthropic), Jerry Liu, METR, Scale AI
original_claim: Whether harness engineering beats simply using a stronger model is contested. Lab voices say reasoning models make scaffolding unnecessary or harmful; harness builders show harness-only gains.
detail: Big Model side: Noam Brown says pre-reasoning scaffolds 'in many ways... makes it worse', and Boris calls Claude Code 'the thinnest possible wrapper over the model'. On measurements, METR finds Claude Code and Codex don't beat a basic scaffold, and SWE-Atlas shows harness effects within noise. Big Harness side: Jerry Liu says 'The Model Harness is Everything', and a Pi experiment improved 15 LLMs by changing only the harness. Latent Space, historically on the Bitter Lesson side, now grants harness engineering 'has real value'.

claim: The source is a prediction in Dan McAteer's guest essay ('I predict that within a year...'), not advice backed by practice. Treat the practice as an inference from that forecast.
quote: It will govern when it’s allowed to interrupt you, when it should keep working, which decisions it can make alone and which decisions need your approval.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness
by: Dan McAteer (guest essay on Latent Space)
original_claim: Give agents an explicit human-attention policy: when they may interrupt, when to keep working, which decisions they make alone and which need approval.
detail: This is a forecast: 'within a year, every company building agentic AI will ship a human attention policy surface in the way that every agentic AI company shipped AGENTS.md.' The essay argues that permissions, identity, trust and legibility are what stays in the harness once models absorb the rest. It cites Lopopolo: 'The only fundamentally scarce thing is the synchronous human attention of my team.'

claim: This is Lilian Weng's personal blog post as quoted by AINews: a respected lab cofounder's opinion, not formal lab guidance.
quote: Even when many harness improvement[s] get eventually internalized into core model, the need to specify goals and context will not disappear.
source: [AINews] Lilian Weng summarizes 35 papers on Harness Engineering for RSI
by: Lilian Weng (Thinking Machines Lab), quoted by AINews / Latent Space
original_claim: Even as harness improvements get absorbed into models, keep specifying goals and context. That need doesn't go away.
detail: This is from Weng's 'Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement' literature review of 35 papers (ACE, meta-harnesses). Paired with the deletion trend above, it defines what should survive in shipped instructions: outcome and context, not procedure. The underlying post was not read in this sweep; the quote is from AINews.

claim: This is Dex Horthy's advice in an AIEWF debate. 'Supervised' is an inference from his 'you never touch the problem' concern. Huntley called factories 'frontier thinking', not yet solved.
quote: he advises to start small and iterate with agent loops — to “build up intuition” and not try to automate end to end from the start.
source: AIEWF Daily Dispatch: The great loops debate and the state of AI engineering
by: Dex Horthy (HumanLayer) at the AIEWF 2026 loops debate, reported by Richard MacManus
original_claim: Build intuition with small, supervised agent loops before automating end to end. The case for full-autonomy 'software factories' is contested at the frontier.
detail: Horthy: 'the hype is outrunning the discipline'. Kubernetes loops are 'deterministic loops', and 'we need to step down an abstraction level, if anything.' Greg Pstrucha says you can't 'orchestrate your problems away by buying more tokens'. The pro-loop side: Geoffrey Huntley says 'It’s inevitable', and Ian Livingstone says verifiability is what matters. AINews 'Loopcraft' (https://www.latent.space/p/loopcraft, 2026-06-12) quotes Steinberger ('you shouldn’t be prompting coding agents anymore. You should be designing loops that prompt your agents') and Boris Cherny ('I write loops, the loops do the work'). Reality check (https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-reality-checks-on-ai-news, 2026-09-17): Steve Yegge shut down his Gas Town orchestrator.

claim: The two weeks comes from Cognition's internal experiments at the 'state of the art in December' (2025), so it is time-bound. 'Regresses to your worst engineer' is Cole's meme about unaudited patterns. Module boundaries come from swyx.
quote: I think we found that the state-of-the-art in December was you can probably, run this for about two weeks.
source: The Age of Async Agents — Cognition's Walden Yan & OpenInspect's Cole Murray
original_claim: Don't run pure auto-merge, no-review agent development for long. Codebases decay within weeks and regress to the worst patterns, so keep reading code, schedule duplication cleanup and enforce module boundaries.
detail: This was Cognition's internal experiment with 'auto merge, no code review at all'. After about two weeks a button existed in 10 variants. Cole Murray: 'your code base regresses to your worst engineer'. He also says not looking at code 'is generally a bad idea' and recommends scheduled cleanup. The debate is open. Lopopolo's OpenAI team ships with 0% human pre-merge review (https://www.latent.space/p/harness-eng). Dex Horthy 'publicly retracted his extremely vibe-coding-pilled call 6 months ago and encouraged people to please read the code' (https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-tasteful-tokenmaxxing, 2026-04-23).

claim: Guest essay by Ankit Jain (Aviator CEO, a vendor). The editor's note says Latent Space is 'not there yet' on the essay's thesis of ending code review.
quote: The fix isn’t to ask the LLM to verify. It’s to ask it to write a script that verifies. Shift from judgment to artifact.
source: How to Kill the Code Review
by: Ankit Jain, Aviator (guest post; editor swyx notes he is 'not there yet' on killing review)
original_claim: Don't ask the model whether its work is correct. Have it produce deterministic verification artifacts (scripts, tests, type checks, lints) and stack imperfect gates.
detail: Proposed guardrail layers: coding guidelines as custom linters, org-wide invariants, domain contracts and task acceptance criteria. 'The agent can’t negotiate with a failing test.' Also proposed: compare multiple agent attempts, and adversarial verifier agents that cannot modify the code.

claim: Same vendor guest essay the editor does not yet endorse. Escalation is stated as: touching auth, schema changes or new dependencies 'should automatically flag for human review'.
quote: Verification criteria need to come from the spec, not from the implementation.
source: How to Kill the Code Review
original_claim: Derive verification criteria from the spec and fix them before code is written. Humans review intent (specs, constraints, acceptance criteria), and risky change types escalate to a human.
detail: 'If the agent writes both the code and the tests, you’ve just moved the problem'. Escalation triggers such as 'touching auth logic, modifying database schemas, adding new dependencies' should 'automatically flag for human review regardless of how confident the agent is'. File scope should be as narrow as the task allows. The claim that humans can stop reading code is contested; see the Cognition finding.

claim: Turn recurring agent 'slop' and reward-hacking patterns into lint or Semgrep rules that fail the PR. Also make the codebase runnable and testable locally so the agent can verify its own work.
quote: we’ve put that in as a lint rule That if you do getattr, your pull request is going to fail.
source: The Age of Async Agents — Cognition's Walden Yan & OpenInspect's Cole Murray
detail: Patterns named: defensive getattr ('It doesn’t want the code to fail'), backwards compatibility at all costs via re-export shims (GPT models, and Claude 4.6 starting to), and untyped dict[str, Any], all catchable with Semgrep or lint. Walden Yan: 'you want your agent to be able to do the full thing, not just write the code, but actually run it and test it', using local DB and Docker Compose without production credentials.

claim: This is Cursor's default for its cloud agents (Jonas), with a /no-test override and per-area AGENTS.md overrides.
quote: The default is to be calibrated. So we tell it, don't test very simple copy changes, but test like more complex things.
source: Cursor's Third Era: Cloud Agents
by: Cursor cloud-agents team (guests on Latent Space)
original_claim: Size verification to the change. The agent should test complex changes end to end before asking for review and skip tests for trivial edits, with AGENTS.md able to override per area.
detail: Their reasoning: a human handing you an untested PR for review would annoy you, so the agent should do the same test-before-review. A /no-test command and agents.md entries override the default. Demo videos and remote VM access give reviewers a cheaper entry point than a large diff. Cursor says these don't replace code review.

claim: One practitioner, Ben Hylak (guest post, 2025-01-12), found that o1/o1 pro worked best when briefed on the what (goal, full context, desired output) rather than the how, leaving planning to the model. He sets this against chat-model framing like 'You are an expert software engineer. Think slowly + carefully'. This is o1-specific experience from January 2025, not tested guidance for reasoning models in general.
quote: I don’t instruct it on the how — only the what. Then let o1 take over and plan and resolve its own steps.
source: o1 isn’t a chat model (and that’s the point)
original_claim: Brief reasoning models on the what (goal, full context, desired output), not the how. Leave planning to the model and drop role or 'think carefully' framing.
detail: 'Don’t Write Prompts; Write Briefs': give much more context, and treat the model like a new hire. The post calls instructions like 'You are an expert software engineer. Think slowly + carefully' 'the opposite of how I’ve found success with o1.' It predates 2025–26 but is still the canonical Latent Space statement of the reasoning-model prompting shift.

claim: This is swyx's tip inside the o1 post ('moving the LLM-as-judge into the prompt and letting o1 run it'), anecdotal and o1-framed.
quote: developing really good criteria for what you consider to be “good” vs “bad” helps you give the model a way to evaluate its own output and self-improve/fix its own mistakes.
source: o1 isn’t a chat model (and that’s the point)
by: swyx (editor's note in Ben Hylak's guest post)
original_claim: Put explicit criteria for good versus bad output into the brief so the model can evaluate and fix its own work.
detail: swyx describes this as 'moving the LLM-as-Judge into the prompt', with the same criteria usable later as evaluators. This supports stating a completion bar inside the instructions rather than leaving 'done' implicit.

claim: The quote is in the episode transcript (Transcript tab). It is OpenAI Platform staff giving opinion in an interview, not formal guidance. The per-model prompting guides and eval-tied prompt optimization are also stated there.
quote: And if anything, it has become more and more entrenched. And I think that there's this interesting trend where it's becoming more and more important.
source: DevDay 2025: Apps SDK, Agent Kit, MCP, Codex and why Prompting is More Important than Ever
by: Sherwin Wu (Head of Engineering, OpenAI Platform) and Christina Huang (OpenAI)
original_claim: Keep investing in prompts, including automated prompt optimization against evals and per-model prompting guides. Practitioners from the platform side say prompting has become more important, not less.
detail: Wu admits 'a lot of us were wrong two years ago' in predicting prompting would die. OpenAI publishes a prompting guide per model because learning 'all the quirks about a new model' is hard. Heavy prompt tuning is called 'zero gradient fine-tuning'. The disagreement is live: Sean Grove's AIEWF 2025 talk was titled 'Prompt Engineering is dead - Everything is a spec', and 2026 loop advocates say to stop prompting and design loops.

claim: The page is swyx's one-line summary of Sean Grove's AIEWF 2025 talk. Grove works on alignment at OpenAI, and the page records a conference talk, not lab guidance. It says only that the best coder will be the best communicator and that well-structured communication, like a spec, is the best approach to alignment and to building anything with AI. It does not call specs the 'primary' or a 'versioned' artifact; that framing would have to come from the linked talk itself.
quote: arguing that the best coder is actually just going to be the best communicator (and well structured communication, like having a spec, is the best approach both to alignment and for creating anything with AI).
source: AI Engineering Goes Mainstream
by: Sean Grove (OpenAI alignment research), 'The New Code' keynote at AIEWF 2025, summarized by swyx
original_claim: Treat well-structured specs as the primary, versioned artifact for communicating intent to models. The best coder becomes the best communicator.
detail: This is Latent Space's recap. Grove used the OpenAI Model Spec as the example of a spec that addresses behavior such as 4o sycophancy. The talk transcript itself was not reachable. By 2026 specs are also a distribution format: OpenAI's Symphony ships as a 'ghost library' spec that a coding agent reassembles (https://www.latent.space/p/harness-eng). Andrew Ng (https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-andrew-ng-gets-into-ai-engineering, 2026-08-25) adds: 'know how to work with a clear spec (and when not to bother doing so)'.

claim: Use one precise, consistent vocabulary ('leading words') for the entities in your skills and instructions. Referring to the same thing in different ways confuses agents.
quote: if you just call everything a ticket, or if you just refer to it in different ways in different places, then it’s going to be really confused and you’re going to get strange behavior.
source: The /wayfinder Skill: Navigating the “Fog of War” of Planning
by: Matt Pocock (AI Skills for Real Engineers), interviewed by Richard MacManus
detail: Pocock: a skill is context management, so design the information flow (a child session gets a 'map' of settled decisions plus its specific 'ticket'). He keeps a shared dictionary so all his skills 'use a consistent dictionary... the same leading words', a 'ubiquitous language between me and the agent'. At AIEWF 2026 he warned of 'skills hell' and 'advises writing fewer and smaller skills, and putting more thought into structure' (https://www.latent.space/p/aiewf26trends).

claim: The page also says a skill meant for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and Codex 'cannot assume they all provide identical capabilities'.
quote: “An adjective with nothing behind it is just a nice apostrophe,” Bakaus said. “You really have to tell the agent what you mean.”
source: Skill engineering and the case against one-shot AI design
by: Paul Bakaus (Impeccable), interviewed by Richard MacManus
original_claim: Give vague qualitative words operational meaning in instructions and skills, spelling out what 'bold' or 'polished' concretely requires. Don't assume skills run identically across harnesses.
detail: Impeccable defines 'bolder' through hierarchy, scale and typography, not gradients. Bakaus notes that Codex and Claude handle subagents and permissions differently, so a skill for Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and Codex cannot assume identical capabilities. He also routes inside a skill to save tokens. He deliberately gives it no auto mode, keeping the human at the point where judgment matters.

claim: The 49 and 26 counts are measured: OpenAI's audit of 138 problem tasks. 'Move toward rubric-based evals' is OpenAI's stated direction for future frontier coding benchmarks (Mia's list, including code quality and design decisions), not a measured result.
quote: 49 tests were too narrowly defined (so that they also reject functionally correct submissions) and 26 tests were “too wide” - looking for extra features that were never mentioned in the problem description.
source: ⚡️The End of SWE-Bench Verified — Mia Glaese & Olivia Watkins, OpenAI Frontier Evals & Human Data
by: Mia Glaese and Olivia Watkins, OpenAI Frontier Evals
original_claim: Validate that eval checks match the task as stated. Tests that are too narrow reject correct solutions, and tests that are too wide demand unstated features. Move coding evals toward rubric-based judgments of design and code quality.
detail: OpenAI audited 138 problem tasks and stopped reporting SWE-Bench Verified; contamination let models reproduce gold patches from task IDs alone. Wanted next: longer-term tasks, open-ended design decisions, code quality and maintainability, and real-world impact. AINews 'FrontierCode' (https://www.latent.space/p/ainews-frontiercode-benchmarking, 2026-06-09) cites METR finding many SWE-bench-passing PRs 'Would Not Be Merged into Main'.

claim: Lilian Weng observes (in an essay about harness evolution and self-improvement) that manual prompt tricks became less central as instruction tuning and reasoning improved, while the need to specify goals, constraints, context and evaluation did not disappear. She does not say newer models no longer need prompt tricks, and she gives no instruction to drop them. This is one researcher's observation, not practitioner consensus.
quote: manual prompt tricks became less central as instruction tuning and model reasoning improved, but the need to specify goals, constraints, context, and evaluation did not disappear.
source: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
original_claim: Drop manual prompt tricks, which newer models no longer need, but always state goals, constraints, context and how the result will be evaluated.
detail: Weng predicts many harness improvements will be internalized into models while the interface to goals, constraints, context and evaluation stays. This supports an audit rule: keep outcome, bounds and completion-bar content, and treat tricks such as emphasis or role framing as candidates for deletion.

claim: The quote is exact and the date is right. Walden Yan (Cognition) states it as a principle; he does not measure it.
quote: Prompt engineering encourages gimmicky techniques like “you’re a senior software engineer” or “think for longer.” Context engineering is more durable and focuses on giving the right context to models while assuming the models become more capable over time.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
original_claim: Avoid persona prompts ('you are a senior engineer') and effort exhortations ('think longer'), and instead give the model the right context, on the assumption that models keep getting more capable.
detail: Cognition's 2026 revision of its 2025 post. For an audit, role or persona lines and 'try harder' lines in an instruction file are low-durability and can be flagged.

claim: The quote is exact and the date is right. It is a Latent Space guest post by Dan McAteer, an opinion piece that says 'keep deleting everything that the model can absorb'. The 80% Claude Code system-prompt deletion it mentions is reported secondhand.
quote: The measure of the pace of agent harness evolution is how much of the harness you get to delete, while retaining the same capability level.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness
by: Latent Space (guest post by Dan McAteer)
original_claim: Regularly delete harness scaffolding and system-prompt text that newer models have absorbed, and measure harness progress by how much can be removed at equal capability.
detail: The post describes the loop as train, absorb, shed, repeat, and reports that Thariq Shihipar said Anthropic deleted 80% of Claude Code's system prompt. It also cites Harness-Bench, where the same model scored 52.4 to 76.2 in different harnesses. The practical consequence is that each shipped sentence needs a periodic check that it still changes behavior on current models.

claim: The quote is exact. The source is about hand-written application and system prompts. It concedes that repetition is 'necessary when the behavior we want is at odds with a model's training', but still presents it as the road to prompt debt.
quote: If unwanted behaviors persist, instructions are repeated, with increasing severity. Pretty soon, the prompt isn’t straightforward and quick fixes regress previous instructions.
source: The Problem is Prompt Debt
original_claim: Don't fix recurring misbehavior by piling on repeated, escalating, all-caps hot-fix instructions: they make the prompt brittle, let each fix regress earlier ones, and tie it to one model's quirks.
detail: Breunig calls repetition 'fighting the weights'. He notes that Claude Code repeats one instruction seven times and says these fixes are 'tailored to a single model's behavior', which locks a project to that model. An audit can detect the pattern directly: the same rule appearing in several places, rising severity markers, and all-caps.

claim: The quote is exact. The scope is building reliable LLM applications: evals, metrics and typed specs, then prompts searched by tools such as DSPy or GEPA so models can be swapped.
quote: The first principle is to specify your system’s behavior with measurements, not prose.
source: The Problem is Prompt Debt
original_claim: Define required behavior with measurements (evals, metrics, typed specs, tests) rather than prose, so prompts can be regenerated or searched and models swapped.
detail: His second principle is to stop hand-writing prompts and let a system such as DSPy or GEPA search for them against the measurements. He adds that tests are 'no longer a safety net but the thing that lets the model cook.' This supports moving rules out of prose and into project-native checks.

claim: The quote is exact. The source says the instruction-count research 'hasn't been investigated in an incredibly rigorous manner'.
quote: This implies that your CLAUDE.md file should contain as few instructions as possible - ideally only ones which are universally applicable to your task.
source: Writing a good CLAUDE.md
original_claim: Keep the always-loaded instruction file to the fewest instructions that apply to every task, because instruction-following degrades as the instruction count grows.
detail: The post cites research that frontier thinking models follow about 150 to 200 instructions reliably and that adherence falls uniformly across all instructions as the count grows. It estimates the Claude Code system prompt at about 50 instructions, and HumanLayer's own root file is under 60 lines. It also notes that Claude Code wraps CLAUDE.md in a 'may or may not be relevant' reminder, so content that does not apply broadly gets ignored.

claim: The quote is in HumanLayer's post, but the '138 agent files' count is wrong. The ETH Zurich study it summarises (Gloaguen et al., arXiv 2602.11988) used 138 task instances from 12 repositories with developer-committed context files, plus 300 SWE-bench Lite tasks. The study found that context files, whether LLM-generated or developer-written, did not generally improve task success and raised inference cost by more than 20%, and that repository overviews were not helpful. It also found that instructions in the files were followed well, and that context files are useful for non-standard practices. Corrected practice: skip codebase overviews and don't auto-generate the files; in a benchmark of 138 tasks across 12 repositories, neither improved success.
quote: Codebase overviews and directory listings didn't help at all; agents discover repository structure on their own just fine.
source: Skill Issue: Harness Engineering for Coding Agents
by: HumanLayer (Kyle), reporting the ETH Zurich agentfile study
original_claim: Don't put codebase overviews or directory listings in agent instruction files, and don't auto-generate the files: in a study of 138 agent files, neither improved results.
detail: This is the ETH Zurich study as HumanLayer reports it: LLM-generated agent files hurt performance while costing more than 20% extra, human-written ones helped about 4%, and agents spent 14 to 22% more reasoning tokens on context-file instructions. Two sources disagree with it: HumanLayer's own Nov 2025 post recommended giving 'a map of the codebase', and Eugene Yan recommends annotated INDEX.md files. OutcomeBound's AGENTS.md repository map is directly in scope. The primary paper should be read.

claim: Point to authoritative sources (file:line references, task-specific docs loaded on demand) rather than copying code or detail into instruction files, which goes stale.
quote: Prefer pointers to copies. Don't include code snippets in these files if possible - they will become out-of-date quickly. Instead, include file:line references to point Claude to the authoritative context.
source: Writing a good CLAUDE.md
detail: This is the post's progressive-disclosure practice: list task docs with one-line descriptions and let the agent decide which to read. Eugene Yan (2026) agrees and warns against @import because it inlines the text. Simon Willison notes that skill frontmatter costs only 'a few dozen extra tokens'.

claim: The source's own example is code style guidelines. It suggests a Stop hook that runs the formatter and linter and shows Claude the errors.
quote: Never send an LLM to do a linter's job. LLMs are comparably expensive and incredibly slow compared to traditional linters and formatters. We think you should always use deterministic tools whenever you can.
source: Writing a good CLAUDE.md
original_claim: Enforce style and mechanical rules with deterministic tools such as linters, formatters and hooks, not with instructions to the model.
detail: The post suggests a Stop hook that runs the formatter and linter and surfaces errors to the agent, and notes that models follow existing code patterns without being told. An audit can flag style-guide prose in instruction files as a candidate to move into a check.

claim: Shape check output deterministically: show a one-line pass on success and the full, focused failure output otherwise, fail fast, and strip noise, so the agent never parses hundreds of passing lines.
quote: Rather than letting the model decide what to truncate, we like to take control of output deterministically.
source: Context-Efficient Backpressure for Coding Agents
detail: Dex also warns that recent models over-correct by piping output to head or tail and then re-running long suites. He sums up: 'deterministic is better than non-deterministic.' The HumanLayer post of 2026-03-12 repeats the point: success is silent and only failures produce verbose output. This is directly relevant to how the engine's validation, quality and ticket reports are printed.

claim: This is HumanLayer's experience with Opus 4.6 1M, after which they switched back to Opus 4.5. The explanation that the instruction budget does not grow with the window is their inference.
quote: More context isn't more capability - the instruction budget doesn't scale with the context window.
source: Long-Context Isn't the Answer
original_claim: Keep each context window small and isolated through sub-agents, progressive disclosure and quiet backpressure rather than relying on 1M-token windows, because a model's instruction budget does not grow with its window.
detail: After weeks of use, HumanLayer reverted from Opus 4.6 1M to Opus 4.5 because instruction adherence got worse even at short lengths, and it now warns at 100k tokens. Amp takes the opposite view (see the Amp '200k Tokens Is Plenty' finding), so this remains contested.

claim: The note itself (Lewis Metcalf) is dated 2025-12-09, but the quoted 'Archived' banner was added later; the page's article:modified_time is 2026-05-27. The quote should be dated about 2026-05-27, not 2025-12-09.
quote: This note was written in December 2025 for an older model and context-window era. Now, auto-compaction makes longer threads work well, and it's fine and productive to go beyond 200k tokens.
source: 200k Tokens Is Plenty (archived)
original_claim: Very short threads to protect context quality are less necessary now: Amp archived its short-thread advice because auto-compaction makes long threads work well.
detail: The original note argued that agents 'get drunk if you feed them too many tokens' and recommended one small task per thread. The archive banner has no date. This disagrees with HumanLayer's March 2026 finding, so context-size guidance should be tied to the model generation rather than written as a timeless rule.

claim: Mitchell Hashimoto says that whenever you see an agent make a mistake, you should engineer a fix so it never recurs: an AGENTS.md line for simple things, or a programmed tool. Each line in Ghostty's AGENTS.md is based on an observed bad behavior, and that almost completely resolved them. He does not say to add lines or tools only in response to observed failures. He also builds tools so agents can verify they are doing a Good Thing. This is an anecdote.
quote: Each line in that file is based on a bad agent behavior, and it almost completely resolved them all.
source: My AI Adoption Journey
original_claim: Add an instruction-file line or a programmed tool only in response to an agent failure you actually saw, so that every line traces to a bad behavior it prevents.
detail: Hashimoto names this practice 'harness engineering': update AGENTS.md for simple issues, and for others write scripts (screenshots, filtered tests) paired with an AGENTS.md pointer. He also writes: 'If you give an agent a way to verify its work, it more often than not fixes its own mistakes.' HumanLayer (2026-03-12) agrees, saying that designing the ideal harness upfront did not work for them and that configuration should be added only after real failures. Every's compound-engineering guide (2025-12-11) asks: 'Would the system catch this automatically next time?'

claim: Delegate large chunks of work by stating intent, constraints and success criteria up front and then letting the model work, and define success criteria before delegating anything you cannot verify.
quote: Explain your intent, constraints, and success criteria upfront, then let the model work. You can’t delegate what you can’t verify, so this requires first defining success criteria and metrics.
source: How to Work and Compound with AI
by: Eugene Yan (personal blog; MTS at Anthropic)
detail: This is close to OutcomeBound's Outcome/Bounds/Completion-bar framing. Yan distinguishes execution drift (checked often) from direction drift (checked occasionally), and uses a fresh-context session to compare the spec against recent turns. Amp (2026-01-14) states the same idea: 'Give it a definition of done, then engineer feedback loops into the prompt itself.'

claim: Treat verification as a ladder and catch each class of error at the cheapest deterministic rung (post-edit format and lint hooks) before tests, evals and LLM or human review.
quote: I think of verification as a ladder. The bottom is cheap and deterministic; the top is expensive and requires judgement. We want to address issues at the lowest possible rung.
source: How to Work and Compound with AI
detail: This maps onto quality-floor design, where fast static checks gate first and broad or judgement checks come later. Yan also says to make verification easy for the model by letting it run the eval, open the browser, or run the code and read the error.

claim: Eugene Yan's full rule keeps an exception: 'Each rule or preference should live in exactly one place (though critical instructions can be repeated in the main CLAUDE.md).' Corrected practice: refactor and prune configs periodically so each rule lives in one place, repeating only critical instructions in the main file, because a rule the model ignores may be contradicted by another rule.
quote: As configs grow, they can overlap or conflict with each other. As a result, if the model ignores a rule, it can be because another rule contradicts it.
source: How to Work and Compound with AI
original_claim: Refactor and prune instruction configs periodically so each rule lives in exactly one place, because a rule the model ignores may be contradicted by another rule.
detail: Yan also mines past transcripts for correction phrases such as 'did you check…' or 'still wrong' as evidence of a missing instruction or verification step. That gives an audit an evidence base beyond reading the file itself. Drew Breunig's 'context clash' (2025-06-22) is the same failure mode.

claim: Willison says a coding agent 'can often' brute-force a solution, and he scopes agentic loops to problems with clear success criteria where trial and error is likely.
quote: If you can reduce your problem to a clear goal and a set of tools that can iterate towards that goal a coding agent can often brute force its way to an effective solution.
source: Designing agentic loops
original_claim: Make agent work succeed by reducing the problem to a clear goal plus tools the agent can loop with, and pick problems with clear success criteria.
detail: Willison says the value of coding agents is 'massively amplified by a good, cleanly passing test suite.' He prefers shell commands with an AGENTS.md usage example over MCP, runs YOLO mode only in sandboxes, and gives agents scoped staging credentials with budget limits.

claim: 'First run the tests' comes from the adjacent chapter (/first-run-the-tests/), which says it 'encompasses a substantial amount of software engineering discipline that's already baked into the models'. The cited page's date matches only its og:updated_time (2026-02-23).
quote: Every good model understands “red/green TDD” as a shorthand for the much longer “use test driven development, write the tests first, confirm that the tests fail before you implement the change that gets them to pass”.
source: Red/green TDD (Agentic Engineering Patterns)
original_claim: Invoke discipline the models already know with compact shorthand ('Use red/green TDD', 'First run the tests') instead of spelling out the procedure.
detail: The companion chapter 'First run the tests' calls that phrase 'a four word prompt that encompasses a substantial amount of software engineering discipline that's already baked into the models.' This supports a terse kernel that names known practices rather than explaining them. Chapters are living documents, so the date given is the guide's launch.

claim: Willison states the advice for end users combining tools: 'the only way to stay safe there is to avoid that lethal trifecta combination entirely'. For application developers he points to design patterns and CaMeL.
quote: LLMs are unable to reliably distinguish the importance of instructions based on where they came from.
source: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
original_claim: Don't rely on prompt instructions to defend against injected instructions; remove one of the three capabilities (private data, untrusted content, external communication) instead.
detail: Willison says telling the model not to obey injected text is unreliable and that guardrail products claiming 95% detection are 'a failing grade.' A guardrail that matters should be enforced by permissions, sandboxing or policy rather than by instruction wording. Treating ticket bodies, tool output and adopter files as data is consistent with this.

claim: Don't hand collaborators agent-produced changes you haven't verified yourself; attach evidence of the verification you did.
quote: Given how easy it is to dump unreviewed code on other people, I recommend including some form of evidence that you've put that extra work in yourself.
source: Anti-patterns: things to avoid (Agentic Engineering Patterns)
detail: This disagrees with Amp's 'Pave The Road' and with Ryan Lopopolo's OpenAI Frontier practice, which has no human review before merge (Latent Space, 2026-04-07). All three sources want evidence-backed claims. They differ on whether a human pre-merge review or automated verification with fast reversibility supplies that evidence.

claim: Amp (Alex Kemper, a vendor opinion piece that promotes its Orbs sandboxes) argues that because producing code has become cheap, the way software organisations handle the risk of shipping bad code should move from preventing mistakes to making them cheap: isolation over permission, quick reversibility over careful review, parallelism over queues. The scope is code shipping in the development lifecycle. Cheap undo is something the system has to provide, not a given. It is not a general case for removing gates on irreversible actions.
quote: from a system based around mistake prevention to one based around the idea that mistakes are cheap: isolation over permission, quick reversibility rather than careful review, and parallelism instead of queues.
source: Pave The Road
original_claim: Replace permission-and-review gates with isolation, fast reversibility and parallelism, since mistakes are now cheap to make and to undo.
detail: Amp reports pushing straight to main from isolated ephemeral sandboxes and a 65% rise in commit velocity. It argues that 'the next model doesn't matter' while the delivery process is the bottleneck. This is the opposing side to Willison's review-before-handoff. For OutcomeBound, the relevant distinction is whether an edge is truly reversible.

claim: The claim comes from Cognition's experience with internal and production experiments. It is not a measured comparison against parallel writers; the only figure given is about review (about 2 bugs per PR, 58% severe). The source also says smart-friend works only when both models are strong (a weaker primary is an open problem), and the manager pattern still has unsolved communication problems. The evidence should be anecdote or practitioner experience, not measured.
quote: multi-agent systems work best today when writes stay single-threaded and the additional agents contribute intelligence rather than actions.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
original_claim: When using several agents, keep writes single-threaded and let the additional agents contribute intelligence (a clean-context reviewer, a consulting 'smart friend', map-reduce under a manager) rather than parallel writes.
detail: This refines 'Don't Build Multi-Agents' (2025-06-12): 'Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results.' Internally, Devin Review catches about 2 bugs per PR, roughly 58% of them severe. The review loop works best when the coding and review agents 'do not share any context beforehand', which supports independent review with separate context. Unstructured swarms are called 'mostly a distraction'.
