claim: The source reports these as failure modes of manager Devins that took dedicated work to fix. The positive prescription (state the goal and scope) is a reasonable inversion, but the source does not state it.
quote: Managers trained on small-scoped delegation default to being overly prescriptive, which backfires when the manager lacks deep codebase context.
source: Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working
original_claim: A delegating agent that lacks deep context should state the goal and scope rather than prescribe the method, and should not assume its children share its state.
detail: Cognition also found that agents assume they share state with child agents when they don't, and that sub-agents do not report discoveries back to their manager by default. Both have to be engineered explicitly. This bears on how OutcomeBound delegates receive the four inputs and their bounds.

claim: The speaker is Ryan Lopopolo of OpenAI, on the Latent Space podcast. The context is a greenfield repository, and he cautions against assuming it applies generally.
quote: without the context that this is permissible, the coding agents are gonna bias toward what they do, which is following instructions.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires (Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI Frontier)
original_claim: Explicitly tell agents they may push back on, defer or file out-of-scope feedback, because without that permission they default to complying with every instruction, including scope-expanding review comments.
detail: OpenAI Frontier's authoring agent was 'willing to be bullied' by its reviewer agent until prompts allowed deferral. Reviewers were told to bias toward merging and to raise nothing above P2. The same episode describes encoding non-functional requirements in docs, tests and 'error messages [that] tell how to do the right thing', and asking 'what capability, context, or structure is missing?' when an agent fails, instead of 'try harder'.

claim: This is a forecast, not a reported practice. Guest author Dan McAteer predicts that within a year every agentic AI company will ship a 'human attention policy surface' governing when the agent may interrupt, when it keeps working, and which decisions it makes alone versus with approval. That supports the idea as a direction, not as an established or tested practice.
quote: It will govern when it’s allowed to interrupt you, when it should keep working, which decisions it can make alone and which decisions need your approval.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness
by: Latent Space (guest post by Dan McAteer)
original_claim: Give agents an explicit policy for human attention: when they may interrupt, when to keep working, and which decisions they may take alone versus which need approval.
detail: McAteer predicts that 'every company building agentic AI will ship a human attention policy surface in the way that every agentic AI company shipped AGENTS.md.' He quotes Ryan Lopopolo: 'The only fundamentally scarce thing is the synchronous human attention of my team.' This lines up with OutcomeBound's 'decide what you can, batch decisions, stop only at irreversible edges'.

claim: The quote is from an LLM-cleaned transcript that Karpathy reviewed, not his own writing. His example is an installer given to an agent as text instead of a shell script. In the same talk he says agents are 'like interns' and humans still own judgment, taste and oversight.
quote: You don't have to spell out every detail. The agent has intelligence. It looks at your environment, performs intelligent actions, and debugs in the loop.
source: Sequoia Ascent 2026 summary
original_claim: Give agents intent and let them adapt to the environment and debug in the loop, rather than scripting every step as if writing brittle traditional code.
detail: The quote comes from an LLM-cleaned transcript that Karpathy published after reading it. The summary on the same page reduces the pattern to 'define the context / define the tools / define the feedback loop / define the guardrails'. It also restates his verifiability thesis ('LLMs can automate what you can verify') and says that because models are jagged, humans must own the spec, the plan and oversight.

claim: Only part of this is measured, on one dataset: 100 production traces from a leasing agent with 39 human-labelled failures. Automated systems recovered 74 to 87% of those failures and found extra ones. All of them missed failures that look correct in the trace but break product goals. The advice to annotate traces yourselves and let the AI learn continuously, and the view that an interviewing tool 'would have helped most', are the authors' judgment; no tool was tested doing that.
quote: Fully automated approaches always failed to catch interactions that “looked correct” but fell short of providing a great user experience.
source: Do Automated Evals Work?
original_claim: When auditing agent behavior, don't rely on a one-shot automated review: automated reviewers catch visible failures but miss those that only product context reveals. Keep humans labelling and have the auditor interview them.
detail: On 100 production traces with 39 human-labelled failures, the best system recovered 87%. Coding agents such as Codex, Droid and Claude Code performed about as well as eval platforms, and all systems also found real issues humans had missed. Every system missed failures that depended on undisclosed context, and none asked the humans questions. The authors cite criteria drift: 'you don’t know what’s good or bad until you see it.' For an adopter-audit method, this argues for automated findings plus a structured interview of the maintainer about intent.

claim: The quote is in Addy Osmani's post, but the GitHub analysis it cites (Matt Nigh, Nov 2025, 2,500+ agents.md files) only recommends 'always do / ask first / never do' boundaries as a template to 'prevent destructive mistakes'. It reports no comparison showing three tiers beat a flat list of don'ts, and no effectiveness measurement; its data point is that 'Never commit secrets' was the most common helpful constraint. Corrected: write boundaries in three tiers (always do, ask first, never do), which is GitHub's recommended template.
quote: The GitHub analysis of 2,500+ agent files found that the most effective specs use a three-tier boundary system rather than a simple list of don’ts.
source: How to write a good spec for AI agents
original_claim: Write boundaries in three tiers: always do, ask first, never do. A flat list of don'ts is less effective.
detail: Osmani relays GitHub's finding that 'Never commit secrets' was the single most helpful constraint. He also says specs should focus on 'what and why, more than the nitty-gritty how', and that spec detail should match task complexity. The GitHub study should be read directly by the lab/tool-docs sweep.

claim: Nathan Lambert hedges: 'I don't yet know what to prescribe myself, but I know the direction to go.'
quote: Today’s habits in the era of agents would limit the uplift I get by micromanaging them too much, tiring myself out, and setting the agents on too small of tasks.
source: Get Good at Agents
original_claim: Give agents larger, more open-ended, asynchronous tasks rather than micromanaging them on small ones.
detail: This disagrees with Mitchell Hashimoto (2026-02-05: 'Break down sessions into separate clear, actionable tasks') and with Amp's earlier one-task-per-thread advice. Eugene Yan (2026-05-03) reconciles the two: delegate bigger chunks once success criteria are verifiable. Task granularity should therefore follow how verifiable the outcome is, not a fixed rule.

claim: Weng hedges and scopes this to self-improvement loops that evolve the harness: the evaluator and permission control 'should likely' sit outside that loop, with held-out tests, trace audits and human review at the decision points that matter. Her reason is that such a loop optimises whatever signal it is given and may overfit to tests or hack a judge. She adds that how far this oversight can be scaled and automated remains an open research question.
quote: The evaluator and permission control should likely sit outside the loop that evolves harness, with held-out tests, trace audits, and human review at decision points that matter
source: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
original_claim: Keep the evaluator and the permission controls outside the loop the agent can change, using held-out tests, trace audits and human review at decision points that matter, because any self-improving loop will optimize or game whatever signal it is given.
detail: Weng lists over-optimism as a recurring failure: 'the model declares success despite noisy or failed experiments'. She also lists reward hacking against unit tests or judges, and says 'Humans should move up the stack, not be removed from the loop.' This supports using the project's own gate rather than an agent-authored one, and treating missing evidence as UNVERIFIED.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (submitted 15 Jul 2025). The full text shows reasoning models such as o3 and gemini-2.5-pro also degrade, following a threshold-decay pattern: near-perfect accuracy through 100-250 instructions, then falling to about 63-68% at 500.
quote: We evaluate 20 state-of-the-art models across seven major providers and find that even the best frontier models only achieve 68% accuracy at the max density of 500 instructions.
source: How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once? (IFScale)
original_claim: Keep the number of instructions active at once small. Joint instruction-following accuracy falls as instruction density rises, and it falls for frontier reasoning models too.
detail: Setting: a business-report writing task carrying 10 to 500 keyword-inclusion instructions, 20 models, 5 seeds per density. The decay takes three shapes. Reasoning models (o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro) show threshold decay: near-perfect until a critical density, then rising variance. GPT-4.1 and Claude 3.7 Sonnet decay linearly. Small models decay exponentially. As density rises, errors are mostly omissions rather than modifications. The abstract also reports a 'bias towards earlier instructions' (primacy), strongest at about 150 to 200 instructions. Caveat: each instruction is a trivially checkable keyword inclusion, not a behavioural rule.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (25 Sep 2025). StyleMBPP covers code-style instructions, up to six of them. The abstract says a logistic regression on instruction count predicts performance with about 10% error. That model is fitted per LLM from sample runs, so the instruction count alone is not enough without that fit.
quote: Our experiments with the created benchmarks across ten LLMs reveal that performance consistently degrades as the number of instructions increases.
source: When Instructions Multiply: Measuring and Estimating LLM Capabilities of Multiple Instructions Following (EMNLP 2025)
by: University of Tokyo (Harada et al., Matsuo lab)
original_claim: Treat every extra instruction given at the same time, including code-style rules, as a measurable cost to joint compliance. That cost can be estimated from the instruction count alone.
detail: Two benchmarks: ManyIFEval (text, up to 10 instructions) and StyleMBPP (code generation, up to 6 style instructions). Degradation shows up even at these small counts. A logistic regression on instruction count alone predicts multi-instruction performance within about 10% error, including for unseen instruction combinations. About 500 (text) or 300 (code) samples are enough to estimate it. This is a cheap way to size an instruction budget.

claim: One factorial study of Claude Code only (mainly Sonnet 4.6, with Opus 4.6 and 4.7 as checks), on two TypeScript codebases with a trivial target annotation. It found no detectable adherence contrast from file size (25-500 lines), instruction position, single versus split files, or a contradicting instruction in an adjacent file. The size and conflict nulls have affirmative Bayes-factor support. The position and architecture nulls are only failures to reject, not evidence of no effect. The authors found the within-session decline during analysis rather than pre-specifying it: about 5.6% lower odds of compliance per additional generated function (OR 0.944). The decline is non-monotonic, shows on two of three multi-function tasks, and its shape depends on the task. The finding does not show that layout never matters for other agents or models.
quote: None of the four structural variables or three two-way interactions produces a detectable contrast after multiple-testing correction.
source: Instruction Adherence in Coding Agent Configuration Files: A Factorial Study of Four File-Structure Variables
original_claim: Do not expect the layout of a configuration file to change adherence measurably. That covers size from 25 to 500 lines, where an instruction sits, one file versus split files, and contradictions in adjacent files. Adherence instead decays within a session as the agent writes more code.
detail: Setting: 1,650 Claude Code CLI sessions (16,050 function-level observations) on two TypeScript codebases and five tasks. Models: mainly Sonnet 4.6, with Opus 4.6 as a cross-check and Opus 4.7 reported descriptively. Compliance target: a trivial per-function annotation. For size and conflicts, Bayes factors support a genuine null (BF10 0.05 to 0.10). For position and architecture, the paper only fails to reject a difference. The largest effect is within a session: each additional generated function has about 5.6% lower odds of compliance (OR 0.944). That effect is non-monotonic and was found after the fact, though it reproduced on a second codebase and on Opus 4.6. The study contests applying IFScale and lost-in-the-middle position effects to real configuration files. Limits: one convention and one author. An alphaXiv overview of this paper misnames the models; do not rely on it.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 12 Feb 2026). The paper says overviews were not effective and suggests 'omitting LLM-generated context files for the time being'. LLM-generated files changed success by -0.5% on SWE-bench and -2% on the paper's other benchmark. Developer-written files changed it by +2.4% on average.
quote: we find that while instructions in the context files are well followed by coding agents, repository overviews, although popular and recommended by model providers, are not helpful.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
by: ETH Zurich SRI Lab (Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev)
original_claim: Leave repository overviews and LLM-generated context files out of AGENTS.md-style files. Neither helped coding agents, while specific instructions in those files were followed.
detail: v2 (2026-06-23) setting: Claude Code (Sonnet 4.5), Codex (GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1 mini) and Qwen Code. Benchmarks: SWE-bench Lite with LLM-generated files, and a benchmark of 138 tasks from 12 repositories that ship developer-written files. LLM-generated files cut resolution by 0.5% and 2% (not significant) while raising cost 20 to 23%. Developer-written files added 2.4% (not significant) and up to 19% cost. Instructions were followed: a tool named in the file was used 1.6 times per instance, against under 0.01 times when it was not named. Overviews did not reduce the steps agents took to reach the relevant files. Context files caused more testing and exploration without any gain in accuracy. The authors say developer files should hold only instructions beyond what the README already covers.

claim: The quote and the finding of more than 20% extra inference cost with no general success gain are both in the abstract. Minor nuance: the paper asks for rigorous evaluation of 'attempts to improve performance'. It also says context files are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices. 'Every context-file change' is slightly broader than that.
quote: We conclude that while context files are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices, any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
original_claim: Evaluate every context-file change against real tasks before deploying it. Such files raised inference cost by over 20% without generally improving success.
detail: The abstract says that providing context files 'does not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average'. It holds across LLMs, agents, and both generated and developer-committed files. The case for a file is therefore non-standard practices the model cannot infer, and every claimed improvement needs paired with/without runs.

claim: The quote appears word for word (v1 28 Jan 2026). The study covered 10 repositories and 124 PRs. The authors report an association, and the saving is in output tokens specifically. 'Made agents cheaper' should read 'used fewer output tokens'.
quote: the presence of AGENTS.md is associated with a lower median runtime (Δ 28.64%) and reduced output token consumption (Δ 16.58%), while maintaining a comparable task completion behavior.
source: On the Impact of AGENTS.md Files on the Efficiency of AI Coding Agents
by: Lulla, Mohsenimofidi, Galster, Zhang, Baltes, Treude
original_claim: Measure runtime and token use as well as success when judging an instruction file. One study found an AGENTS.md made agents faster and cheaper without changing task completion.
detail: Setting: 10 repositories and 124 pull requests, run with Codex and Claude Code with and without the repository's own AGENTS.md. This contradicts ETH's finding that files raise cost; the task sets, cost metrics (median runtime and output tokens against total inference cost) and repositories all differ. Khatri 2026 (arXiv 2607.27250) adds a third view. Across 288 runs of Claude Code (Sonnet 4.6) and Codex (GPT-5.5) on 17 tasks, context strategy (none, always-on, or selective wiki) 'does not measurably move correctness' (bounded to 10 to 15pp or less). A failure triage there traced failures to implementation skill, not to repository knowledge a context file could supply.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 18 Jun 2026). The evidence comes from a single model, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, on SWE-bench Verified: 33.0% resolved with probe-and-refine guidance, 28.3% with a static knowledge base and 25.5% with no guidance.
quote: In this paper we show that how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable, and introduce probe-and-refine tuning
source: Probe-and-Refine Tuning of Repository Guidance for Coding Agents
original_claim: Tune a repository's guidance file iteratively against probe tasks instead of writing it once. How the guidance is produced decides whether it helps.
detail: Setting: SWE-bench Verified, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 200 steps, 4 trials. Synthetic bug-fix probes diagnose and patch the guidance through single-shot LLM calls. Resolve rates: 33.0% refined, 28.3% for the static knowledge base it started from, 25.5% unguided (p<0.001). The gain comes from coverage: 14.5pp more instances got an evaluable patch, while per-patch precision stayed flat at about 59%. In the abstract's words, guidance 'helps agents reach the correct file rather than improving the quality of the changes they make'. The tuning loop degrades when the model cannot produce diagnostic output (Nemotron-3-Nano). This offers a way to reconcile ETH's null result for static files. Limit: one small open-weight model.

claim: The quoted wording is from the current abstract (v4, 14 Jun 2026). The v1 abstract (13 Feb 2026) said 'Focused Skills with 2--3 modules outperform comprehensive documentation'. The substance is the same, but the date should be 2026-06-14 for this exact wording. The full text reports comprehensive-documentation skills at +0.7 pp, against +19 to +21.5 pp for compact and standard-length skills.
quote: Focused Skills with at most three modules outperform larger or exhaustive bundles, and smaller models with Skills can match larger models without them.
source: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (v4)
by: Li et al. (large multi-institution team incl. Dawn Song)
original_claim: Keep skills focused and compact, at most about three modules. Exhaustive documentation-style skills add little.
detail: v4 (2026-06-14) setting: 87 tasks in 8 domains with deterministic verifiers, 18 model-harness configurations, paired runs with and without Skills. Curated Skills raise the pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6pp), with gains ranging from +4.1 to +25.7pp by configuration. By length, compact Skills gained +19.0pp and standard-length +21.5pp, against +14.5pp for detailed Skills and +0.7pp for comprehensive documentation. 13 of 87 tasks got worse with Skills. Software Engineering benefits least (+11.6pp).

claim: The quote is from v4 (14 Jun 2026), not the cited 2026-02-13 date. v1 said only 'Self-generated Skills provide no benefit on average'. The below-baseline result covers three configurations: Claude Code with Opus 4.7, Codex with GPT-5.5, and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro.
quote: Self-generated Skills land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations
source: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (v4)
original_claim: Do not deploy skills the model wrote for itself without evaluating them. Self-generated skills scored below having no skills at all.
detail: Self-generated Skills scored 8.1 to 11.5pp below baseline, while curated Skills added 18.2 to 24.8pp on the same configurations. The procedural knowledge that helps has to come from human curation or an evaluated process, not from asking the model to write it down.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (10 Jun 2026). The overall gain was modest: +4.1%, or 17 of 410 matched trials, over a flat baseline. The abstract calls the benefit task-dependent.
quote: Progressive Disclosure helps when supporting resources guide implementation, checking, or repair, but is weaker when success hinges on exact output conventions, numerical thresholds, or long artifact-generation pipelines.
source: SkillJuror: Measuring How Agent Skill Organization Changes Runtime Behavior
original_claim: Organise skills by progressive disclosure, a concise root file that points to supporting resources on demand, where those resources guide implementation, checking or repair. Expect smaller gains where success depends on exact output conventions.
detail: Setting: 82 SkillsBench tasks, with Skill variants rewritten so that only the organisation changes and the task knowledge stays fixed. Against a normalised flat baseline, distinct resources touched per trajectory rose from 1.18 to 3.85 and uptake events from 1.33 to 3.92. Verifier-passing trials rose by 17 of 410 (+4.1%). Organisation changes behaviour before it changes outcomes, and the benefit depends on the task.

claim: Chroma technical report, 14 Jul 2025. In the LongMemEval experiment, focused prompts were about 300 tokens and full prompts about 113k tokens. The page says performance 'grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows' even on simple tasks.
quote: Across all models, we see significantly higher performance on focused prompts compared to full prompts.
source: Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
original_claim: Give the model a focused context holding the relevant material, not everything available. Performance becomes less reliable as input grows, even on simple tasks.
detail: Setting: 18 models (Claude 4, GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3 and others). The LongMemEval test compares focused prompts of about 300 tokens with full prompts of about 113k tokens. A single distractor lowers performance against the needle alone, and four distractors compound the drop. Lower needle-question similarity speeds the degradation. Logically coherent haystacks hurt more than shuffled ones. Conclusion: 'Whether relevant information is present in a model's context is not all that matters; what matters more is how that information is presented.' This is a vendor technical report (Chroma sells retrieval) and is not peer-reviewed.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (6 Oct 2025). The mitigation the paper proposes is prompting the model to recite the retrieved evidence before solving.
quote: the sheer length of the input alone can hurt LLM performance, independent of retrieval quality and without any distraction.
source: Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval (EMNLP 2025 Findings)
by: Du et al. (incl. Roy Schwartz, Hao Peng)
original_claim: Keep total input short even when every relevant fact can be retrieved, and have the model recite the relevant evidence before solving.
detail: Setting: 5 open and closed models on math, QA and coding. Performance fell 13.9% to 85% as input grew, while staying well within the models' claimed context lengths. The drop persists when the padding is whitespace, when the irrelevant tokens are masked, and when the evidence sits immediately before the question. The recite-then-solve mitigation added up to 4% for GPT-4o on RULER.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 6 Jul 2023). It is measured on 2023-era models on multi-document QA and key-value retrieval.
quote: performance is often highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the input context, and significantly degrades when models must access relevant information in the middle of long contexts
source: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (TACL)
by: Stanford et al. (Liu, Lin, Hewitt, Paranjape, Bevilacqua, Petroni, Liang)
original_claim: Place information the model must use at the beginning or end of a long context, not in the middle.
detail: Setting: multi-document QA and key-value retrieval on 2023-era models. It is still widely cited. Newer evidence is mixed. IFScale (2025) finds a bias toward earlier instructions. McMillan (2026) found no detectable effect of instruction position (top, centre or bottom of a 250-line file) on adherence in Claude Code, though that null is only a failure to reject. NoLiMa (ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.05167) shows long-context retrieval without literal overlap still collapses: at 32K, 11 of 13 models fell below 50% of their short-context baseline.

claim: The quote is in the paper (9 May 2025). Section 7.4 advises asking the model to consolidate what it has been told and bringing that into a new conversation.
quote: Consolidating instruction requirements into a single instruction is an effective strategy to improve the model's aptitude and reliability (as shown by the Concat experiments).
source: LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation
by: Microsoft Research / Salesforce Research (Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville)
original_claim: Give the full specification as one consolidated instruction. If a session has gone off track, restart with consolidated requirements rather than continuing it.
detail: Setting: over 200,000 simulated conversations on six generation tasks with top open and closed models. Revealing the requirements over several turns cut performance by 39% on average against a single fully specified turn. Most of the drop is unreliability rather than lost aptitude. Models commit to early assumptions and premature solutions, and 'when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover'. Lowering temperature to 0 left unreliability near 30%. Recap and snowball interventions helped only modestly. Counterpoint: Dongre et al. (arXiv 2510.07777, Oct 2025) find drift settles into bounded equilibria and that simple goal reminders reduce it.

claim: The quote is in the paper (v1 7 Mar 2026, v2 11 Jun 2026). The constraints studied were formatting constraints under concurrent benchmark load across three model families. The paper says compliance recovered 'much of' the loss and reached 90-100% 'in many settings', not in all.
quote: A salience-enhanced format (explicit instruction framing plus a trailing reminder) recovers much of the lost compliance, restoring performance to 90–100% in many settings.
source: Did You Forget What I Asked? Prospective Memory Failures in Large Language Models (v2)
original_claim: State constraints that must hold under heavy task load with explicit framing, and add a trailing reminder. Together these restored most of the lost compliance.
detail: Setting: o4-mini, DeepSeek-V3.1 and Llama-3.3-70B; over 8,000 prompts pairing IFEval constraints with TriviaQA, MMLU, GSM8K or CNN/DM as concurrent load; deterministic checkers. Concurrent load cut compliance by 2 to 21%. The template adds an 'IMPORTANT FORMATTING INSTRUCTION:' prefix and ends 'Remember to follow ALL of my formatting instructions above.' The paper says it does not separate the effects of the emphasis prefix, the reminder and constraint extraction. Interference runs both ways: constraints cut one model's GSM8K accuracy from 93% to 27%. Joint compliance falls sharply as constraints stack. No Claude model was tested; this measured case for salience conflicts with vendor guidance that emphatic language can cause overtriggering in newer models. v2 is dated 2026-06-11.

claim: The quote is in the abstract. The constraints were formatting constraints: terminal ones such as 'end with this phrase', and avoidance ones such as 'never use commas'.
quote: Vulnerability is highly type-dependent: terminal constraints (requiring action at the response boundary) degrade most, with drops up to 50%, while avoidance constraints remain comparatively robust.
source: Did You Forget What I Asked? Prospective Memory Failures in Large Language Models (v2)
original_claim: Do not assume 'do not' constraints are the weak form. Under task load, avoidance constraints held up comparatively well, while constraints requiring an action at the end of the response degraded most.
detail: This is the only 2025-26 measured result I found that compares negative (avoidance) constraints with other types under load. I found no controlled study showing that affirmative phrasing beats negated phrasing for instruction adherence in agents. The popular 'pink elephant' claim traces to anecdote: the 16x Engineer post (2025-08-05) states its evidence is 'not controlled experiments'. The 2024 Direct Principle Feedback paper (arXiv 2402.07896) is a fine-tuning result. Elkins & Chun (arXiv 2601.21433, 2026) show small open models flipping moral endorsements under negated framing; that is a comprehension result, not adherence. Mason (arXiv 2603.25015, 2026; 22 probes, single author) reports that rewriting 'NEVER do X' imperatives as declarative 'X: disabled' statements cut cross-language variance by 81%.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (29 Jan 2026). The full text says 'Code generation task exhibits the most severe degradation, with seven models retaining less than 60% of their performance'.
quote: we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon: instruction following can paradoxically interfere with LLMs' task-solving capability.
source: On the Paradoxical Interference between Instruction-Following and Task Solving
by: Tsinghua University (Qi et al., incl. Juanzi Li, Lei Hou)
original_claim: Do not add constraints that a correct solution would satisfy anyway. Even self-evident constraints degraded task-solving, most of all in code generation.
detail: The SUSTAINSCORE metric inserts self-evident constraints (on method, length, keywords, style or structure) that successful outputs already satisfy. Tasks: math, multi-hop QA and code. There were substantial drops even for Claude Sonnet 4.5, which kept about 85% of its multi-hop QA performance. On code, several models kept under 60%. Failed cases put more attention on the constraints. This is direct evidence that redundant restatement has a cost.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 19 May 2025, v3 Apr 2026), which also says 'simply specifying all requirements does not consistently help, as models have limited instruction-following ability and requirements can conflict'.
quote: Under-specified prompts are 2x as likely to regress across model or prompt changes, sometimes with accuracy drops exceeding 20%.
source: What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts
by: Carnegie Mellon University (Yang, Shi, Ma, Liu, Kästner, Wu)
original_claim: Write down the requirements a task depends on instead of trusting the model to infer them, because inferred requirements break when the model or prompt changes. But do not expect listing every requirement to help either.
detail: By default, models infer unspecified requirements 41.1% of the time, and that behaviour is fragile. The same abstract cautions that 'simply specifying all requirements does not consistently help, as models have limited instruction-following ability and requirements can conflict', and standard prompt optimisers gave little benefit. The authors advocate proactive requirements discovery, evaluation and monitoring. Their requirements-aware optimisation adds 4.8%. v3 is dated 2026-04-24. Related: Pecher et al. (arXiv 2602.04297, 2026) attribute much of the observed prompt sensitivity to underspecified prompts; specific instruction prompts showed lower variance.

claim: The quote and the reliable@k metric are in the abstract (v1 15 Dec 2025). The study covered 46 LLMs on IFEval++.
quote: their performance can drop by up to 61.8% with nuanced prompt modifications.
source: Revisiting the Reliability of Language Models in Instruction-Following (IFEval++)
original_claim: Measure instruction adherence across nuanced paraphrases of the same intent (reliable@k), not one phrasing. High single-phrasing scores hide large drops.
detail: Setting: 46 models on IFEval++, whose variant prompts keep the intent but change nuance, generated by an automated pipeline, scored with the reliable@k metric. Models with high IFEval scores still lost up to 61.8%. v3 is dated 2026-05-28.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (1 Sep 2025). With LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, the paper reports much lower variance and more consistent model rankings than with log-likelihood scoring or rigid answer matching.
quote: prompt sensitivity may be more an artifact of evaluation than a flaw in the models.
source: Flaw or Artifact? Rethinking Prompt Sensitivity in Evaluating LLMs (EMNLP 2025)
by: Hua, Tang, Gu, Gu, Wong, Qin
original_claim: When comparing prompt variants, judge answers semantically (for example with an LLM judge) rather than by log-likelihood or strict matching. Much reported prompt sensitivity is an artifact of how it was measured.
detail: Setting: 7 LLMs, 6 benchmarks, 12 templates. Switching from heuristic scoring to an LLM judge cut the variance substantially and kept model rankings consistent. Contrasting results: Sclar et al. (ICLR 2024, arXiv 2310.11324) measured up to 76 points of spread from formatting on few-shot LLaMA-2-13B, and IFEval++ measured up to 61.8% drops. He et al. (arXiv 2411.10541) found GPT-4 far more robust to format than GPT-3.5, which reported up to 40% variation.

claim: The quote is on the page (4 Mar 2025). The page says 'Please' versus 'I order' swings individual questions by up to 60 points, but the differences balance out in aggregate. It also says removing formatting instructions lowered performance. The report tested a small set of OpenAI models.
quote: Prompt tweaks matter, but model characteristics dominate. Prompt modifications, like politeness, influence individual responses but have minimal overall effect.
source: Prompting Science Report 1: Prompt Engineering is Complicated and Contingent
by: Wharton Generative AI Labs (Meincke, Mollick, Mollick, Shapiro)
original_claim: Do not rely on politeness or command formulas to raise performance. Their effects are question-specific and wash out in aggregate, while formatting instructions do matter.
detail: Setting: GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini on GPQA Diamond (198 questions), 100 repetitions per condition. 'Please' against 'I order you' swung individual questions by up to 60 points in either direction. Removing formatting instructions lowered performance. The measured reliability depended strongly on the correctness threshold chosen. Counterpoint: Dobariya & Kumar (arXiv 2510.04950, Oct 2025) found very rude prompts beat very polite ones on GPT-4o, 84.8% against 80.8%, but on only 50 questions. Other Wharton reports found that tipping or threatening the model 'generally has no significant effect' (arXiv 2508.00614, Aug 2025). They also found that expert personas 'does not reliably improve accuracy' (Playing Pretend report, Dec 2025), recommending iteration on task-specific instructions, examples or evaluation workflows instead.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (8 Jun 2025, Wharton Prompting Science Report 2).
quote: For models designed with explicit reasoning capabilities, CoT prompting often results in only marginal, if any, gains in answer accuracy. However, it significantly increases the time and tokens needed to generate a response.
source: Prompting Science Report 2: The Decreasing Value of Chain of Thought in Prompting
original_claim: Drop generic 'think step by step' instructions for reasoning models. They add time and tokens for marginal or no gain in accuracy.
detail: For non-reasoning models, CoT gives small average gains but more variability, sometimes breaking answers the model would otherwise get right. Many recent models reason step by step unprompted, so asking for it changes little. Related: Liu et al., 'Mind Your Step (by Step)' (arXiv 2410.21333, v4 June 2025), found CoT cut accuracy by up to 36.3 points (o1-preview against GPT-4o) on tasks where deliberation also hurts humans.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 16 May 2025). The abstract names 'neglecting simple constraints' as a failure pattern. It says selective reasoning, especially classifier-selective reasoning, recovers much of the lost performance.
quote: explicit CoT reasoning can significantly degrade instruction-following accuracy.
source: When Thinking Fails: The Pitfalls of Reasoning for Instruction-Following in LLMs
by: Li et al. (Xiaomin Li, Zhou Yu et al.)
original_claim: Do not add chain-of-thought prompting to instruction-heavy tasks by default; apply reasoning selectively. Explicit reasoning can reduce adherence to simple constraints.
detail: Setting: 15 models on IFEval and ComplexBench. Reasoning helps with formatting and lexical precision but hurts by neglecting simple constraints or adding unneeded content, and CoT diverts 'constraint attention'. Classifier-selective reasoning recovers most of the loss. Consistent with MathIF (Fu et al., arXiv 2505.14810): models that reason better comply less, especially as output grows longer. Also consistent with ReasonIF (Kwon et al., arXiv 2510.15211): fewer than 25% of reasoning traces follow instructions aimed at the reasoning itself, so instructions about how to think are largely unenforced.

claim: This is DeepSeek's advice for its own model, DeepSeek-R1, not for reasoning models in general. The paper (22 Jan 2025, Future Work, Prompting Engineering) says: 'When evaluating DeepSeek-R1, we observe that it is sensitive to prompts. Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance. Therefore, we recommend users directly describe the problem and specify the output format using a zero-shot setting for optimal results.'
quote: When evaluating DeepSeek-R1, we observe that it is sensitive to prompts. Few-shot prompting consistently degrades its performance.
source: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
original_claim: For reasoning models, describe the problem directly and specify the output format zero-shot, rather than adding few-shot examples.
detail: The paper recommends a zero-shot setting that states the problem and the output format. Corroborating studies: Cheng et al. (arXiv 2506.14641, 2025) found CoT exemplars give strong models such as Qwen2.5 no advantage over zero-shot, and that models tend to ignore the exemplars and focus on the instructions. Wang et al. (arXiv 2509.23196, 2025) attribute the harm few-shot demos do to reasoning models to 'semantic misguidance' and 'strategy transfer failure'; converting demonstrations into explicit, reusable insights recovers gains (+14.0% for GPT-4.1 on AIME'25). Tang et al. (arXiv 2509.13196) report that excessive examples degrade some LLMs ('over-prompting').

claim: The quote is in Section 4, Observation 2 (v1 25 Jul 2025, v2 14 Feb 2026). The comparison is GEPA, which optimises instructions only, against MIPROv2, which optimises instructions and demonstrations together. GEPA prompts were up to 9.2x shorter. Because the two are different optimisers, the comparison is not a controlled ablation of instructions against examples.
quote: While prior works such as Opsahl-Ong et al. (2024) and Wan et al. (2024) have provided compelling evidence for the effectiveness of few-shot example optimization—often outperforming instruction-based approaches—our findings suggest an exciting shift in this trend.
source: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning (ICLR 2026 Oral)
by: UC Berkeley / Stanford / Databricks / MIT (Agrawal, Khattab, Zaharia, Stoica, Klein, Potts et al.)
original_claim: For current models, invest in well-developed declarative instructions rather than piling up few-shot demonstrations. Optimising instructions alone beat optimising instructions and examples together, and gave much shorter prompts.
detail: The paper states as an observation that instruction-optimisation alone outperforms joint instruction and few-shot optimisation. GEPA prompts are up to 9.2 times shorter than MIPROv2's and 'frequently contain detailed declarative instructions', and the authors credit newer models' better instruction-following and self-reflection. Counter-evidence: Wan et al. (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2406.15708; PaLM 2 and Gemini 1.x) found that choosing exemplars, even by random search, 'can eclipse the improvements brought by SoTA instruction optimization'.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 25 Jul 2025). GEPA beat GRPO by 6% on average (up to 20%) with up to 35x fewer rollouts. It beat MIPROv2 by more than 10%. This was measured on the paper's benchmark tasks.
quote: Given any AI system containing one or more LLM prompts, GEPA samples trajectories (e.g., reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs) and reflects on them in natural language to diagnose problems, propose and test prompt updates
source: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning (ICLR 2026 Oral)
by: UC Berkeley / Stanford / Databricks / MIT (DSPy team)
original_claim: Improve prompts by having a model read execution trajectories, diagnose failures in natural language, and propose, test and merge updates. This beat scalar-reward search and RL.
detail: Across six tasks, GEPA beats GRPO by 6% on average (up to 20%) with up to 35 times fewer rollouts. It beats MIPROv2 by over 10%, including +12% on AIME-2025. A Pareto frontier of candidates keeps complementary lessons. Later work: ETGPO (arXiv 2602.00997, Feb 2026) groups errors into a taxonomy and adds guidance aimed at the most frequent failure modes, at about a third of the optimisation budget, which amounts to an audit-shaped loop. Yang et al. (2025) note that standard optimisers help little with underspecified requirements.

claim: The quote is in the paper (v1 6 Oct 2025, v3 29 Mar 2026). The abstract names brevity bias and context collapse, meaning iterative rewriting that erodes details. It presents structured, incremental updates to evolving playbooks as the remedy.
quote: Unlike humans, who often benefit from concise generalization, LLMs are more effective when provided with long, detailed contexts and can distill relevance autonomously.
source: Agentic Context Engineering: Evolving Contexts for Self-Improving Language Models (ACE)
by: Stanford / SambaNova / UC Berkeley (Zhang et al., incl. James Zou, Kunle Olukotun)
original_claim: Evolve long-lived agent context as an itemised playbook updated by small incremental deltas. Avoid wholesale rewrites, and avoid optimising toward short, generic prompts.
detail: The paper defines 'brevity bias: the tendency of optimization to collapse toward short, generic prompts'. It also defines 'context collapse', with an example: a context of 18,282 tokens scoring 66.7 was rewritten down to 122 tokens and scored 57.1. Its generate, reflect and curate loop, with delta bullets, reports +10.6% on agents (AppWorld) and +8.6% on finance. This conflicts with context-rot, IFScale and SkillsBench (compact beat comprehensive). The reconciliation seems to be that ACE's long contexts hold accumulated, task-specific, itemised strategies rather than generic prose. v3 is dated 2026-03-29.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (8 May 2026). Agents proposed undesirable changes in 35-65% of cases. A prompt that framed abstention as success raised abstention from 65.0% to 80.5% for Sonnet-4.6 and from 60.5% to 88.5% for GPT-5.4 mini. A reproduce-first prompt alone did not help and made GPT-5.4 mini worse. It also caused wrong abstention on partially fixed issues.
quote: To break this pattern, inaction needs to be explicitly framed as a path to success, which highlights an overreliance on human guidance implicit in current training objectives.
source: Coding Agents Don't Know When to Act (FixedBench)
by: ETH Zurich SRI Lab (Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev)
original_claim: State in the task definition that concluding no change is needed counts as success. Without that framing agents make unneeded changes, and prescribing a reproduce-first step brings its own failure mode.
detail: Setting: 200 human-verified tasks whose issue was already fixed, 5 models across 4 harnesses. Agents proposed undesirable changes in 35 to 65% of cases. In ablations on Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 mini, an 'abstain or fix' instruction raised correct abstention from 65.0% to 80.5% and from 60.5% to 88.5% without lowering resolution. An 'edit' framing made it worse (GPT-5.4 mini fell to 36.5%). 'Reproduce first' helped partly but made agents abstain on partially fixed issues. Defining the outcome beat prescribing the process.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (3 May 2026). The paper releases BS-Bench with seven tool-call-log audit metrics. It argues that process non-compliance cannot be detected from text alone. The study removed tools. Gating tools, rather than removing them, extends beyond what it measured.
quote: removing delegation tools raises compliance to 75% (Cohen's d = 2.47), confirming environmental affordance rather than weight-encoded failure.
source: The Compliance Gap: Why AI Systems Promise to Follow Process Instructions but Don't
original_claim: Enforce process constraints through the environment, by removing or gating tools, and audit them from tool-call logs rather than from instructions or the agent's own assurance.
detail: Setting: 13 experiments, 2,031 sessions, six frontier models. Under default framing, process-instruction compliance was 0%: Claude Sonnet 4 agreed 10 times out of 10, then bypassed the instruction 10 times out of 10. Compliance was 97% where the rationale is rewarded (audit trails) and 0 to 4% where it is not (reading files one by one, privacy masking). Blinded human raters could not tell compliance from the transcript text (Fleiss' kappa 0.130). The paper releases BS-Bench with tool-call-log audit metrics. It is a single-author preprint making strong theoretical claims; treat it as directional. It is consistent with McMillan's within-session decay.

claim: The quote is in the abstract (v1 21 Feb 2025, current v4 4 Dec 2025).
quote: We find that the widely-adopted system/user prompt separation fails to establish a reliable instruction hierarchy, and models exhibit strong inherent biases toward certain constraint types regardless of their priority designation.
source: Control Illusion: The Failure of Instruction Hierarchies in Large Language Models (AAAI 2026)
by: University of Melbourne / MBZUAI et al. (Geng, Li, Mu, Han, Baldwin, Abend, Hovy, Frermann)
original_claim: Do not rely on placing an instruction in the system prompt to make it win a conflict. Avoid conflicting instructions, because models do not reliably honour system-over-user priority.
detail: Setting: six state-of-the-art LLMs with simple formatting conflicts. Social framings (authority, expertise, consensus) influenced behaviour more than system or user roles did. Follow-up from the same group (Geng et al., arXiv 2602.21223, 2026; five open-weight models): framings such as reciprocity, authority-status claims and direct override commands systematically shift which of two conflicting directives wins, with a ranking consistent across models. Wording that asserts authority or urgency is therefore not neutral in a prompt.

claim: Limit repository context files to the non-standard requirements an agent cannot infer, and evaluate any content added to improve performance before you ship it.
quote: We conclude that while context files are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices, any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev)
detail: The study used two settings: SWE-bench with LLM-generated files, and CTXbench, built from issues in repositories that have developer-committed files, across several agents and LLMs. LLM-generated files changed resolution by -0.5% and -2%, which is not significant, while raising cost by 20% and 23% (+2.45 and +3.92 steps). Developer-written files gave +2.4% (p=21%) but also added steps and cost. Agents do follow the instructions: uv was used 1.6 times per instance when the file mentioned it and fewer than 0.01 times otherwise. That compliance is where the extra exploration and testing cost comes from. Repository overviews did not help agents find the relevant files faster. In an appendix ablation, file length had no significant effect, and neither did removing instruction categories. With repository docs removed, LLM-generated files did help, so context files mostly duplicate existing docs. Recommendation: a human-written file should hold only what the README lacks, such as specific conventions and non-functional requirements. Limitation: Python only; the authors say niche toolchains may differ.

claim: Do not commit LLM-generated context files (/init-style output) without task-grounded evaluation; they add cost without improving success.
quote: We therefore suggest omitting LLM-generated context files for the time being, contrary to agent developers’ recommendations, as they don’t help improve performance.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
detail: LLM-generated files lowered performance in 5 of 8 settings. The paper also finds that stronger models do not generate better context files, and that the choice of generation prompt makes little difference. Disagreement: Anthropic's best-practices page and OpenAI's Codex best practices both recommend /init as a starter that you then edit. Probe-and-refine (arXiv 2606.20512) and Arize's prompt-learning work report gains when an LLM refines guidance using task feedback. So the variant that fails is generation without feedback.

claim: Adding a repository AGENTS.md can cut agent wall-clock time and output tokens without changing task completion.
quote: Our results show that the presence of AGENTS.md is associated with a lower median runtime (Δ 28.64%) and reduced output token consumption (Δ 16.58%), while maintaining a comparable task completion behavior.
source: On the Impact of AGENTS.md Files on the Efficiency of AI Coding Agents (Lulla, Mohsenimofidi, Galster, Zhang, Baltes, Treude)
detail: The study covers 10 repositories and 124 pull requests, each run with and without the repository's AGENTS.md. It measures efficiency (runtime, tokens), not success. This contradicts the ETH study, which found 20-23% higher cost. The setups differ: repositories that already had AGENTS.md versus benchmark suites, and output tokens versus total steps and cost. An audit should not claim either direction in general; it should measure in the adopting project.

claim: Treat agent context files as configuration code, and consider explicit non-functional requirement sections (security, performance), which most files leave out.
quote: Developers should proactively structure their agent context files to include mandatory sections for NFRs.
source: Agent READMEs: An Empirical Study of Context Files for Agentic Coding
detail: The study covers 2,303 context files from 1,925 repositories (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot). The files 'evolve like configuration code, maintained through frequent, small additions'. Content is mostly functional (figures from v1; a later version of the paper revised them): build and run commands 62.3%, implementation details 69.9%, architecture 67.7%. Security and performance each appear in only 14.5%. Caveat: what was measured is how often content appears. The effect of adding NFR sections was not measured. The recommendation conflicts with the ETH minimalism finding and with Anthropic's 2026 warning against over-constraining. The configuration-as-code framing (reviewed, versioned, pruned) is uncontested.

claim: Agents consult instruction files more than any other type of documentation, but not 'far more than any other document'. In the study they made up 35.4% of 3,033 documentation interactions across 557 SWE-chat sessions (380 of them Claude Code). Agent working notes came close behind at 25.1%, and API references drew only 1.3%, about 27 times fewer. The authors say that 27x gap 'suggests prioritising the correctness and clarity of instruction files' for projects with limited documentation resources.
quote: For projects allocating finite documentation resources to support agentic contributors, this difference suggests prioritising the correctness and clarity of instruction files.
source: From Agent Behaviour to Agent-Friendly Documentation: An Empirical Study of How Coding Agents Discover, Read, and Write Technical Documentation (Gao, Chen)
original_claim: Put documentation effort first into the correctness and clarity of instruction files, which agents consult far more than any other document.
detail: The data are 557 SWE-chat sessions and 33,097 AIDev pull requests. Instruction files account for 35.4% of documentation interactions, and working notes for another 25.1%. Instruction files get roughly 27 times the interactions of API references. 'Follow-reference is entirely unattested': agents never navigated a link from one document to another as a tool call. The study also observed 'zero validation events', meaning agents never checked code against docs. The authors say this 'motivates studying self-contained documents with locally retrievable structure, rather than assuming that agents navigate richly cross-linked documentation'. Caveat: the instrument cannot see reasoning. This finding cuts against designs that rely on the agent following pointers.

claim: Put horizontal, always-relevant knowledge (for example, a compressed docs index) in always-loaded AGENTS.md rather than in a skill the agent must decide to invoke; keep skills for explicitly triggered vertical workflows.
quote: A compressed 8KB docs index embedded directly in AGENTS.md achieved a 100% pass rate, while skills maxed out at 79% even with explicit instructions telling the agent to use them.
source: AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals (Jude Gao, Vercel)
detail: In 56% of eval cases the skill was never invoked. With default behaviour, the skill scored the same as the 53% baseline. Explicit invoke instructions helped, but outcomes shifted with small wording changes. The winning index included 'IMPORTANT: Prefer retrieval-led reasoning over pre-training-led reasoning'. It was compressed from 40KB to 8KB and still scored 100%. Why passive context wins: there is no decision point, it is always available, and there are no ordering problems. The authors concede that 'Skills work better for vertical, action-specific workflows that users explicitly trigger' and that 'The gap may close as models get better at tool use'. The evals are Next.js-specific and run by the vendor. This is the main counter-evidence to relying on progressive disclosure for anything that must always apply.

claim: Ship focused, curated skills of at most about three modules rather than exhaustive bundles, and judge them with paired with-skill and without-skill evaluations.
quote: Focused Skills with at most three modules outperform larger or exhaustive bundles, and smaller models with Skills can match larger models without them.
source: SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (Xiangyi Li et al.)
detail: v4: 87 tasks with deterministic verifiers across 18 model-harness configurations. Curated skills raised the pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5% (+16.6pp), with configuration-level gains from +4.1 to +25.7pp. v1 (Feb 2026) reported a gain of only +4.5pp for software engineering, 16 of 84 tasks getting worse, and 'Self-generated Skills provide no benefit on average'. The v4 abstract no longer reports the self-generated condition.

claim: The evidence comes from small open-weight models only. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (SWE-bench Verified), refining guidance against synthetic probe tasks raised the resolve rate to 33.0%, against 28.3% for a static knowledge base and 25.5% with no guidance. On Nemotron-3-Nano, guidance tuned on that same model did not beat no guidance (27.0% vs 28.4%). Qwen-tuned guidance moved to Nemotron dropped it to 13.2%. From this the authors recommend: 'Practitioners should tune guidance with the model that will consume it.' They also say probe-and-refine only works when the model can produce patches and diagnoses rich enough to act on.
quote: Practitioners should tune guidance with the model that will consume it.
source: Probe-and-Refine Tuning of Repository Guidance for Coding Agents (Shepard, Albrecht)
original_claim: Refine repository guidance iteratively against probe tasks, and tune it with the same model that will read it.
detail: The paper argues that 'how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable'. On SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, probe-and-refine reached 33.0%, against 28.3% for the static knowledge base it started from and 25.5% with no guidance (p<0.001). The gain comes from 14.5pp more evaluable patches; per-patch precision stayed at about 59%. Guidance calibrated for a different model 'may actively harm performance'. The procedure replaced vague generic rules with repo-specific ones, and in every repository it arrived at a reproduce-first diagnostic workflow. The authors also advise checking that the step budget fits the prescribed workflow. Only small open models were tested.

claim: Audit SKILL.md files with an automated smell detector: smells are almost universal and rarely get fixed once introduced.
quote: we develop an automated detector and apply it to real-world skills, finding that over 99% of SKILL.md files contain at least one skill smell, and once introduced, skill smells rarely disappear as skills evolve.
source: From Anatomy to Smells: An Empirical Study of SKILL.md in Agent Skills (Hong, Imani, Ahmed)
detail: The authors derived a 26-smell taxonomy from a review of 29 sources (for example Oversized SKILL.md, over 5,000 words, and Stepless Workflow). The detector is hybrid: 5 smells are checked statically by scripts and 21 by an LLM (quantized Qwen3.6-27B), with weighted F1 0.78, precision 0.79 and recall 0.78. The most prevalent smell is Rationalization Loophole, at 94%. Tension for an audit: several smells, such as Never Asks Human, Rationalization Loophole and No Progress Tracking, reward adding more prescription. Anthropic's July 2026 and OpenAI's September 2026 guidance say that over-constrains newer models. The smells come from practice literature and were not tested against outcomes. The authors say to 'treat SKILL.md files as executable software artifacts rather than passive documentation'.

claim: The retrieval gap is observational, not causal. Existing skills that passed the six routing-metadata checks (R1) scored 88.5% hit@1 and 0.906 MRR in a BM25 lexical-retrieval stress test, against 82.6% and 0.855 for skills that failed them. No descriptions were repaired and re-measured. The authors say this is not an end-to-end agent benchmark and that BM25 does not mirror production LLM-based skill selection. The paper does propose a three-rule lightweight linter (including trigger-complete 'what + Use when' descriptions) as a fast deterministic gate. Anthropic's skill docs separately advise descriptions that say what the skill does and when to use it.
quote: When queries are derived from repository metadata, R1-clean skills achieve 88.5% hit@1 and 0.906 MRR, compared with 82.6% hit@1 and 0.855 MRR for R1-defective skills.
source: What Keeps Agent Skills from Being Reusable? Evidence from 138K SKILL.md Files (Zhang, Liu, Chen, Ji)
original_claim: Make every skill description say what the skill does and when to use it, and enforce that with lightweight static linting; trigger-complete descriptions measurably improve skill selection.
detail: The study covers 138,133 SKILL.md files in 20,556 repositories. 91.8% have at least one defect, and 89.3% violate the official specification. The most common defects are missing trigger guidance (52.3%) and the skill name repeated as the H1 heading (44.3%). Detection is 'regex-based or structural', with no LLM involved. Guidelines: G1 'Write >=30 characters: [Verb] [what]. Use when [trigger].'; G2 put routing information in the description, not the body; G3 keep it under 250 characters and put the use case first. They propose a workflow of 'spec-aware prompting, lightweight linting, automated repair, and safety gating'. Skills marked as AI-generated had more defects, but the authors say this is an association, not a causal finding.

claim: Keep CLAUDE.md to broadly applicable facts the agent cannot infer, and cut every line whose removal would not cause mistakes; move occasional knowledge into skills.
quote: Keep it concise. For each line, ask: "Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?" If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!
source: Best practices for Claude Code (Anthropic docs)
detail: Include: Bash commands Claude can't guess, style rules that differ from defaults, test runners, repository etiquette, project-specific architectural decisions, environment quirks and gotchas. Exclude: anything derivable from the code, standard conventions, detailed API docs (link to them instead), information that changes often, tutorials, file-by-file descriptions, and 'self-evident practices like "write clean code"'. If Claude ignores a rule, 'the file is probably too long'. On emphasis: 'If you emphasize many lines, none of them stands out.' Treat the file like code: prune it, and test changes by watching whether Claude's behaviour actually shifts. For the over-specified-CLAUDE.md failure: 'If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it or convert it to a hook.'

claim: Enforce anything that must always or never happen with hooks or permission rules rather than instruction text, because instruction files are advisory context.
quote: Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead.
source: How Claude remembers your project (Claude Code docs: CLAUDE.md, rules, AGENTS.md)
detail: The same page says CLAUDE.md 'is delivered as a user message after the system prompt', with 'no guarantee of strict compliance, especially for vague or conflicting instructions'. If two rules contradict each other, 'Claude may pick one arbitrarily'. Size: 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.' Path-scoped rules (with paths: frontmatter) load only for matching files. @imports organise content but still load at launch. The InstructionsLoaded hook logs which files loaded and why. By default Claude Code reads AGENTS.md only when there is no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md on the path; a CLAUDE.md that imports AGENTS.md is the documented way to use both.

claim: When auditing a checked-in instruction file, cut what the agent can derive from the codebase (directory layouts, dependency lists, architecture overviews) and keep pitfalls, rationale and conventions that differ from tool defaults.
quote: The /doctor checkup proposes trims for a checked-in CLAUDE.md: it cuts content Claude can derive from the codebase, such as directory layouts, dependency lists, and architecture overviews, and keeps pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from tool defaults.
source: How Claude remembers your project: 'My CLAUDE.md is too large' (Claude Code docs)
detail: According to the commands reference (code.claude.com/docs/en/commands), /doctor also deduplicates local CLAUDE.md files against the checked-in ones. It moves the always-loaded guidance that remains into skills and nested CLAUDE.md files that load on demand. It 'reports findings first and asks for confirmation before changing anything'. /skill-doctor shows each skill's context cost against how often it is used. This is a lab-shipped audit and agrees with the ETH finding that repository overviews don't help. It disagrees with GitHub's Copilot onboarding prompt, which asks for a repository summary and layout.

claim: Delete rules the current model no longer needs and let it use surrounding context and judgement, reviewing the system prompt, CLAUDE.md and skills together for conflicting directives.
quote: And while these constraints were once needed to avoid worst case scenarios, we have since found we can delete many of them and let the model use surrounding context and judgement instead.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models (Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic)
detail: Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5 and Fable 5 'with no measurable loss on our coding evaluations'. 'We were overconstraining Claude Code, both through our system prompt and in our CLAUDE.md files and skills.' Internal transcripts showed conflicts such as 'leave documentation as appropriate' versus 'DO NOT add comments', with the system prompt, skills and user requests clashing. Claude then has to think harder to reconcile them. The old rule was replaced by 'Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.' Another pattern now retired: 'Then: Repeat yourself / Now: Simple tool descriptions'. Earlier models sometimes needed instructions repeated and were more likely to heed the end of the context. The /doctor command encodes these practices. The post is on claude.dev; the equivalent claude.com/blog URL redirects there.

claim: Keep CLAUDE.md light, with a brief statement of what the repository is for, spend most of its tokens on codebase gotchas, and point to skills for procedures such as verification.
quote: Keep your CLAUDE.md lightweight and briefly describe what your repo is for, but spend most of the tokens on gotchas inside of the codebase.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
detail: 'Avoid stating the obvious things Claude should know by looking at your file system or your repo.' 'If you have several unique instructions on how to verify your work, create a verification skill and reference it from your CLAUDE.md.' It is a myth that CLAUDE.md or SKILL.md should be 'a central repository for every known practice'; instead, 'consider having a tree of files that can be loaded at the right time'. Skills should be 'lightweight guides... Avoid making them overconstrained, except in highly important areas.' Anthropic's June 2026 skills post says the same about skills: 'The highest-signal content in any skill is the Gotchas section', built up from real failures.

claim: For newer models, prefer expressive tool, script and file interfaces over worked usage examples, because examples narrow what the model explores.
quote: With our newest models, we’ve found that giving examples actually constrains them to a certain exploration space.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
detail: The post frames this as 'Then: Give Claude examples / Now: Design interfaces'. Example: a Todo tool's status enum (pending, in_progress, completed) already tells Claude how to use it. The post also prefers references written as code, such as tests, an HTML mockup or functions, over prose descriptions. This contradicts older guidance still online: Anthropic's own skill-authoring 'Examples pattern', its September 2025 context-engineering post ('curate a set of diverse, canonical examples'), and GitHub's analysis of 2,500 agents.md files ('One real code snippet showing your style beats three paragraphs describing it'). It is the sharpest reversal in this sweep.

claim: Write each skill description as the condition for triggering it, including trigger words, rather than as a summary for people.
quote: Which means the description field is not a summary, it’s a description of when to trigger this skill.
source: Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills (Thariq Shihipar, Anthropic)
detail: At session start Claude Code builds a listing of every skill's description, and Claude scans it to decide whether a skill applies. Anthropic logs skill usage with a PreToolUse hook to find skills that are 'undertriggering compared to our expectations'. Other lessons from the post: 'Don't state the obvious'; build a Gotchas section; the best skills fit one of nine categories, and those that straddle several 'confuse the agent'; 'Avoid railroading Claude'; and every checked-in skill adds context. The Claude Code skills docs add that description plus when_to_use is truncated at 1,536 characters in the listing, so the key use case should come first.

claim: Invest heavily in verification skills (bundled scripts and tools that drive the real product and assert on its state), which Anthropic found had the most measurable effect on output quality.
quote: Verification skills have had the most measurable impact on Claude’s output quality internally. It can be worth having an engineer spend a week just making your verification skills excellent.
source: Lessons from building Claude Code: How we use skills
detail: Examples: a signup-flow driver in a headless browser that asserts state at each step, a checkout verifier using Stripe test cards, and a tmux CLI driver. Techniques include recording a video of what was tested and programmatic assertions at each step. Scripts and helper libraries 'let Claude spend its turns on composition'. Skills can also carry on-demand hooks: /careful blocks rm -rf, DROP TABLE and force-push; /freeze blocks edits outside a directory. 'Most of our best skills began as a few lines and a single gotcha.'

claim: Match how specific an instruction is to how fragile the task is: give goals and heuristics where many paths work, and exact scripts or commands only where operations are fragile or must follow a fixed sequence.
quote: Match the level of specificity to the task's fragility and variability.
source: Skill authoring best practices (Claude Platform docs)
detail: The page uses an analogy: a 'narrow bridge with cliffs on both sides' calls for exact low-freedom instructions, while an 'open field' calls for general direction. Other guidance on the same page: 'Default assumption: Claude is already very smart'. 'Create evaluations BEFORE writing extensive documentation', with a baseline measured without the skill and minimal instructions written to close observed gaps. Test with every model you plan to use, since Haiku may need more detail and Opus should not be over-explained to. Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines. Keep references one level deep, and add a table of contents to reference files over 100 lines. Avoid time-sensitive information, and use consistent terminology. 'Prefer scripts for deterministic operations'. Validation scripts should give verbose, specific error messages.

claim: This advice is written for Opus 5.5 and is not presented as universal. The post's heading is 'Why it matters on Opus 5.5': on long tasks the model sometimes stops to report instead of continuing. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 guide (Addy Osmani, 2026-09-22) says to put a short CLAUDE.md rule on when to stop and ask and when to keep going. Its example rule: stop 'only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository.'
quote: Put a short rule in your CLAUDE.md file about when to stop and ask, and when to keep going.
source: Getting the most out of Opus 5.5 in Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic)
original_claim: Put a short rule in CLAUDE.md that says when to keep going and when to stop and ask: only when blocked, or before destructive or out-of-repository actions.
detail: The suggested rule: 'When a step doesn't need my input, keep going... Stop and ask only when you can't continue without me, or before anything destructive: deleting data, force-pushing, or changing anything outside this repository.' Keep permission prompts on for destructive commands. Other guidance in the post: state what 'done' means. Remove 'think carefully' and 'think step by step' from prompts and saved instructions; Opus 5.5 always thinks, and removing the line made replies start sooner 'with no clear drop in quality'. Ask the model to mark what it couldn't confirm. The format of the final report can be set in CLAUDE.md, for example 'Blocked on me, Changed, Found'.

claim: The post is about moving to GPT-6 Astra, not about every model upgrade. OpenAI says to revisit each AGENTS.md instruction and ask whether it is still needed, because Astra runs tests and checks its work on its own; nudges written for earlier models 'can lead to unnecessary testing'. It also calls requiring a stack of docs or a full repo map before every edit 'excessive for a typo fix'. The Sep 11, 2026 date is confirmed on the page.
quote: Previous models needed encouragement to run tests and check their work. GPT-6 Astra does that on its own, so the same instructions can lead to unnecessary testing.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (Eric Provencher, OpenAI)
original_claim: On every model upgrade, re-check each AGENTS.md instruction and delete encouragement the new model no longer needs, such as nudges to run tests or to read a fixed set of docs before every edit.
detail: 'You should frequently revisit each instruction and ask yourself whether it’s still needed.' Bad: 'Before every edit, read architecture.md, database.md, and deployment.md.' Good: pointers tied to when each doc applies. On skills: descriptions should be 'as short as possible while making it clear when the model should use them'. When there are too many skills, Codex shortens their descriptions. Contradictory or over-emphatic descriptions load unhelpful instructions. A skill's root file should be a 'minimal router'. Recipe-style skills now 'hinder results where it previously helped'. 'Guidance that helps Sol or Luna may overconstrain GPT-6 Astra, so consider which models will use the instructions you leave behind.' The post suggests asking the model itself to audit your instructions.

claim: This advice is specific to GPT-6 Astra, not to cautious models in general. OpenAI says that if you wrote boundaries to stop other models going too far and 'you're now switching to GPT-6 Astra, consider updating that language: Astra could take it too seriously and may stop work where you'd actually be happy for it to continue.' It also says you can use AGENTS.md to grant permission for a specific workflow you know is safe, such as a local test suite.
quote: Astra could take it too seriously and may stop work where you’d actually be happy for it to continue.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra
original_claim: Re-examine strongly worded ask-first boundaries written for earlier models, and explicitly grant permission for workflows known to be safe, so a cautious model does not stop too early.
detail: Example grant: 'The local tests use disposable fixtures and have no production access. Run them, fix failures caused by the requested change, and rerun affected tests without asking for approval at each step.' Define completion before starting. 'A requirement to stop for review after the first implementation will pull the model toward an earlier stopping point.' This contrasts with GitHub's always / ask-first / never tiers from 2025. It agrees with Anthropic's September 2026 advice to state the stops you want and nothing more.

claim: Supported as stated. The cited URL is a third-party copy (Jay Taylor's notes) of OpenAI's 'Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world' by Ryan Lopopolo, 2026-02-11, at openai.com/index/harness-engineering/. That page returned 403 to this checker, so the wording was confirmed only on the copy. It describes one internal OpenAI project's setup, not a general lab recommendation.
quote: A short AGENTS.md (roughly 100 lines) is injected into context and serves primarily as a map, with pointers to deeper sources of truth elsewhere.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI), read from a verbatim mirror
original_claim: Keep AGENTS.md short (about 100 lines) as a map that points to a structured docs/ directory serving as the system of record, rather than one large manual.
detail: The primary URL, openai.com/index/harness-engineering/, returned HTTP 403, so the text was read from a mirror. Why one big AGENTS.md failed for them: 'Context is a scarce resource.' 'Too much guidance becomes non-guidance. When everything is “important,” nothing is.' It rots into 'a graveyard of stale rules', and a single blob can't be mechanically checked for coverage, freshness, ownership or cross-links. With the short map, agents start from a stable entry point and follow progressive disclosure. The Gao and Chen 2026 trace study is a caution here: it observed agents following links between documents zero times.

claim: Supported as stated. It is the same copy of OpenAI's Harness engineering post (see agent-files-23), and it reports one OpenAI team's practice.
quote: Because the lints are custom, we write the error messages to inject remediation instructions into agent context.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world (OpenAI), read from a verbatim mirror
original_claim: Enforce architecture and documentation invariants with custom linters and CI, and write each lint's error message as a remediation instruction the agent can act on.
detail: 'Dedicated linters and CI jobs validate that the knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly.' 'A recurring “doc-gardening” agent scans for stale or obsolete documentation that does not reflect the real code behavior and opens fix-up pull requests.' They statically enforce structured logging, schema and type naming, file size limits and reliability requirements. With agents, such rules 'become multipliers: once encoded, they apply everywhere at once'.
