claim: Supported as stated. The URL now redirects (308) to https://learn.chatgpt.com/guides/best-practices. The same page also says: 'When Codex makes the same mistake twice, ask it for a retrospective and update AGENTS.md,' and to reference task-specific markdown files once AGENTS.md grows large.
quote: Keep it practical. A short, accurate AGENTS.md is more useful than a long file full of vague rules. Start with the basics, then add new rules only after you notice repeated mistakes.
source: Codex Best practices (OpenAI; redirects to learn.chatgpt.com/guides/best-practices)
original_claim: Keep AGENTS.md short and accurate, start with the basics, and add a rule only after a repeated mistake (found through a retrospective); move task-specific material into referenced files.
detail: A good AGENTS.md covers repository layout, how to run the project, build/test/lint commands, conventions and PR expectations, constraints and do-not rules, and 'What done means and how to verify work'. The /init scaffold is a starting point that you should then edit. Nested files apply, with the closest winning. When the file grows, keep the main file concise and reference task-specific markdown for planning, review or architecture. 'When Codex makes the same mistake twice, ask it for a retrospective and update AGENTS.md.' For task prompts: Goal, Context, Constraints, Done when. The Codex AGENTS.md docs cap combined instruction files at project_doc_max_bytes, 32 KiB by default.

claim: Supported. The sentence comes from GitHub's sample prompt that asks Copilot's cloud agent to generate copilot-instructions.md. It is not a direct instruction to human authors. The same prompt asks for documenting errors and the workarounds used.
quote: Each command should be validated by running it to ensure that it works correctly as well as any preconditions and postconditions.
source: Adding repository custom instructions for GitHub Copilot (GitHub Docs)
original_claim: Validate every build, test and lint command in an instruction file by actually running it, and record its preconditions, failures and workarounds.
detail: This comes from the prompt GitHub provides for Copilot cloud agent to generate .github/copilot-instructions.md. The same prompt requires that instructions be 'no longer than 2 pages' and 'not task specific'. It asks for a repository summary and the project layout, and ends: 'explicitly instruct the agent to trust the instructions and only perform a search if the information in the instructions is incomplete or found to be in error.' That overview-and-trust approach is contested by ETH (overviews don't help) and by Anthropic's /doctor (which cuts layouts). Copilot also reads AGENTS.md (nearest file wins) or a root CLAUDE.md or GEMINI.md. The docs advise avoiding conflicting instruction sets across personal, repository and organisation levels.

claim: Leave style guides and commonly known commands out of rules (use a linter), reference canonical files instead of copying code, and add rules only for repeated mistakes.
quote: Copying entire style guides: Use a linter instead. Agent already knows common style conventions.
source: Rules (Cursor docs)
detail: 'Good rules are focused, actionable, and scoped.' Keep rules under 500 lines and split them into composable rules. 'Reference files instead of copying their contents—this keeps rules short and prevents them from becoming stale as code changes.' Avoid documenting every possible command, edge cases that rarely apply, and duplicates of the codebase. 'Start simple. Add rules only when you notice Agent making the same mistake repeatedly.' Rule types: Always Apply, Apply Intelligently (by description), Apply to Specific Files (glob), and Apply Manually. AGENTS.md is supported as a simpler alternative. HumanLayer (2025-11) makes the same point: 'Never send an LLM to do a linter's job.'

claim: Supported. This is an opinion guest post by Dan McAteer on Latent Space (2026-08-22), not measured evidence. Its metric: 'how much of the harness you get to delete, while retaining the same capability level.' It cites Anthropic deleting 80% of Claude Code's system prompt.
quote: Once the models absorb the harness capabilities, the harness can shed the scaffold. It’s production by reduction.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness (Dan McAteer, Latent Space)
original_claim: As models absorb what the harness used to do, delete the scaffolding (prompts and instructions) that made up for it, and measure progress by how much you can remove at equal capability.
detail: The essay relays Thariq Shihipar's statement that Claude Code's team 'recently deleted 80% of Claude Code's system prompt'. 'The measure of the pace of agent harness evolution is how much of the harness you get to delete, while retaining the same capability level.' It predicts an 'attention-interface': a policy surface for when the agent may interrupt and which decisions it makes alone, which 'every company' will ship the way they shipped AGENTS.md.

claim: Supported as an anecdote. The line comes from an AI-generated AINews recap of X posts (2026-02-03) and is attributed to one user (@nbaschez). It is not a measured result.
quote: A concrete best practice for CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md: Add a “test-first” instruction: when a bug is reported, write a reproducing test first; then fix; then prove via passing test
source: [AINews] OpenAI Codex App: death of the VSCode fork, multitasking worktrees, Skills Automations (Latent Space)
original_claim: Add a test-first instruction to CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md: on a bug report, write a reproducing test, then fix the bug, then prove the fix with the passing test.
detail: This practitioner claim is 'framed as the single biggest improvement to agent performance and sanity'. It agrees with probe-and-refine, which independently arrived at a reproduce-first workflow for small open models. It is contested by OpenAI's September 2026 note that testing encouragement causes unnecessary testing with GPT-6 Astra, and by the ETH finding that followed instructions add testing and exploration cost. Whether this helps depends on the model.

claim: The source is vendor marketing for AgentLint, with no measurement showing that whole-harness auditing improves outcomes. The page treats AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, tool-specific rules, CI, pre-commit hooks and .gitignore together as the agent harness. It scores them with 33 checks across five weighted dimensions (Findability 20%, Instructions 30%, Workability 20%, Continuity 15%, Safety 15%). The page never calls its own checks deterministic: in the quote, 'deterministic' describes CI, hooks and .gitignore, not AgentLint's checks.
quote: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are the persistent rules. .cursor/rules and copilot-instructions.md are the tool-specific layers. CI, pre-commit hooks, and .gitignore are the deterministic constraints the agent cannot override.
source: AgentLint: Lint your CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, and AI agent harness
original_claim: Audit the whole harness (instruction files plus CI, hooks and .gitignore) with deterministic, weighted checks rather than reviewing the instruction file alone.
detail: 33 checks in five weighted groups. Findability (20%): entry files, indexes, resolvable references, naming. Instructions (30%): emphasis density, specificity, file length, a claimed 40K-character hard limit. Workability (20%): commands, CI, real tests, linter, 256 KB ceiling, hook speed. Continuity (15%): freshness, handoffs, changelogs, plans. Safety (15%): .env gitignored, SHA-pinned Actions, workflow permissions, secrets. It claims its reference values come from tracking 265 versions of Claude Code's system prompt (for example, IMPORTANT cut from 12 uses to 4). I could not verify that, and the site offers no evidence that the score predicts agent outcomes. Other tools found: AgentLinter (v2.3.0, 2026-03-14; eight scored dimensions), cclint, skill-lint, and the Agent Skills spec's 'skills-ref validate' (frontmatter and naming only).

claim: Run several isolated trials of every task, each starting from a clean environment, because a single run of a non-deterministic agent is not a measurement.
quote: Because model outputs vary between runs, we run multiple trials to produce more consistent results.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: The same article requires isolation: shared state between runs (leftover files, cached data, resource exhaustion) causes correlated failures that come from the infrastructure, not the agent. In OutcomeBound's eval runner this means a fresh worktree per trial.

claim: Pick pass@k or pass^k to match the product: pass^k (all k trials succeed) is the metric for behavior that must be reliable every time, and it drops quickly as k grows.
quote: pass^k measures the probability that all k trials succeed. As k increases, pass^k falls since demanding consistency across more trials is a harder bar to clear.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Worked example from the article: 75% per-trial success over 3 trials gives about 42% pass^3. At k=1 the two metrics are equal. By k=10 they point opposite ways. pass^k comes from Sierra's tau-bench (arXiv 2406.12045, June 2024), which found gpt-4o at 'pass^8 <25% in retail'. An instruction that should always hold, such as reporting UNVERIFIED instead of claiming success or stopping before an irreversible edge, should be scored on pass^k, not pass@1.

claim: Keep capability evals, which start at a low pass rate and leave room to improve, separate from regression evals, which should pass nearly 100% of the time and exist to catch backsliding.
quote: Capability or “quality” evals ask, “What can this agent do well?” They should start at a low pass rate, targeting tasks the agent struggles with and giving teams a hill to climb.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: The same article says regression evals 'should have a nearly 100% pass rate' and that a saturated capability eval can graduate into the regression suite. This split answers the headroom question: a prompt change can only show an improvement on the capability set. The regression set can only show harm.

claim: Watch for saturation: an eval every configuration passes can still catch regressions but cannot show that a change helped, so add harder tasks or new dimensions.
quote: An eval at 100% tracks regressions but provides no signal for improvement. Eval saturation occurs when an agent passes all of the solvable tasks, leaving no room for improvement.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Hamel Husain's FAQ (2026-09-18) agrees: 'If you’re passing 100% of your evals, you’re likely not challenging your system enough.' It also advises retiring or running less often an eval where 'everything keeps passing'.

claim: With frontier models, Anthropic advises reading a 0% pass rate over many trials (0% pass@100) as most often a sign of a broken task rather than an incapable agent, and as a reason to double-check the task specification and graders. It recommends a reference solution for each task and the test that two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict. This is lab guidance backed by audit anecdotes (Terminal-Bench, METR, CORE-Bench), not a measured result. The source limits it to frontier models and says 'most often', not always.
quote: With frontier models, a 0% pass rate across many trials (i.e. 0% pass@100) is most often a signal of a broken task, not an incapable agent, and a sign to double-check your task specification and graders.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
original_claim: Read a 0% pass rate over many trials as a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent. Validate each task with a reference solution and the two-expert agreement test.
detail: Same article: 'A good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict'; 'Ambiguity in task specifications becomes noise in metrics'; every task needs a reference solution that passes all graders. Measured example: Opus 4.5 scored 42% on CORE-Bench until grading bugs and ambiguous specs were fixed, then 95%.

claim: Start early with a small set of tasks drawn from real failures. Small samples are enough only while effects are large, so grow the set as the remaining effects shrink.
quote: 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a great start. After all, in early agent development, each change to the system often has a clear, noticeable impact, and this large effect size means small sample sizes suffice.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: OpenAI gives similar sizing for skills: 'a small set of 10–20 prompts is enough to surface regressions and confirm improvements early' (Testing Agent Skills Systematically with Evals, 2026-01-22). The size rule depends on effect size, which leads straight to the power-analysis finding below.

claim: Grade what the agent produced, not the exact path it took. Assertions that require a specific tool sequence punish valid alternative solutions.
quote: So as not to unnecessarily punish creativity, it’s often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Disagreement: Google Cloud's agent-evaluation guidance (2025-11-18) gives trajectory analysis its own pillar because of 'silent failures', where the output is correct but the process was wrong. Hamel Husain's FAQ resolves this by ordering: measure end-to-end task success first, then use step-level diagnostics to find out why a task fails. Anthropic also recommends partial credit for multi-component tasks.

claim: Build balanced problem sets that cover both cases where a behavior should happen and cases where it should not, so that optimizing the prompt does not make the agent over-apply it.
quote: Test both the cases where a behavior should occur and where it shouldn’t. One-sided evals create one-sided optimization.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: The article's example: testing only whether the agent searches when it should produces an agent that searches for almost everything. OpenAI's skill-eval post includes should_trigger=false negative controls. Anthropic's skill-creator asks for near-miss should-not-trigger queries. For OutcomeBound this means scenarios where a mechanism (spec, failing test first, review) should not be used, which is the overengineering side.

claim: Calibrate LLM judges against human experts, give each judge a structured rubric for a single dimension, and give it an explicit 'Unknown' answer so it does not hallucinate a verdict.
quote: LLM-as-judge graders should be closely calibrated with human experts to gain confidence that there is little divergence between the human grading and model grading. To avoid hallucinations, give the LLM a way out
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: The article's example of a way out is an instruction to return 'Unknown' when information is insufficient. The other labs agree: OpenAI ('Maintain agreement: Use human feedback to calibrate automated scoring') and Google Cloud (align the judge to human output before deployment). Eugene Yan (Nov 2025) recommends one evaluator per dimension and warns against a single 'God Evaluator'.

claim: Validate a judge against human labels on a held-out test split, and report its true positive rate and true negative rate separately rather than raw agreement.
quote: Raw agreement can be misleading when classes are imbalanced. Treat the human labels as ground truth and report the judge’s True Positive Rate and True Negative Rate separately.
source: Using LLM-as-a-Judge For Evaluation: A Complete Guide
detail: Page modified 2026-09-01. The 2026 FAQ adds: label 100–200 examples per failure mode; split them roughly 10–20% train, 40–45% dev, 40–45% test, with 30–50 Pass and 30–50 Fail in each of dev and test. It also warns that tuning the judge prompt on dev results overfits even when dev examples never enter the prompt. Eugene Yan (Nov 2025) uses precision, recall and Cohen's kappa and notes 'The benchmark is human performance, not perfection.'

claim: Label and judge with binary pass/fail instead of 1–5 Likert scores. Adjacent Likert points are subjective and inconsistent across annotators, detecting statistical differences needs larger samples, and annotators drift to middle values. To track gradual progress, use separate binary checks on sub-components. The cited FAQ does not recommend pairwise win/lose judgments, so that part is not supported here. The FAQ page is dated 2026-09-18, but this question was first published 2025-05-29.
quote: Binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling. Likert scales introduce significant challenges: the difference between adjacent points (like 3 vs 4) is subjective and inconsistent across annotators
source: AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know (Evals FAQ)
original_claim: Label and judge with binary pass/fail, or pairwise win/lose, instead of 1–5 Likert scores, which are inconsistent between annotators and need larger samples to detect differences.
detail: The same answer adds that Likert differences need larger samples to reach statistical significance. OpenAI agrees: judges should do 'pairwise comparisons, classification, or scoring against specific criteria instead of open-ended generation'. So does Eugene Yan: 'Focus on binary pass/fail or win/lose labels'. Tension: Anthropic's agent guidance recommends partial credit for multi-component tasks, and its older Claude docs still show Likert LLM-grading examples. One reconciliation is binary checks per component, aggregated into partial credit.

claim: Counter LLM-judge position bias by randomizing or swapping the order of the options, and watch for self-preference, where a judge favors outputs from its own model family.
quote: Positional bias: LLMs usually prefer the first answer, so you can’t naively give them options and ask them to rank them, but you also have to mix up the order in which they appear.
source: Benchmarks 201: Why Leaderboards > Arenas >> LLM-as-Judge (Latent Space, with Clémentine Fourrier)
detail: The same piece reports self-preference: a judge 'will also prefer models from its own family'. Eugene Yan (Nov 2025) runs every pairwise judgment twice with the order swapped and records a tie when the verdict flips. Contested: Hamel's FAQ says using the same model as judge 'is usually fine' because what matters is measured alignment with humans. This bears on OutcomeBound's cross-family setup, where codex judges claude transcripts: validate the judge's alignment rather than assuming the family choice removes bias.

claim: Give LLM judges an expert-written reference answer. Without one, judges agree with experts only on items they could have solved themselves.
quote: when not provided with a correct reference, judges show high agreement with human experts only on questions the judges were able to correctly answer themselves. We demonstrate that providing the judges with expert-written references largely mitigates this issue
source: No Free Labels: Limitations of LLM-as-a-Judge Without Human Grounding
detail: Based on 1,200 expert-graded responses (BFF-Bench and an MT-Bench subset). This matches Anthropic's requirement that every task have a reference solution. For hard agent scenarios, where headroom tasks sit exactly, the judge rubric should include the expected outcome, not only the criteria.

claim: Read transcripts and grades from many trials. It is the only way to know whether graders measure what matters and whether failures are real or artifacts of the eval.
quote: You won't know if your graders are working well unless you read the transcripts and grades from many trials.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Hamel's FAQ: 'Error analysis is the most important activity in evals'. Review at least 100 traces, annotating the first 30 yourself before letting an agent suggest failures, and continue until 'theoretical saturation'. Anthropic's tool-writing post (2025-09-11) also says to review raw transcripts including tool calls. For an instruction-file audit, the failure taxonomy should come from reading real adopter transcripts, not from imagined rules.

claim: Contested: whether to write evaluators before building features (eval-driven development). Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar say 'Generally no': start with error analysis, and write evaluators only up front for specific constraints where success is exactly known, such as 'never mention competitors'. Anthropic's January 2026 evals article calls its roadmap 'eval-driven agent development'. The cited page does not show that OpenAI or Eugene Yan endorse the practice. The page's published date is 2025-07-27, not 2026-09-18.
quote: Generally no. Eval-driven development (writing evaluators before implementing features) sounds appealing but creates more problems than it solves. Unlike traditional software where failure modes are predictable, LLMs have infinite surface area for potential failures.
source: Q: Should I practice eval-driven development? (Evals FAQ)
original_claim: Contested: whether to write evaluators before building features (eval-driven development). Hamel Husain advises against it except for known constraints and prefers error analysis first. Anthropic, OpenAI and Eugene Yan endorse it.
detail: Hamel's exception: a constraint where success is exactly known (e.g. 'never mention competitors') can get an evaluator early. The other side: Anthropic (Jan 2026) 'Build evals to define planned capabilities before agents can fulfill them', OpenAI 'Adopt eval-driven development: Evaluate early and often', and Eugene Yan (Apr 2025) 'Eval-driven development (EDD) helps us build better AI products.' Shankar's 'criteria drift' (arXiv 2404.12272) supports Hamel: 'users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria.' Possible reconciliation for OutcomeBound: write evals up front for the bounds and guardrails the kernel names, and find quality failures by error analysis.

claim: When comparing two prompt or model variants on the same tasks, analyze paired per-task differences with standard errors, not two independent means. Pairing removes task-difficulty variance at no extra cost.
quote: Since the question list is shared across models, conducting a paired-differences test lets us eliminate the variance in question difficulty and focus on the variance in responses.
source: A statistical approach to model evaluations
detail: Other recommendations in the post: report the SEM with every score, cluster standard errors on the unit of randomization (e.g. tasks from the same repo), and resample several answers per question, averaging per question. Frontier models' per-question scores correlate at 0.3–0.7, which makes pairing 'a “free” variance reduction technique'. Eugene Yan's Nov 2025 guide still links this 'deep dive'.

claim: Before running an A/B comparison, do a power analysis: choose the smallest effect worth detecting and compute how many tasks you need, because small evals only register large differences.
quote: If an eval doesn’t have very many questions, confidence intervals associated with any statistical tests will tend to be wide. This means that models will need to have a large underlying difference in capabilities
source: A statistical approach to model evaluations
detail: The post shows how to 'formulate a hypothesis (such as Model A outperforms Model B by 3 percentage points)' and compute the required number of questions. A 2026 context-file ablation (arXiv 2607.27250) reports that detecting a 10pp effect at 80% power needed about 120–200 tasks. Its 3-repeat design caught even large effects only part of the time. So a 20-task instruction A/B can only rule on large effects.

claim: Screen candidate scenarios for each agent to find the borderline band, where the agent sometimes passes and sometimes fails. Tasks at the floor or ceiling cannot show any effect of an instruction change.
quote: The “borderline is agent-specific” finding explains prior contradictions and implies that future ablation studies must screen tasks per-agent to achieve informative dynamic range.
source: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
detail: The authors ran a screening sweep over 84 candidate tasks 'to avoid a floor/ceiling design—where every task is too easy or too hard for any manipulation to register'. Task difficulty correlated only about 0.75 (Spearman) between Claude Code and Codex, so a borderline set calibrated on one agent is mostly floor/ceiling for the other. DeltaSelect (arXiv 2609.19607, Sep 2026) takes a similar approach: keep only the tasks whose single-run results track the full benchmark (22 of 113 in DeepSWE), 'intended for repeated baseline-versus-candidate comparisons during development, not model rankings.' This is the most direct method for building scenarios with headroom.

claim: To gain statistical power for comparing strategies, add more distinct tasks rather than more repeats per task, because variance between tasks dominates.
quote: Task-level variance dominates: scaling requires more tasks, not more repeats.
source: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
detail: This is a Monte Carlo power analysis over 288 runs (tasks × 3 strategies × 3 repeats). It is in tension with the common advice to run more trials (Anthropic's resampling recommendation, skill-creator's 3 runs per query). Repeats reduce within-task noise and are needed for pass^k, but they add little power for a between-strategy comparison once the task set is the bottleneck.

claim: Hold infrastructure constant across compared runs and document it. Treat small score gaps as noise until the configuration matches, because resource settings alone move agentic coding scores by several points.
quote: leaderboard differences below 3 percentage points deserve skepticism until the eval configuration is documented and matched.
source: Quantifying infrastructure noise in agentic coding evals
detail: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, the gap between the most- and least-resourced setups was 6pp (p<0.01). Recommendations: specify guaranteed allocation and kill threshold separately for each task, run 'at multiple times and on multiple days', and expect pass rates to vary with time of day. Epoch AI (2025-12-23) adds that switching scaffold alone moved SWE-bench Verified by up to 11% for GPT-5. So an instruction A/B must run both arms in the same harness adopters use, interleaved in time.

claim: One audit tested 3 tool-calling endpoints on the BFCL function-calling benchmark at temperature 0, where reruns were nearly deterministic. There, semantics-preserving prompt rewordings produced median paired SDs 11x to 58x larger than reruns. So measure how sensitive results are to wording before crediting an instruction change. The measured effect is specific to BFCL tool-calling and was not tested on coding agents or on instruction-file changes.
quote: Semantics-preserving prompt perturbations create the larger floor on all endpoints, with median perturbation paired SDs 11x to 58x larger than rerun paired SDs.
source: Noise Floor Audit for Agent Benchmarks
original_claim: Measure how sensitive results are to wording before crediting an instruction change. Semantics-preserving rewordings can move scores far more than simple reruns.
detail: Measured on BFCL tool calling at temperature 0, not on long-horizon coding agents, so the multipliers may not transfer. In an agent setting, Vercel (Jan 2026) found 'Same skill. Same docs. Different outcomes based on subtle wording changes.' Practical consequence: when a prompt change 'wins', check whether a paraphrase of the old prompt wins by the same margin.

claim: Harden an instruction eval before trusting it: remove test leakage and contradictions, assert on observable behavior rather than implementation details, and target knowledge absent from training data so a baseline has room to improve.
quote: We hardened the eval suite by removing test leakage, resolving contradictions, and shifting to behavior-based assertions. Most importantly, we added tests targeting Next.js 16 APIs that aren't in model training data.
source: AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals
detail: Results on the hardened suite: baseline 53%, skill 53% (the skill was never invoked in 56% of cases), skill plus explicit invocation instruction 79%, compressed docs index in AGENTS.md 100%. The authors say configurations were run 'with retries to rule out model variance' but report no N or intervals, so treat the numbers as indicative. The initial suite had 'tests that validated implementation details rather than observable behavior'.

claim: Contested: whether repository instruction files improve coding-agent outcomes. Rigorously evaluate any instruction-file change against a no-file baseline, including its token cost, before deploying it.
quote: We conclude that while context files are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices, any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
by: ETH Zurich SRI Lab (Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev)
detail: Main result: context files 'do not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average'. Instructions are followed, but repository overviews do not help (v2 2026-06-23). Other studies disagree. Vercel reports 53%→100%. A two-agent ablation (Jul 2026) bounds the effect to ≤10–15pp. Probe-and-refine (arXiv 2606.20512, Jun 2026) reports 33.0% vs 25.5% unguided (p<0.001, 4 trials) and argues 'how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable'. Latent Space AINews (2026-03-05) cites SWE-Atlas: harness choice was 'essentially noise within the margin of error'. The disagreement is itself the lesson: the effect depends on content, task headroom and agent, so it has to be measured each time.

claim: Benchmark an instruction or skill change against a baseline run in the same batch: no skill for a new skill, a snapshot of the old version for an edit. Aggregate mean ± stddev and flag assertions that do not discriminate between the two.
quote: For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later.
source: skill-creator SKILL.md (anthropics/skills)
detail: The benchmark aggregates pass rate, time and tokens as mean ± stddev with a delta. The analyzer (agents/analyzer.md) flags an assertion that 'always pass[es] in both configurations? (may not differentiate skill value)', one that always fails in both (possibly broken), and 'highly variable' evals (flaky). Description optimization splits queries 60/40 train/test, runs each query 3 times, and selects 'by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting'. Anthropic's tool-writing post (2025-09-11) also uses 'held-out test sets to ensure we did not overfit'.

claim: DATE WRONG: the cited page was published 2025-06-29 (modified 2026-09-01), not 2026-09-18. The practice and quote are supported. The source calls CI datasets 'small (in many cases 100+ examples)' and says to add examples of new production failure patterns to the CI dataset.
quote: Since CI tests are run frequently, the cost of each test has to be carefully considered (that’s why you carefully curate the dataset). Favor assertions or other deterministic checks over LLM-as-judge evaluators.
source: Q: How are evaluations used differently in CI/CD vs. monitoring production? (Evals FAQ)
original_claim: Keep the per-change regression suite small, curated and cheap. Prefer deterministic assertions over LLM judges there, and add every new production failure to it.
detail: CI sets cover core features, regression tests for past bugs and known edge cases. Production monitoring samples live traces, runs reference-free judges asynchronously and tracks confidence intervals, and new failure patterns found there go back into CI. OpenAI similarly advises continuous evaluation 'to run evals on every change'. This fits OutcomeBound's policy of deterministic support: code checks gate, and judges advise.

claim: For each instruction change, write a targeted eval that checks that only the intended behavior changed, rerun the full suite before merging, and set explicit per-eval failure budgets.
quote: Write a targeted eval alongside every instruction change that asks not just "does this work" but "did only this change."
source: CI/CD for Context in Agentic Coding: Same Pipeline, Different Rules
detail: Same post: 'When you make a context change, rerun your full eval suite before merging. Unexpected failures elsewhere are the signal.' On non-determinism: 'Run the same eval twice and you can get different results with nothing changed'. The recommended model is 'error budgets, not pass/fail', with budgets set per eval type because 'it's a product call, not a technical one'. Schedule evals independent of commits when agent versions or external context change.

claim: Do not treat a passing test suite as the outcome. Add reviewer-style quality judgments, and calibrate reviewer noise against a golden baseline of known-good human changes.
quote: roughly half of test-passing SWE-bench Verified PRs written by mid-2024 to mid/late-2025 agents would not be merged into main by repo maintainers, even after adjusting for noise in maintainer merge decisions.
source: Many SWE-bench-Passing PRs Would Not Be Merged into Main
detail: Maintainers accepted only 68% of the original merged human patches, so scores are reported as a percentage of that golden baseline. Maintainer merge decisions ran about 24pp below the automated grader. Rejection reasons were core functionality failure, breaking other code, and code quality. Related: Anthropic says Claude Code added evals for 'over-engineering', and Cognition's FrontierCode (Latent Space AINews, 2026-06-09) grades scope, cleanliness and regression safety. OutcomeBound's over- and under-engineering axis needs graders beyond test pass.

claim: Measure guardrail instructions on scenarios built to expose the targeted behavior, such as tasks whose spec conflicts with their tests so that any pass is a cheat. Standard success benchmarks can show no difference between prompts that differ sharply on these.
quote: While these prompts do not produce statistically significant performance difference on the original benchmarks, we find they lead to significantly different cheating propensity on Conflicting-LiveCodeBench
source: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
detail: The cheating rate is the pass rate on the impossible variants. Hiding tests 'reduces cheating success rate to near zero' but hurts normal performance. Read-only tests are a middle ground. Multiple submissions raised cheating on Conflicting-SWEbench from 33% to 38%. An instructed abort option (submit flag_for_human_intervention) was 'quite effective for OpenAI models' and 'much less pronounced for Claude Opus 4.1'. This is a direct template for testing OutcomeBound's 'report UNVERIFIED / stop before crossing an edge' wording.

claim: Anecdote: in a May 2025 Latent Space interview, the Claude Code team (Boris Cherny) said they chose agentic search over RAG mostly on internal 'vibes', with 'some internal benchmarks also', because it outperformed 'by a lot'. The interview covers this one decision, not large-effect design decisions in general. It does not say the team later added targeted evals as the product scaled, and it never uses the word dogfooding.
quote: This was just vibes, so internal vibes. There's some internal benchmarks also, but mostly vibes. It just felt better.
source: Claude Code: Anthropic's Agent in Your Terminal (Latent Space podcast)
by: Latent Space (Boris Cherny, Cat Wu of Anthropic)
original_claim: Contested: making large-effect design decisions by intensive dogfooding and internal 'vibes' rather than formal evals. The Claude Code team did this early, then added targeted evals as the product scaled.
detail: Boris Cherny was explaining the choice of agentic search over RAG. Anthropic's Jan 2026 evals post places this in time: 'Claude Code started with fast iteration based on feedback from Anthropic employees and external users. Later, we added evals—first for narrow areas like concision and file edits, and then for more complex behaviors like over-engineering.' It warns that building without evals breaks down when 'users report the agent feels worse after changes'. OpenAI lists 'Vibe-based evals' as an anti-pattern. The positions fit together: vibes work while effects are large, and evals are needed once changes are subtle or regressions are costly.

claim: Outdated: tracking frontier coding progress on a saturated, contaminated benchmark. Audit test suites for tests that are too narrow (reject correct solutions) or too wide (require unstated features), and prefer held-out, uncontaminated tasks.
quote: Progress has kind of stalled. And basically we realized that this is because the eval is effectively saturated and also highly contaminated.
source: The End of SWE-Bench Verified — Mia Glaese & Olivia Watkins, OpenAI Frontier Evals & Human Data (Latent Space)
detail: From the episode write-up: '49 tests were too narrowly defined (so that they also reject functionally correct submissions) and 26 tests were “too wide” - looking for extra features that were never mentioned in the problem description'. All frontier models could reproduce gold patches from the task ID alone. OpenAI now reports SWE-bench Pro. Its own post (openai.com) could not be fetched. Lesson for a scenario corpus: public, memorizable tasks lose their headroom, and over-specified tests measure guessing, not capability.

claim: When documentation fails to hold a rule, promote the rule into code (custom linters, structural tests): enforce invariants centrally and leave the agent free in how it meets them.
quote: Human taste is fed back into the system continuously. Review comments, refactoring pull requests, and user-facing bugs are captured as documentation updates or encoded directly into tooling. When documentation falls short, we promote the rule into code
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
detail: Same post: 'By enforcing invariants, not micromanaging implementations, we let agents ship fast' and 'enforce boundaries centrally, allow autonomy locally.' When the agent struggles, the question was 'what capability is missing, and how do we make it both legible and enforceable for the agent?', never 'try harder.' Mitchell Hashimoto's origin post (mitchellh.com, 2026-02-05) says the same thing: each agent mistake becomes either an AGENTS.md line or a 'programmed tool', and he wants 'fast, high quality tools to automatically tell it when it is wrong.' Caveat from the post: the setup is greenfield and 'should not be assumed to generalize without similar investment.'

claim: Write the error messages of your custom checks for the agent: a failing lint should say how to fix the problem, not only what is wrong.
quote: Because the lints are custom, we write the error messages to inject remediation instructions into agent context.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
detail: Böckeler (martinfowler.com, 2026-04-02) independently calls this 'custom linter messages that include instructions for the self-correction - a positive kind of prompt injection.' In the Latent Space interview (2026-04-07), Lopopolo adds that 'we add links where the error messages tell how to do the right thing' so that non-functional requirements reach the agent at the moment it fails.

claim: Keep the always-loaded instruction file a short map (about 100 lines) that points to a structured docs tree, and check that knowledge base mechanically in CI (freshness, cross-links, structure) instead of maintaining one large manual.
quote: It’s hard to verify. A single blob doesn’t lend itself to mechanical checks (coverage, freshness, ownership, cross-links), so drift is inevitable.
source: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
detail: The discouraged practice is the 'one big AGENTS.md'. It failed in four ways: context crowding, 'Too much guidance becomes non-guidance', instant rot, and being unverifiable. The replacement is a short AGENTS.md as the table of contents plus 'Dedicated linters and CI jobs validate that the knowledge base is up to date, cross-linked, and structured correctly', and a recurring doc-gardening agent opens fix-up PRs. This bears directly on auditing instruction files: the file's structure should itself be checkable.

claim: Build guardrails from what the model already produces and was trained on (code, tests, lints). Avoid separate scaffolds that restrict its output; those tend to be thrown away as models improve.
quote: If we were building an entire separate rust scaffold around Codex to restrict its output, that I think would be like additional harness that would be prone to being scrapped.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires (Latent Space podcast, Ryan Lopopolo)
by: Latent Space (swyx, Vibhu) with Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI
detail: swyx summarises this as an 'on policy harness, which is already within distribution'. Lopopolo says the team's guardrails 'actively degrade' nothing, because 'really all they're doing is running tests'. In the same episode he says reasoning models let 'the harness be the whole box' with options to choose from, where older models had to be put in 'boxes with a predefined set of state transitions.' Other practices from the episode: keep the inner build loop under one minute, and treat a slow build as a signal to decompose.

claim: Make command output quiet on success and short on failure (only the failing tests, only a formatted-or-not verdict). Wrap noisy tools so the agent never reads walls of passing output.
quote: You’re gonna want to patch dash silent to prettier because the agent doesn’t care that every file was already formatted.
source: Extreme Harness Engineering for Token Billionaires (Latent Space podcast, Ryan Lopopolo)
by: Latent Space with Ryan Lopopolo, OpenAI
detail: Same segment ('Agent Friendly CLI Output'): recursive pnpm output 'produces a absolute mountain of text' that is all for passing suites, so they wrapped it in a script that emits only the failing parts. CLIs are called 'super token efficient' and 'can be made more token efficient really easily'. Policy can be as simple as giving the agent the gh CLI 'with some text that say CI has to pass.'

claim: Pair feedforward guides with feedback sensors. Computational sensors are cheap and fast enough to run on every change. Spread the costlier inferential sensors across the change lifecycle by cost, speed and criticality: a basic code-review agent can still run before commit, and broader LLM review or mutation testing runs post-integration. Böckeler says LLM semantic checks are 'not on every commit', not that they belong only late in the lifecycle. This is one practitioner's article (Birgitta Böckeler on martinfowler.com), not a measured consensus.
quote: Computational sensors are cheap and fast enough to run on every change, alongside the agent. Inferential controls are of course more expensive and non-deterministic, but allow us to both provide rich guidance, and add additional semantic judgment.
source: Harness engineering for coding agent users
original_claim: Pair feedforward guides with feedback sensors. Run cheap deterministic (computational) sensors on every change, and save costlier inferential checks (LLM review, judges) for later in the lifecycle.
detail: Either half alone fails: 'you get either an agent that keeps repeating the same mistakes (feedback-only) or an agent that encodes rules but never finds out whether they worked (feed-forward-only).' 'Keep quality left': fast checks run before commit, and expensive ones (mutation testing, broad review) run after integration. Continuous drift sensors run outside the change lifecycle. The article's examples put AGENTS.md and skills in the inferential feedforward row and structural tests in the computational feedback row. It also lists open questions: harness coherence, and whether silent sensors mean quality or blind spots.

claim: State the outcome clearly. No sensor can establish correctness against an intent that was never specified, and the highest-impact failures (misdiagnosis, overengineering, misread instructions) slip past both deterministic and LLM checks.
quote: Correctness is outside any sensor's remit if the human didn't clearly specify what they wanted in the first place.
source: Harness engineering for coding agent users
detail: Computational sensors reliably catch structural issues: duplication, complexity, coverage, architectural drift, style. 'Neither catches reliably some of the higher-impact problems: Misdiagnosis of issues, overengineering and unnecessary features, misunderstood instructions.' The behaviour harness (functional correctness) is 'the elephant in the room', and trusting AI-written tests is 'not good enough yet.' Conclusion: 'A good harness should not necessarily aim to fully eliminate human input, but to direct it to where our input is most important.'

claim: Give the agent a check it can run that returns pass or fail, choose how hard that check gates completion (in the prompt, a goal, a Stop-hook gate, or an independent reviewer), and ask for evidence rather than a claim of success.
quote: Claude stops when the work looks done. Without a check it can run, "looks done" is the only signal available, and you become the verification loop: every mistake waits for you to notice it.
source: Best practices for Claude Code
detail: The escalation ladder is: in one prompt; across a session with a /goal condition checked by a separate evaluator; 'As a deterministic gate: a Stop hook runs your check as a script and blocks the turn from ending until it passes' (overridden after 8 consecutive blocks); and a second-opinion verification subagent. 'Each step trades setup for attention.' Also: 'Have Claude show evidence rather than asserting success.' On adversarial review, the page warns that a reviewer asked to find gaps will find some, and chasing every one 'leads to over-engineering'.

claim: Claude Code guidance: use hooks for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions, because CLAUDE.md instructions are advisory while hooks are deterministic. Prune CLAUDE.md ruthlessly: if Claude already does something correctly without an instruction, delete the instruction or convert it to a hook. The source covers actions a hook can run in Claude Code, not every instruction, and it does not address AGENTS.md.
quote: Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.
source: Best practices for Claude Code
original_claim: Move any instruction that must hold every time out of CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md and into a hook. Prune any prose line the model already follows without being told.
detail: Pruning test: 'Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' Fix for an over-specified file: 'If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it or convert it to a hook.' The exclude list includes 'Anything Claude can figure out by reading code' and 'Self-evident practices'. The hooks guide adds that hooks give 'deterministic control: certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them.' HumanLayer (2025-11-25) agrees: 'Never send an LLM to do a linter's job' and put the formatter and linter in a Stop hook.

claim: In Claude Code auto mode, the permission classifier treats boundaries you state in conversation as a block signal. It does not store them as rules. It re-reads them from the transcript on each check, so a boundary can be lost if context compaction removes the message that stated it. For a hard guarantee, add a deny rule. The source is about conversational boundaries under the auto-mode classifier, not about prose instruction files in general.
quote: Boundaries are not stored as rules. The classifier re-reads them from the transcript on each check, so a boundary can be lost if context compaction removes the message that stated it. For a hard guarantee, add a deny rule instead.
source: Permission modes (Claude Code docs)
original_claim: Put hard boundaries in permission rules (deny/ask), not in conversation or prose. A boundary stated in text is re-read from the transcript each time and can disappear when context is compacted.
detail: Auto mode has been the default for Pro/Max/Team since 2026-08-14. The Claude blog (2026-08-07) justifies it with 'users approve 97% of permission prompts', i.e. reflexive clicking, and still recommends reviewing high-stakes production changes yourself. A practitioner summary (beri.net, 2026-08-10) uses the headline 'Prompts Aren't Policy' and quotes managed permissions.deny as the only setting that 'can't be overridden'. Hence the split: what the agent must never do goes in deterministic permission settings; what it should aim for goes in prose.

claim: Anthropic's auto-mode classifier is deliberately conservative. The prompt establishes what is authorized, and everything the agent chooses on its own is unauthorized until the user says otherwise. The past incidents Anthropic cites from its internal log (deleted remote branches, an uploaded auth token, an attempted production migration) all came from overeager initiative. Anthropic does not currently see misalignment in practice. So it tuned the classifier to overeager behavior and honest mistakes, but it also names prompt injection and misalignment as threats. The post does not call overeagerness the dominant real-world failure.
quote: The classifier is deliberately conservative. The prompt establishes what is authorized; everything the agent chooses on its own is unauthorized until the user says otherwise.
source: How we built Claude Code auto mode: a safer way to skip permissions
original_claim: Read authorization narrowly: any action the agent picks on its own initiative, beyond what the user named, counts as unauthorized. Overeager initiative, not malice, is the dominant real-world failure a guardrail has to catch.
detail: Incident-log examples include scope escalation ('clean up old branches' leading to a remote delete), credential exploration, agent-inferred targets, sharing via an external service, and a safety-check bypass (retrying with a skip-verification flag). Design choices: the gate judges actions, not the agent's prose ('We strip assistant text so the agent can't talk the classifier into making a bad call'). A denial comes back as a tool result telling the agent to find a safer path, and the run escalates after 3 consecutive or 20 total denials. Honest limit: 17% false negatives on 52 real overeager actions, so it 'is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.' Allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution are dropped on entry.

claim: Define filesystem and network isolation boundaries (both are needed) within which the agent can work freely. In Anthropic's internal usage, sandboxing reduced permission prompts by 84%. It did not remove them: new network domains still prompt the user for confirmation. That reduces approval fatigue rather than making it go away.
quote: In our internal usage, we've found that sandboxing safely reduces permission prompts by 84%. By defining set boundaries within which Claude can work freely, they increase security and agency.
source: Making Claude Code more secure and autonomous with sandboxing
original_claim: Replace per-action approval prompts with predefined isolation boundaries covering both filesystem and network, so the agent can act freely inside them and approval fatigue goes away.
detail: 'effective sandboxing requires both filesystem and network isolation.' The web sandbox keeps credentials outside it and pushes through a scoped proxy that only allows the configured branch. Stripe (stripe.dev, 2026-02-19) runs agents with full permissions and no confirmation prompts because each runs in a quarantined devbox with no production access. Simon Willison (2025-09-30) adds scoping credentials to test/staging with 'a tight budget limit.'

claim: Design tool responses for the agent: actionable error messages instead of opaque codes, truncation that tells the agent how to narrow its request, sensible pagination and filter defaults, and a concise/detailed verbosity switch.
quote: if a tool call raises an error (for example, during input validation), you can prompt-engineer your error responses to clearly communicate specific and actionable improvements, rather than opaque error codes or tracebacks.
source: Writing effective tools for AI agents—using AI agents
detail: Claude Code caps tool responses at 25,000 tokens by default, and 'We expect the effective context length of agents to grow over time, but the need for context-efficient tools to remain.' The post recommends semantic identifiers over UUIDs (these 'significantly' improved retrieval precision), fewer tools consolidated around workflows ('More tools don't always lead to better outcomes'), and 'enforcing with strict data models' for inputs. Tool quality should be judged by held-out evals, avoiding verifiers so strict that they reject correct responses.

claim: Grade agents on the outcome they produce, not on whether they followed a prescribed path, and prefer deterministic graders where they can decide.
quote: So as not to unnecessarily punish creativity, it’s often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took.
source: Demystifying evals for AI agents
detail: Checking exact tool-call sequences was 'too rigid and results in overly brittle tests, as agents regularly find valid approaches that eval designers didn't anticipate.' Their recommendation is 'choosing deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary or for additional flexibility, and using human graders judiciously.' Code-based graders are fast, cheap, objective and reproducible but brittle to valid variation. Also: build in partial credit. Rigid grading can make a capable model look broken: Opus 4.5 went from 42% to 95% on CORE-Bench once grading bugs were fixed and the scaffold was loosened.

claim: Treat every harness component as an assumption about what the model cannot yet do. Stress-test those assumptions one component at a time and remove the ones that stop carrying weight when a new model ships.
quote: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be incorrect, and because they can quickly go stale as models improve.
source: Harness design for long-running application development
detail: Observed obsolescence: context resets were essential on Sonnet 4.5 ('context anxiety'), but 'Opus 4.5 largely removed that behavior on its own, so I was able to drop context resets'. With Opus 4.6 the sprint decomposition was also removed. Radical cuts failed; removing one component at a time worked. The separate skeptical evaluator held its value: 'tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical turns out to be far more tractable than making a generator critical of its own work.' But 'the evaluator is not a fixed yes-or-no decision. It is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo.' The planner was told to constrain deliverables rather than implementation, 'let them figure out the path'.

claim: For Claude Opus 5 specifically (Anthropic's prompting guide for that model): remove explicit verification and re-check instructions, and legacy harness scaffolding that adds separate verification steps. Opus 5 verifies its own work without being told, and such instructions cause over-verification that wastes tokens with no loss in quality when removed. This is guidance for one model, not for frontier models in general.
quote: If your prompt contains explicit verification instructions ("include a final verification step for any non-trivial task," "use a subagent to verify"), remove them: instructions like these cause over-verification on Claude Opus 5
source: Prompting Claude Opus 5
original_claim: For the newest frontier models, remove prose instructions to verify or re-check and any legacy scaffolding that adds separate verification steps, because the model now verifies on its own and extra instructions cause over-verification.
detail: The page continues: 'The same applies to legacy harness scaffolding that adds separate verification steps.' It also says to avoid 're-verify before responding'-style instructions, and to set 'deterministic caps on how many agents can be launched' (environment variables and a budget option) instead of relying only on prose. The general best-practices page says the same about self-check prompts, which help older models but cause over-verification on Opus 5. Tension with the measured finding below (progress mirage): what becomes outdated is prose telling the model to self-verify, not out-of-band deterministic checks, which that research calls structurally necessary.

claim: When output must follow a schema, enforce it with constrained decoding (structured outputs or strict tool use) rather than prompt wording.
quote: Without structured outputs, Claude can generate malformed JSON responses or invalid tool inputs that break your applications.
source: Structured outputs (Claude API docs)
detail: 'Structured outputs guarantee schema-compliant responses through constrained decoding' ('Always valid', 'No retries needed for schema violations'), and strict tool use guarantees schema validation of tool names and inputs. A nuance from the prompting best-practices migration note: 'newer models can reliably match complex schemas when told to, especially if implemented with retries.' So prompting plus a validator is the fallback, and the constraint is the guarantee.

claim: Run agents inside a code-defined workflow ('blueprint') that mixes deterministic nodes (run linters, push branch) with open agent nodes (implement, fix CI), and bound the costly loops, for example to one or two CI rounds before handing back to a human.
quote: writing code to deterministically accomplish small decisions we can anticipate—such as “always lint changes at the end of a run”—saves tokens (and CI costs) at scale and gives the agent a little less opportunity to get things wrong.
source: Minions: Stripe’s one-shot, end-to-end coding agents—Part 2
detail: Scale: more than 1,300 merged PRs a week with no human-written code (all human-reviewed). 'putting LLMs into contained boxes' compounds into system-wide reliability. They shift feedback left by looping on a deterministic lint node locally before pushing, then allow one CI round with autofix and one more agent attempt, citing 'diminishing marginal returns if an LLM is running against indefinitely many rounds of a full CI loop.' Rule files are scoped to subdirectories rather than global, and each agent gets a curated 'smaller box' of tools.

claim: Split the work: the instruction file gives the why and examples and maps each guideline to a lint RuleID, while the linter supplies the how and the guarantee. 'Lint green' then becomes the definition of done.
quote: AGENTS.md = the “why” and the examples. It maps each guideline to a RuleID and links to rule docs/ADRs. Linting = the “how” and the guarantee.
source: Using Linters to Direct Agents
detail: Named failure modes of prose-only guidance: 'Ambiguity' (agents think they complied when they did not), 'No guarantees: advice does not cause builds to fail', and 'Limited reach: prose can’t verify cross‑file imports, architectural boundaries, or error semantics.' The lint cycle: observe drift, have an LLM draft the rule, surface violations, remediate with agents, then put the rule on the hot path (pre-commit, CI, agent toolchain) with time-boxed waivers.

claim: Design CLIs agent-first: machine-readable output, runtime schema introspection instead of docs pasted into prompts, field masks to protect context, input validation that treats agent input as adversarial, and --dry-run before mutations.
quote: Agents don’t need GUIs. They need deterministic, machine-readable output, self-describing schemas they can introspect at runtime, and safety rails against their own hallucinations.
source: You Need to Rewrite Your CLI for AI Agents
detail: 'Human DX optimizes for discoverability and forgiveness. Agent DX optimizes for predictability and defense-in-depth.' Static API docs in a system prompt are 'expensive in tokens and goes stale'; make 'the CLI itself the documentation'. Validate against agent-typical errors: path traversal, embedded query parameters, double-encoding, control characters. Ship skill files for the invariants that --help cannot convey. Suggested order: --output json, input validation, schema/--describe, --fields, --dry-run, context/skill files, MCP. Armin Ronacher (2025-06-12) makes the same point: 'Tools need to be protected against an LLM chaos monkey using them completely wrong.'

claim: Reduce the problem to a clear goal plus tools that can iterate toward it, and let the agent brute-force the solution in a loop. The approach suits problems with clear success criteria, and a cleanly passing test suite amplifies it.
quote: If you can reduce your problem to a clear goal and a set of tools that can iterate towards that goal a coding agent can often brute force its way to an effective solution.
source: Designing agentic loops
detail: 'The value you can get from coding agents and other LLM coding tools is massively amplified by a good, cleanly passing test suite.' Unattended ('YOLO') mode is 'so dangerous' yet 'key to getting the most productive results', so pair it with a sandbox that limits files, secrets and network, plus credentials scoped to test/staging with tight budget limits. Suited to 'Problems with clear success criteria where finding a good solution is likely to involve (potentially slightly tedious) trial and error.'

claim: LangChain wrapped its deepagents-cli loop in deterministic middleware for Terminal Bench 2.0 with gpt-5.2-codex. A PreCompletionChecklistMiddleware intercepts the agent before it exits and reminds it (it does not force it) to run a verification pass against the task spec. A LocalContextMiddleware injects directory and tool context at start. A LoopDetectionMiddleware adds a 'reconsider your approach' nudge after N edits to the same file. The measured 13.7-point gain (52.8 to 66.5) is for all harness changes together, including prompting and the reasoning budget; no single middleware's contribution was isolated. The authors expect such guardrails to become unnecessary as models improve.
quote: We use a PreCompletionChecklistMiddleware that intercepts the agent before it exits and reminds it to run a verification pass against the Task spec.
source: Improving Deep Agents with harness engineering
original_claim: Use deterministic middleware or hooks around the loop: intercept completion to force a verification pass against the task spec, inject environment context at start, and detect doom loops. These can be retired as models improve.
detail: Changing only the harness (fixed gpt-5.2-codex) raised Terminal Bench 2.0 from 52.8 to 66.5. The most common failure: the agent 'wrote a solution, re-read its own code, confirmed it looks ok, and stopped.' LoopDetectionMiddleware adds a nudge after N edits to the same file. The authors flag these as temporary: 'As models improve, these guardrails will likely be unnecessary.' They also say 'Tailor Harnesses to Models': the same harness scored lower with Opus 4.6 because it had not been tuned for that model.

claim: Vercel's d0 text-to-SQL agent on Claude Opus 4.5 dropped its specialized tools and its heavy constraining prompt engineering in favour of a single bash tool with direct access to its semantic-layer files. On 5 representative queries it went from 4/5 to 5/5 success, 3.5x faster and with 37% fewer tokens. This is one team's agent and a 5-query benchmark, not a general measurement across strong models. It worked only because the underlying files were already legible documentation.
quote: We were constraining reasoning because we didn’t trust the model to reason. With Opus 4.5, that constraint became a liability. The model makes better choices when we stop making choices for it.
source: We removed 80% of our agent’s tools
original_claim: With strong current models, remove specialized tools and 'guardrail' prompting that pre-chew the model's reasoning, and give it direct access to well-documented sources with general tools (bash, grep). This only works if the underlying material is itself legible.
detail: The text-to-SQL agent went from 80% to 100% success, 3.5x faster, with 37% fewer tokens and 42% fewer steps, after replacing specialized tools (schema lookup, query validation, error recovery) and heavy prompt constraints with a filesystem agent. Precondition: 'This only worked because our semantic layer was already good documentation.' What became outdated is deterministic support that does the model's thinking for it, not support that verifies its result.

claim: Contested: how much scaffolding to build around reasoning models. Model labs say the harness should be minimal and that scaffolds can hurt; harness builders report large gains from the harness alone.
quote: And then it turns out we just created reasoning models and they, you don’t need this complex behavior. In fact, in many ways, it makes it worse.
source: [AINews] Is Harness Engineering real?
by: Latent Space (swyx), quoting Noam Brown (OpenAI) and Boris Cherny (Anthropic)
detail: The Big Model side: Boris Cherny calls Claude Code 'the thinnest possible wrapper over the model'; METR reports that Claude Code and Codex don't beat a basic scaffold; Scale's SWE-Atlas finds harness choice within noise. The Big Harness side: Jerry Liu ('The Model Harness is Everything') and a harness-only change that improved 15 LLMs. Latent Space now grants that harness engineering 'has real value.' At AIEWF 2026 (latent.space/p/aiewf26trends), Dex Horthy (HumanLayer) argued that 'the hype is outrunning the discipline' and that control loops worth trusting are 'deterministic loops'. One way to reconcile the two: minimal scaffolding for how the model reasons, deterministic checks for what counts as done.

claim: Put harness investment into what models will not absorb (permissions, identity, trust, legibility, and when to spend human attention), and delete model-facing scaffolding as models absorb it.
quote: What’s left at the end of this deletion and absorption process are the human-centric agent capabilities. Things like permissions, identity, trust and legibility.
source: The Evolution of the Agent Harness
detail: The cycle is 'train -> absorb -> shed -> repeat'. Measure harness progress by 'how much of the harness you get to delete, while retaining the same capability level.' Thariq Shihipar (Anthropic) reportedly deleted 80% of Claude Code's system prompt. 'A model that absorbs permissions into itself has dissolved permissions.' Cited measurement: Harness-Bench runs the same model across harnesses and scores span 52.4 to 76.2. Prediction: an 'attention-interface', a policy surface for when the agent may interrupt and what it may decide alone, will become as standard as AGENTS.md.

claim: For self-improvement loops that evolve their own harness, Lilian Weng argues that the evaluator and permission control should likely sit outside the loop, backed by held-out tests, trace audits and human review at decision points that matter. Her example is a system whose verifier, tracer, runs directory and LLM config are read-only. Her reason: the loop optimizes whatever signal it is given and may overfit to tests or reward-hack a judge. The source is hedged ('should likely', 'may') and scoped to harness self-improvement, and it is one researcher's essay rather than a practitioner consensus.
quote: The evaluator and permission control should likely sit outside the loop that evolves harness, with held-out tests, trace audits, and human review at decision points that matter
source: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
original_claim: Keep the evaluator and permission controls outside anything the agent can modify (read-only verifier and config, held-out tests, trace audits, human review at key decisions), because an optimizing loop will game whatever signal it is given.
detail: Preceding sentence: 'A self-improvement loop optimizes whatever signal it is given. If the reward comes from unit tests, the agent may overfit to tests; if it comes from a judge model, it may learn reward hacking tricks specific to this judge'. Cited design: 'the runs directory, tracer, verifier, and LLM configuration are read-only, which disables a set of reward hacking'. Anthropic's prompting guide warns about the same overfitting at the prompt level: 'Tests are there to verify correctness, not to define the solution.'

claim: Even as prompt tricks lose value, keep specifying goals, constraints, context and evaluation, and keep the harness interface to tools and external context simple, with complexity encapsulated behind it.
quote: manual prompt tricks became less central as instruction tuning and model reasoning improved, but the need to specify goals, constraints, context, and evaluation did not disappear.
source: Harness Engineering for Self-Improvement
detail: Same paragraph: 'Eventually it is possible that many harness improvements will be internalized into core model behavior, but the interface with external context and tools should remain.' On design: 'Similar to an OS, a harness should encapsulate complicated logic while keeping the interface simple.' This supports an outcome-plus-bounds contract whose wording can shrink while the goal, constraint and evaluation slots stay.

claim: Do not let an agent's self-report or an in-band LLM judge gate its own progress on open-ended goals. Gate on an out-of-band, externally grounded check of world state that the agent cannot fake.
quote: For open-ended objectives whose success signal lives outside the transcript, scaling up the judge is not enough; out-of-band evaluation with real-world access is a structural requirement.
source: When Do Agent Loops Mistake Stagnation for Progress? Self-Evaluation Bias and Externally Grounded Verification in Long-Running Autonomous LLM Agent Loops
detail: Across 54 cycles, a frontier agent claimed improvement every time, yet 56% had zero or negative measured delta. The self-verdict gate became accept-all and eroded the best deployed state by 19%. The strongest in-band judge accepted cycles of which 44% were real regressions. When success was verifiable from the artifact itself, the gap vanished. The benefit sits in the gate's grounding, not in feedback content: a sign-only verdict performed about as well as full feedback.

claim: Put effort into how tools are structured and exposed (structured low-level interfaces, code-execution-style tools) rather than text-based 'cognitive scaffolding' tools such as tools for recording reasoning.
quote: lightweight text-based cognitive-scaffolding tools, such as tools that let the agent record intermediate reasoning, have limited effect on actor behavior.
source: The Devil Is in the Interface: Evaluating How Tool Architecture Shapes Coding Agent Behavior
by: Xu, Saghir, Wu, Côté, Wang, Lakkaraju, Pei, Zhang
detail: The study compared 11,700 trajectories across six tool architectures with similar underlying capability. Against a bash-only baseline, structured low-level interfaces improved consistency across repeated attempts by up to 4.7x; natural-language search increased access to relevant files by more than 11%; and Python CodeAct-style interfaces matched task performance with 41.6% fewer steps and 56.3% fewer tokens. How capability is exposed changes behaviour even when the capability is the same.

claim: Discouraged: putting repository overviews into AGENTS.md-style context files to raise task success. Such files add cost without improving outcomes. Reserve prose for non-standard practices and evaluate any addition before shipping it.
quote: we find that while instructions in the context files are well followed by coding agents, repository overviews, although popular and recommended by model providers, are not helpful.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
by: Gloaguen, Mündler, Müller, Raychev, Vechev (ETH Zürich SRI Lab)
detail: Context files 'do not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average', across LLMs, agents, and both LLM-generated and developer-written files. Conclusion: 'context files are useful for specifying non-standard coding practices, any attempts to improve performance should be rigorously evaluated before deployment.' A later two-agent ablation (arXiv 2607.27250, 2026-07-28, Claude Code and Codex, 288 runs) likewise found that context strategy 'does not measurably move correctness', because failures come from implementation skill rather than missing repository knowledge. The counterpoint (arXiv 2606.20512) finds that guidance tuned through synthetic probes does help a smaller model, and argues that 'how the guidance is produced is the decisive variable'. The evidence therefore favours moving load-bearing rules into checks and testing whatever prose remains.

claim: Carrying a large, constraint-heavy system prompt forward to a new model generation is outdated: Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for Claude 5 models with no measurable loss on coding evals.
quote: We removed over 80% of Claude Code’s system prompt for models like Claude Opus 5 and Claude Fable 5 with no measurable loss on our coding evaluations.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
detail: This is the strongest observed data point for the whole sweep. Anthropic applied the same lesson to CLAUDE.md files and skills, and shipped a /doctor ('claude doctor') command to 'rightsize your skills, and CLAUDE.md files'. The post frames the old practices as 'myths' and gives six then/now shifts: rules to judgment, examples to interface design, everything upfront to progressive disclosure, repetition to simple tool descriptions, memory in CLAUDE.md to auto-memory, simple specs to rich references.

claim: For Claude 5 generation models, Anthropic found it could delete many of the hard constraints once needed to keep older models from worst cases, and let the model use surrounding context and judgment instead; some of those rules were wrong for a subset of prompts. The article says 'many', not all, and still advises constraints in highly important areas. It does not say models do better when told the intent; that point comes from Anthropic's Fable 5 guide.
quote: And while these constraints were once needed to avoid worst case scenarios, we have since found we can delete many of them and let the model use surrounding context and judgement instead.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
original_claim: Hard 'always/never' rules written to protect older models from worst cases are outdated; newer models do better when told the intent and left to use surrounding context and judgment.
detail: Worked example: the old rule 'default to writing no comments. Never write multi-paragraph docstrings...' became 'Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.' Transcripts also showed conflicting instructions stacking up across the system prompt, skills and user requests ('leave documentation as appropriate' versus 'DO NOT add comments'), and the model 'must think more carefully about these overlapping and conflicting messages'.

claim: Giving tool-usage examples is outdated for the newest models because the examples narrow the model's exploration; put the effort into expressive tool, script and file interfaces instead (for example, enum-typed parameters).
quote: With our newest models, we’ve found that giving examples actually constrains them to a certain exploration space.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
detail: The post says 'The number one rule for tool usage was to give Claude examples' and replaces it with interface design: a Todo tool's status enum (pending, in_progress, completed) already tells the model how to use it. This conflicts with Anthropic's own general prompting page, which still calls examples one of the most reliable ways to steer output (see the separate finding). Read together: examples are fading for tool use and exploration, and remain in use for output format and style.

claim: Do not make CLAUDE.md or SKILL.md a central store of every practice. Keep the always-loaded file light (what the repo is for, plus its gotchas) and load deeper guidance from a tree of files when it is needed.
quote: A common myth is that you want to make these a central repository for every known practice that you might run into, because Claude would not find it otherwise.
source: The new rules of context engineering for Claude 5 generation models
detail: The same post says: 'Instead, consider having a tree of files that can be loaded at the right time.' And: 'Keep your CLAUDE.md lightweight and briefly describe what your repo is for, but spend most of the tokens on gotchas inside of the codebase... Avoid stating ‘the obvious’.' Skills should be 'lightweight guides', 'Avoid making them overconstrained, except in highly important areas', and they work best when they encode opinions particular to your team. Anthropic moved Claude Code's verification and code-review guidance out of the system prompt into skills that load when called.

claim: Lean system prompts: remove repeated instructions and examples and simplify tool descriptions, one group at a time, re-running the same evals after each cut. OpenAI measured higher eval scores at far lower token cost.
quote: In a sample of internal coding-agent eval runs, configurations with leaner system prompts improved evaluation scores by roughly 10–15% while reducing total tokens by 41–66% and cost by 33–67%.
source: Using GPT-5.6 (OpenAI API docs, 'Favor leaner prompts')
detail: The method the page gives: 'Start with a prompt and tool set that already works. Remove one group of instructions, examples, or tools at a time, then rerun the same evals.' 'State each instruction once.' 'Keep examples and style guidance when they encode a product requirement or correct a measured gap.' OpenAI calls the ranges directional and tells readers to validate on their own tasks. The page also says broad brevity instructions ('Be concise') may now be unnecessary and can make responses too brief.

claim: Define autonomy and approval boundaries once, as a compact policy by kind of request: report-only for review and diagnosis, in-scope local changes for fix requests, confirmation for external, destructive, costly or scope-expanding actions. Do not repeat 'ask first'-style rules.
quote: Keep the policy in one place and state each rule once. Repeating instructions such as “ask first,” “do not mutate,” or “wait for approval” can cause unnecessary approval requests for safe, expected actions.
source: Using GPT-5.6 (OpenAI API docs, 'Define autonomy and approval boundaries')
