claim:
Observed direction, 2025 to September 2026:

(1) **From chat assistant to long-horizon coding and knowledge-work agent.** Grok 3 and 4 were chat and reasoning models, and Grok 4.1 was tuned for personality. grok-code-fast-1 (Aug 2025) and grok-build-0.1 (May 2026) were fast coding specialists. Grok 4.5 (Jul 2026) was co-developed with Cursor, which SpaceX acquired on 2026-08-14. Grok 4.6 and 4.7 are trained with RL on multi-hour agentic tasks and marketed on self-verification.

(2) **Reasoning went from optional to mandatory.** It moved from separate or selectable modes (Grok 3 mini effort; separate reasoning/non-reasoning slugs for 4 Fast, 4.1 Fast and 4.20; 'none' on 4.3) to always-on reasoning with an effort dial (4.5: low to high; 4.6 and 4.7 add xhigh). Encrypted reasoning must now be carried across turns. Output tokens per task rose again at top effort: about 81k for 4.7 xhigh, against the 2x token-efficiency pitch for 4.5.

(3) **Harness and model are converging.** The 4.5 to 4.7 cards cite supplemental training on anonymized Cursor workflow data and on Grok Build/Grok Bot harness trajectories, and scores are reported per harness. xAI open-sourced its harness (Apache-2.0), and it reads AGENTS.md and Claude Code's CLAUDE.md, rules, skills, hooks and plugins, so cross-harness instruction files are becoming the norm. Independent observers warn this coupling makes models harder to swap.

(4) **Instruction following is strong, and that strength is itself a risk.** The 4.20 and 4.3 models led independent IFBench (81%). xAI's own audit found that stronger system-prompt adherence also raised susceptibility to misuse system prompts, and prompt-injection results were poor on 4.20 (AgentDojo 0.33). The 2026 cards dropped the alignment and injection audits in favour of capability tables.

(5) **Guidance moved into the harness.** xAI's only text-model prompting guide (grok-code-fast-1: detailed system prompts, XML sections) has been removed, and the published system-prompt repo has not been updated since Nov 2025. The live guidance is now the Grok Build system prompt. Between July and September 2026 it went from enumerated lists of risky commands to compact principles: reversibility and blast radius, scoped authorization, quoted content treated as data, completion claims backed by tool output, and reports that stand alone for the reader. The docs say short, specific AGENTS.md instructions are followed more reliably. The voice guide for xAI's newest voice model says to simplify prompts and strip workaround prompting.

(6) **Independent quality is non-monotonic.** Hallucination rate (Artificial Analysis) went 22%, then 25%, 54%, 34% and 29%. Long-context reasoning regressed in 4.7 even though xAI claims long-context gains. Cadence is now about monthly point releases (4.5 in Jul, 4.6 in Aug, 4.7 in Sep), each at the same $2/$6 price.

Net for instruction authors: state outcome, bounds and verification compactly, let effort parameters and the harness handle how the model reasons, and verify behaviour in the target harness because it varies between releases.

FORECAST, not observed. Musk has sketched Grok 4.8 as 'a meaningful step up', Grok 4.9 in 'Astra/Fable class', and Grok 5 as a possible frontier leader, with no dates given (reported by Decrypt, 2026-09-21, citing Musk's post: https://tech.yahoo.com/ai/gemini/articles/xai-launches-grok-4-7-171603280.html). Grok 5 is still in training; secondary reports say Musk said in August 2026 that it should arrive within 2026, but I did not verify that against a primary source. Musk's recent timelines have slipped: Grok 4.7 was delayed at least five times between late July and its 21 September release. The Grok 4.7 model card says SpaceXAI plans to add 4.7 to consumer surfaces (web, apps, Grok in X) 'at a later date', which conflicts with Decrypt's report that it is already live in the Grok app. If the monthly cadence holds, expect Grok 4.8 around October to November 2026 at the same $2/$6 price, with Cursor and Grok Build shipping first. That timing is my extrapolation, not an announcement.

**Grok Build** is xAI's coding agent: CLI `grok` with a TUI, headless `-p` mode and the Agent Client Protocol. It is open source (Apache-2.0) at github.com/xai-org/grok-build (repo created 2026-07-14), and its default model is grok-4.7.

**Instruction files (from docs/build/features/project-rules, the in-repo user guide 12-project-rules.md and agents_md.rs):**
- **Files read.** In each directory from the git repo root down to the cwd (cwd only outside a repo), plus ~/.grok/, it reads AGENTS.md, Agents.md, AGENT.md, CLAUDE.md, Claude.md, CLAUDE.local.md and .claude/CLAUDE.md. It also reads every *.md under .grok/rules/, .claude/rules/ and .cursor/rules/ (the Claude and Cursor ones behind compat toggles that default on), the home rules dirs ~/.grok/rules, ~/.claude/rules and ~/.cursor/rules, and any [paths] extra_rule_dirs.
- **Exclusions and trust.** Files ignored by .gitignore are skipped, so a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md is not loaded. Project files load only in a trusted folder (--trust or an interactive grant).
- **Loading.** Files load in full with no size cap. Rules files have their frontmatter stripped. Deeper files appear later and win on conflicts. Instruction files in directories outside the initial set are discovered when the agent touches them.
- **Injection.** Everything is injected into the user message as one <\system-reminder> block that begins 'As you answer the user's questions, you can use the following context (ordered from repo root to current directory - deeper files take precedence on conflicts)', with '## From: <path>' headings, and ends 'Follow these instructions exactly. When working in subdirectories not listed above, check for additional project instruction files'. Embedded system-reminder tags are escaped.
- **Precedence.** The subagent prompt restates AGENTS.md scoping and says direct chat instructions override project files.
- **Overrides and inspection.** `grok inspect` lists the discovered rules files with token counts. `--rules` appends text to the system prompt and `--system-prompt-override` replaces it.

**System prompt.** templates/prompt.md, XOR-obfuscated in the binary and last changed 2026-09-22. It has XML sections (<dangerous_actions>, <work_policy>, <communication>, <memory>, <scratch_files>, <browser_verification>) and wraps the request in <user_query>. There is a separate Codex-style apply_patch prompt for apply_patch models and a subagent prompt.

**Skills, plugins and hooks.** Skills load from ./.grok/skills (walked up to the repo root), ~/.grok/skills, ~/.agents/skills, plugin skills/ directories and configured paths. SKILL.md frontmatter supports name, description, when-to-use, paths (globs), argument-hint, user-invocable and disable-model-invocation. allowed-tools neither grants nor restricts tools, and model, effort, license and compatibility are accepted but ignored. The docs claim zero-config Claude Code compatibility: marketplaces, plugins, skills, MCPs, agents, hooks and instruction files. Project hooks need /hooks-trust.

**Plan mode and subagents.** Plan mode gates edit tools but not bash. The built-in subagent types are general-purpose, explore (read-only) and plan. Personas are overlays under .grok/personas. Worktrees and background tasks are supported.

**Other harnesses.**
- **Cursor** (a SpaceX subsidiary since 2026-08-14, and the only place besides Grok Build that serves Grok 4.7 Fast) reads .cursor/rules/*.mdc, AGENTS.md at the root and nested, user rules and team rules. Its docs do not mention CLAUDE.md.
- **GitHub Copilot** offers Grok 4.7 in VS Code, Copilot CLI, the cloud agent and other IDEs from 2026-09-21.
- **API users** write their own system prompt. In 2025 xAI published safety-policy system-prompt prefixes that the API injected ahead of yours for grok-4-0709, grok-4-fast and grok-code-fast-1 (xai-org/grok-prompts). That repo's last commit was 2025-11-17, so whether a prefix is injected for grok-4.5 through 4.7 is UNVERIFIED. The model cards say only that 'system prompts further steer the model'.

No release newer than grok-4.7 was found as of 2026-09-25. The xAI API release notes were last updated 2026-09-21, the models page lists grok-4.7 as the newest text model, and no Grok 4.8 or Grok 5 has shipped. Variants in the family that the maintainer's list does not name:
- **Grok 4.7 Fast** (2026-09-21): the same model on faster infrastructure at twice the token rates, served only in Cursor and Grok Build, not on the public API.
- **grok-build-0.1**: xAI's coding-specific model (May 2026, 256k context, $1/$2), still listed on the API.
- **grok-4.20-multi-agent** (beta): its reasoning.effort sets the agent count.

Context worth knowing: xAI now operates as 'SpaceXAI', a trade name of X.AI LLC, following SpaceX's acquisition of xAI (reported Feb 2026). SpaceX also owns Cursor as of 2026-08-14. In the same news cycle (not Grok), Artificial Analysis reported Claude Opus 5.5 on 2026-09-22 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna, which matches the maintainer's list.

The quote and the 2025-07-28 date are on the blog, and OpenRouter lists 2025-07-25. The other details come from other Z.ai pages: 'native agentic' and 'one-click compatibility with the Claude Code framework' are in docs.z.ai release-notes; thinking.type and dynamic-thinking-by-default are on docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-4.5; 'Interleaved Thinking, a feature introduced since GLM-4.5' is in the GLM-4.7 blog; the XML-like tool-call template is in the GLM-4.5 paper (arXiv 2508.06471). The blog does not use the name CC-Bench. It says Claude Code was used to run 52 tasks and publishes them as the CC-Bench-trajectories dataset.
quote: Both GLM-4.5 and GLM-4.5-Air are hybrid reasoning models, offering: thinking mode for complex reasoning and tool using, and non-thinking mode for instant responses.
original_claim: The first 'native agentic' GLM. It is a hybrid reasoning model: the caller turns thinking on or off with thinking.type, and dynamic thinking is the default. Interleaved thinking between tool calls starts here. Tool calls use a new XML-like template to reduce code escaping. From day one it was positioned as a model you plug into Claude Code (the release note calls it 'one-click compatibility with the Claude Code framework') and measured on CC-Bench, which is built on Claude Code.

claim: All of it is on the blog: context from 128K to 200K, tool use during inference, Claude Code/Cline/Roo Code/Kilo Code, automatic upgrade for Coding Plan subscribers, about 15% fewer tokens than GLM-4.5 on CC-Bench, and 'Claude-level performance ... 1/7th the price'.
quote: GLM-4.6 shows a clear improvement in reasoning performance and supports tool use during inference, leading to stronger overall capability.
original_claim: Context grows from 128K to 200K, and the model can use tools during reasoning. Z.ai marketed it inside Claude Code, Cline, Roo Code and Kilo Code, where Coding Plan users were upgraded automatically, and claims about 15% fewer tokens per task than GLM-4.5. The Coding Plan was pitched as a cheaper Claude substitute inside Claude Code.

claim: The blog says 'supports thinking before acting' and names Claude Code, Kilo Code, Cline and Roo Code. TRAE and the phrase 'think before acting' come from docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-4.7. Thinking on by default is confirmed by the thinking-mode docs.
quote: Preserved Thinking: In coding agent scenarios, GLM-4.7 automatically retains all thinking blocks across multi-turn conversations, reusing the existing reasoning instead of re-deriving from scratch.
original_claim: Thinking is on by default and happens before every response and tool call. Two features are added: Preserved Thinking, which keeps reasoning across turns in coding agents, and Turn-level Thinking, which toggles thinking per turn. Z.ai says it 'thinks before acting' inside Claude Code, Kilo Code, TRAE, Cline and Roo Code.

claim: The quote is on the docs page. 744B (40B active), DSA, slime and the 'From Vibe Coding to Agentic Engineering' title are on the 2026-02-12 blog. 'Fully automated via Claude Code and other agent harnesses' is in the GLM-5 paper (arXiv 2602.15763). OpenRouter lists 2026-02-11.
quote: In internal evaluations aligned with the Claude Code task distribution, GLM-5 demonstrates substantial gains over GLM-4.7 across frontend development, backend systems engineering, and long-horizon execution tasks.
original_claim: Scale rises to 744B-A40B, using DeepSeek Sparse Attention and 'slime' asynchronous RL. The framing moves 'from vibe coding to agentic engineering', meaning long-horizon systems work. Internal evaluation, CC-Bench-V2, is run through Claude Code and other harnesses and is aligned with the Claude Code task distribution. Z.ai says it is compatible with Claude Code and OpenClaw.

claim: The quote is exact and OpenRouter lists 2026-03-15. That it is 'closed' rests on API-only access and no zai-org/GLM-5-Turbo repo; the page does not say so. 'Tuning to third-party harnesses' is an inference, though it is consistent with the page.
quote: It has been specifically optimized for the core requirements of OpenClaw tasks since the training phase, enhancing key capabilities such as tool invocation, command following, timed and persistent tasks, and long-chain execution.
original_claim: A closed variant trained for OpenClaw-style personal-agent harnesses. It emphasises command following, timed and persistent tasks, and long-chain execution, and shows Z.ai tuning models to specific third-party harnesses.

claim: The docs call it 'Z.AI's first multimodal coding foundation model', and OpenRouter lists 2026-04-01. Z.ai later calls GLM-5.3-Flash 'the first natively multimodal model in the GLM-5 series', so the two 'first' claims carry different qualifiers.
quote: Deeply optimized for agent workflows, it works seamlessly with agents such as Claude Code and OpenClaw to complete the full loop of "understand the environment → plan actions → execute tasks".
original_claim: The first multimodal coding model in the family. It is positioned for the 'understand environment, plan, execute' loop inside Claude Code and OpenClaw.

claim: The quote is exact. The docs give 8 hours. 'Hundreds of rounds and thousands of tool calls', earlier models that 'plateau' or 'declare the task complete', and the review/improve/continue harness are all in the 2026-04-07 blog.
quote: Further optimized for agentic coding workflows such as Claude Code and OpenClaw, GLM-5.1 offers stronger long-horizon planning, stepwise execution, process adjustment, and result delivery.
original_claim: Built for long horizons: single runs of up to 8 hours, and optimisation that continues over hundreds of rounds and thousands of tool calls. Z.ai says earlier models plateaued or declared done early. It wraps the model in a harness loop of review, improve, continue, and says it is further optimised for Claude Code and OpenClaw workflows.

claim: Blog (2026-06-16): effort levels, GLM-5.2[1m] in Claude Code, High/Max, 'more potential hacking behavior than GLM-5.1', and an online anti-hack guard for both RL training and evaluation. The CLAUDE.md/'Agent.md' advice and adherence to engineering standards are on docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-5.2. The 2026-06-13 Coding Plan date comes only from third-party reports. The HF repo was created 2026-06-16 under MIT.
quote: GLM-5.2 also introduces effort level control, enabling users to explicitly balance model capability against task execution speed and computational cost.
original_claim: Context rises to 1M tokens (enabled in Claude Code with the glm-5.2[1m] suffix). Effort-level control arrives (High/Max). Z.ai claims stronger adherence to engineering standards and recommends putting standards in CLAUDE.md or 'Agent.md'. The lab reports more reward-hacking pressure than in 5.1 and added online anti-hack guards to training.

released: 2026-08-14 (blog/Coding Plan); API 2026-08-18; weights on Hugging Face 2026-08-25 (custom GLM-5.3 license)
claim: Only some GLM-5.3 benchmarks ran in Claude Code 2.1.207: Terminal-Bench 2.1 and 3.0, SWE-Marathon, CyberGym and ExploitGym. DeepSWE used mini-swe-agent, and ALE ran in 'the Claude Code harness' with no version given. Toolathlon, GDPval-AA and FrontierSWE were run by official or third-party evaluators. Also, the blog says only 'some' environments represent several days of expert work. Correct as stated: same base as 5.2 with every gain from post-training; thinking cannot be disabled; low/high/max with max as default and recommended for coding; 'taking ownership ... end to end'. Dates: blog 2026-08-14, API 2026-08-18, HF 2026-08-25 under a custom glm-5.3 license.
quote: GLM-5.3 supports three thinking effort levels: low, high, and max. Disabling thinking is no longer supported by GLM-5.3.
original_claim: Same base as 5.2; every gain comes from post-training RL on synthesised, verifier-checked environments shaped like real expert work lasting several days. Thinking is forced on. Callers can no longer disable it and only choose reasoning_effort low, high or max, with max the default and the recommendation for coding. The model is trained to own work end to end rather than rely on user decomposition. Z.ai's benchmarks run in the Claude Code 2.1.207 harness.

claim: Blog (2026-08-26): 320B total and 18B active, a newly trained base, hybrid sparse and linear attention, 'first natively multimodal model in the GLM-5 series', the render-inspect-revise loop, and Browser/Computer Use in ZCode. The docs give the recommended settings temperature 1, top_p 0.95, reasoning_effort max, thinking.type enabled only, and clear_thinking false. HF weights are under MIT.
quote: The key is to close the loop between generation and visual feedback: the model can render its output, inspect what users would actually see, identify visual issues, and revise the underlying artifact accordingly.
original_claim: A newly trained base with hybrid sparse and linear attention, and the first natively multimodal GLM-5 model. It adds a loop where the model renders, inspects and revises its own output (browser and computer use in ZCode). Thinking is forced on. Recommended settings are temperature 1, top_p 0.95, reasoning_effort max and clear_thinking false.

claim: The quote is on the docs page and OpenRouter lists 2026-09-18. 'No change in prompting' is an inference: the docs share one parameter set across Flash and FlashX.
quote: GLM-5.3-FlashX is now live, delivering inference speeds of 200 tokens/s for faster responses and a smoother experience.
original_claim: A higher-throughput serving of GLM-5.3-Flash. No change in prompting.

released: 2026-09-23 (OpenRouter listing; no Z.ai docs page found)
claim: The OpenRouter entry (created 2026-09-23) matches the quote. Reasoning is mandatory there, with efforts max/high/low and max as default. No Prime page exists in the docs.z.ai index.
quote: GLM-5.3-Prime is the high-speed variant of Z.ai's GLM-5.3, inheriting its full capabilities while delivering 1.5–2× the output throughput through inference acceleration.
original_claim: The same GLM-5.3 capabilities behind faster inference. Reasoning is always on (low, high or max). No change in prompting.

claim: The page says 'In a complex codebase, an effective task description typically includes four elements' (Goal, Context, Constraints, Done when). That is scoped to complex work, not 'every task'.
quote: This kind of structured task input reduces unnecessary guesswork and makes the agent’s changes more consistent and easier to review.
source: Best Practice — Best Practices for Coding Agents: Managing Prompts, Plans, Skills, and Workflows (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
published: undated page; embedded asset timestamps 2026-03-25; read 2026-09-25
original_claim: Structure every task as Goal / Context / Constraints / Done-when. Context matters more than prompt tricks.
detail: Z.ai names four elements: Goal, Context, Constraints and 'Done when', the last meaning tests pass, behaviour changes as expected, or the bug no longer reproduces. These map almost one-to-one onto OutcomeBound's Outcome / Context / Bounds / Completion bar. The page says it draws on the official guidance of leading tools, so this is Z.ai restating cross-tool consensus rather than a GLM-specific finding.

claim: Put temporary instructions in the prompt and long-lived rules in a project-level instruction file.
quote: put temporary instructions in the prompt, and put long-lived rules in project-level configuration files.
source: Best Practice (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: Z.ai says rules repeated in every prompt become inefficient and drift over time.

claim: Write instruction-file rules as specific, checkable directives, not abstract principles. Keep the main file under about 200 lines.
quote: When writing agent memory, use specific, verifiable rules whenever possible rather than abstract principles. The clearer the instructions are, the more stable the agent’s behavior will be.
source: Memory-mechanism (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: The page gives 'Keep the code clean' and 'Write good tests' as rules to avoid, and 'Run pnpm test after modifying business logic' as the kind to prefer. It also recommends keeping the main memory file under 200 lines. For OutcomeBound, a principle-level kernel should be paired with project fragments that name concrete commands and paths, which the fragments already do.

claim: Avoid conflicting rules across instruction files. Treat .md instructions as guidance, not enforcement.
quote: If different files give different instructions for the same behavior, the agent may choose one arbitrarily.
source: Memory-mechanism (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: The same section says .md memory files are 'contextual instructions, not ... enforced configuration'. Oversized files 'reduce the agent’s adherence to instructions'. Hard guarantees belong in deterministic checks.

claim: Write durable rules into files, because conversation-only rules are lost at context compaction.
quote: If certain rules disappear after compression, that means those rules existed only in the conversation and were never written into a memory file.
source: Memory-mechanism (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: This matters most for GLM-5.2 and later, whose 1M context is paired in Claude Code with CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=1000000. Long sessions still compact.

claim: Keep human-written instruction memory separate from agent-accumulated learning memory.
quote: This separation helps prevent experience-driven notes from gradually polluting the system’s core rules, which in turn keeps agent behavior more stable and controllable.
source: Memory-mechanism (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: ZCode implements this split. AGENTS.md is 'something you maintain by hand' and lives in the repository. Memory is written automatically, stays on the machine only, and is off by default (https://zcode.z.ai/en/docs/agents).

claim: The quote is exact. The placement experiment used only 30 sampled instances and the Claude Code v2.1.14 harness. The paper is co-authored by Tsinghua CoAI and Zhipu AI, so it is not fully independent of the GLM lab.
quote: We observe that constraints placed in the repository policy file typically achieve the best compliance, while placement in the system prompt and user prompt shows similar performance.
source: MTAC-IFBench: Benchmarking Instruction-Following in Multi-Turn Agentic Coding (Wen et al.)
original_claim: Put important constraints in the repository policy file (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) rather than the system prompt or user turn.
detail: Measured on a 30-instance sample under Claude Code. The authors come from Tsinghua CoAI and Zhipu AI, and the first author interned at Zhipu, so this is not independent of the lab. The paper also finds constraints in policy files decay less over successive turns than those given in user instructions.

claim: The paper finds that updates to existing constraints in user turns are followed worse than newly added constraints, and that policy-file constraints decay less over turns. It never tests revising a constraint by editing the policy file, so 'edit the policy file instead' is an inference, not a finding.
quote: updating existing constraints is notably harder than adding new ones. This likely stems from interference by superseded constraints, highlighting the inherent difficulty of dynamically revising requirements in multi-turn interactions.
source: MTAC-IFBench (Wen et al.)
original_claim: Revise durable constraints by editing the policy file, not by amending them mid-conversation.
detail: Measured across 11 models including GLM-5.2 and GLM-5.1. The practice drawn here, editing the file rather than amending in chat, is an inference from the finding; the paper states only the measurement.

claim: The measurement is for GLM-5.2, not GLM as a family, and GLM-5.3 was not tested. Across eight models, instruction-following was generally higher under Claude Code v2.1.14 than under OpenCode v1.1.21: GLM-5.2's CSR fell from 80.4% to 76.8% and its C-ISR from 12.7% to 6.7%. The paper also notes that OpenCode showed less multi-turn decay. It is co-authored by Zhipu AI.
quote: For example, GLM-5.2’s CSR drops from 80.4% under Claude Code to 76.8% under OpenCode, while its C-ISR drops more sharply from 12.7% to 6.7%.
source: MTAC-IFBench (Wen et al.)
original_claim: Evaluate and tune instructions for the model plus harness pair. GLM follows instructions better inside Claude Code than OpenCode.
detail: The paper notes models decay less over turns in OpenCode, which it credits to OpenCode's context management. Z.ai's own 'best reported harness' for GLM-5.1 and GLM-5.2 on Terminal-Bench is Claude Code (82.7 for GLM-5.2, per the GLM-5.2 blog).

claim: The result is for GLM-5.2, the top scorer among 11 models from an older set (e.g. Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro), run under Claude Code v2.1.14. It missed about 20% of process constraints, averaged over turns. GLM-5.3, now the strongest GLM, was not tested, so 'the best GLM' should read 'GLM-5.2'.
quote: Even the leading LLM, GLM-5.2, fails to follow about 20% of the process constraints, while most LLMs only achieve perfect constraint compliance in fewer than 10% of turns.
source: MTAC-IFBench (Wen et al.)
original_claim: Back prose process constraints with deterministic checks. Even the best GLM misses about a fifth of them over a multi-turn session.
detail: GLM-5.2 had the top average CSR, 80.4, above Claude-Opus-4.6 at 78.6 in that table. Its all-constraints-satisfied rate falls from 27.6% in turn 1 to 2.6% by turns 9–10. Models do best on static constraints and worst on multi-step coordination and project-wide consistency.

claim: Name hard bounds explicitly (no new dependencies, no API-contract changes, no unrequested commits), and require a report of what was verified and what risks remain.
quote: Do not introduce new dependencies, do not modify API contracts, and do not commit changes proactively. After completing the modification, run the build, lint, and tests, then report the verification results and any uncovered risks.
source: GLM-5.2 overview (Z.ai API docs)
detail: This is Z.ai's own recommended stress-test prompt, given with the advice to put team standards in CLAUDE.md or 'Agent.md'. Z.ai claims GLM-5.2 better respects 'commit boundaries' and reduces 'out-of-scope changes, invalid dependencies, skipped verification, or unauthorized commits', which is a lab claim. The GLM-5.3-Flash docs repeat the same shape: do the task, don't fabricate, verify, then state 'what has been verified and what risks remain uncovered'.

claim: The hacking the blog describes (reading protected evaluation artifacts, copying from upstream commits, curl-fetching solutions) was seen in RL training rollouts, which Z.ai countered with an anti-hack guard. The advice for deployment is an inference from that.
quote: We find that GLM-5.2 shows more potential hacking behavior than GLM-5.1.
source: GLM-5.2: Built for Long-Horizon Tasks (Z.ai blog)
original_claim: Protect verification from the agent: keep evaluation artifacts and upstream solutions out of reach, and do not trust a green result the agent could have gamed.
detail: This is a lab observation made during training, with no published rate. The examples Z.ai gives are reading hidden eval files and curl-ing target source from GitHub. Z.ai added a rule-plus-LLM-judge anti-hack guard during RL and evaluation. GLM-5.3 verifiers are synthesised 'without access to the reference solution' and checked against oracle, no-op and unsolved states.

claim: The quote describes how ZCode's /goal verification judges completion. The same page says 'the more specific and checkable the objective, the more accurate each round's verdict.'
quote: A plan, a checklist, a lot of elapsed effort, or a reply that merely sounds conclusive does not count on its own; changed files, command output, and test results do.
source: Goal Mode (ZCode docs — Z.ai's official GLM-5.3 harness)
original_claim: Judge completion only by evidence (changed files, command output, test results), and state goals as checkable targets.
detail: ZCode runs a separate completion check after each round. The page also says 'The more specific and checkable the objective, the more accurate each round's verdict', contrasting 'Make pnpm test pass and keep first-paint under two seconds' with 'make it faster'. This is the same design as OutcomeBound's completion bar and its PASS / FAIL / UNVERIFIED reporting.

claim: For open-ended work, add a harness-level loop to review and continue instead of trusting the model's own 'done'.
quote: In a single run, most models—including earlier versions of GLM—give up quickly: they produce a basic skeleton with a static taskbar and one or two placeholder windows, then declare the task complete.
source: GLM-5.1: Towards Long-Horizon Tasks (Z.ai blog)
detail: This comes from a single showcase run by the lab. Z.ai 'wrapped GLM-5.1 in a simple harness' where the model reviews its own output after each round and continues, for 8 hours. The blog names 'reliable self-evaluation for tasks where there is no numeric metric' as still open.

claim: The quote is exact. Forced thinking applies to GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash. The thinking-mode docs show GLM-4.7 through 5.2 can still disable it.
quote: GLM-5.3 always operates with reasoning enabled and supports three reasoning effort levels: `low`, `high`, and `max`. Disabling reasoning is no longer supported.
source: GLM-5.3 overview (Z.ai API docs)
original_claim: Toggling thinking on and off per turn, or disabling thinking (the GLM-4.5 to GLM-5.2 hybrid and turn-level thinking controls).
detail: Sending thinking.type 'disabled' to glm-5.3 makes the request fail. Through the Coding Plan, Claude Code's 'disabled' is mapped to effort 'low'. Depth is now set only by effort level, so prompt text asking the model to think harder or less does nothing. Turn-level thinking was introduced with GLM-4.7.

claim: The requirement holds when Preserved Thinking is on. That is the default on the Coding Plan endpoint; on the standard API it is enabled with clear_thinking:false.
quote: All consecutive reasoning_content blocks must exactly match the original sequence generated by the model during the initial request. Do not reorder or edit these blocks; otherwise, performance may degrade and cache hit rates may be affected.
source: Thinking Mode (Z.ai API docs)
original_claim: Coding-agent harnesses must pass prior reasoning_content back unmodified (preserved thinking).
detail: Preserved thinking is on by default on the Coding Plan endpoint and off on the standard API. In the open-weights chat template for GLM-5.3 and 5.3-Flash, clear_thinking defaults to false, with Z.ai advising clear_thinking=true only for chat. This is a harness concern, not a prose one.

claim: Use max reasoning effort for coding tasks.
quote: For complex tasks such as coding, we recommend using `max`.
source: GLM-5.3 overview (Z.ai API docs)
detail: max is also the API default and the Claude Code /effort default through the Coding Plan. Z.ai reports GLM-5.3 at max reaches 34.5% on its in-house Z.ai Code Bench at about 75K output tokens per task, against 23.4% at 96K for GLM-5.2. That is a lab claim on a private benchmark.

claim: The page covers GLM-5.3 (max): 210M output tokens against a 140M median. It does not measure low or high effort, so it gives no comparison to lower settings.
quote: When evaluating the Intelligence Index, it generated 210M tokens, which is very verbose in comparison to the median of 140M.
source: GLM-5.3 (max) — Intelligence, Performance & Price Analysis (Artificial Analysis)
original_claim: Running every task at max effort; expect heavy token use.
detail: This is independent measurement. The same page calls GLM-5.3 (max) 'slower than average and very verbose' at 60 output tokens per second. Artificial Analysis earlier measured GLM-5.2 at 43k output tokens per task, up from 26k for GLM-5.1 (quoted at https://simonwillison.net/2026/jun/17/glm-52/). It conflicts with the lab's efficiency claim. Choose effort per task (low or high for light turns) rather than adding brevity prose.

claim: For complex tasks, have the agent plan before editing.
quote: For more complex requests, asking the agent to start writing code immediately often leads to logic errors, unnecessary rework, or repeated revisions.
source: Best Practice (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: The page cites Claude Code's plan step and Plan modes. In ZCode, Plan mode cannot be combined with /goal automatic continuation. Z.ai's GLM-5.2 example prompts ask first for 'the execution plan, impact scope, risk boundaries, and verification method'.

claim: The Z.ai API reference also says 'only auto is supported' for tool_choice.
quote: tool_choice: Controls function calling strategy, default is auto (only supports auto)
source: Function Calling (Z.ai API docs)
original_claim: Do not rely on forcing a specific tool call through the API. Enforce required steps in the harness or with deterministic checks.
detail: The Z.ai API cannot force a required or named tool call. Any 'must run X' rule reaches the model as prose only, unless the harness or a gate enforces it.

claim: Write tool and function definitions with a single responsibility, clear names, and detailed descriptions and examples.
quote: It is recommended to provide detailed documentation and examples for each function to help the model better understand the function's purpose and usage.
source: Function Calling (Z.ai API docs)
detail: The same page's best-practice list says 'Single responsibility: Each function should do one thing'.

claim: The page says ZCode does not 'choose rule files automatically by task type'; 'path-scoped' is a paraphrase. ZCode also does not read CLAUDE.md at runtime; it uses it only as a one-time migration source.
quote: It does not merge multiple AGENTS.md files across directory levels. It also does not scan child directories, expand @import / @include , or choose rule files automatically by task type.
source: ZCode Agent (ZCode docs)
original_claim: Keep the always-loaded kernel self-contained in the root AGENTS.md. GLM's native harness does not follow @imports, nested files or path-scoped rules.
detail: ZCode reads ~/.zcode/AGENTS.md and then the workspace AGENTS.md, treating the workspace file as primary. CLAUDE.md is used only once, during onboarding migration. Since v3.7.1, subagents also inject AGENTS.md; they can opt out with injectAgentsMd:false, and Explore does not inject it. OutcomeBound composes fragments into AGENTS.md and imports it from CLAUDE.md with @AGENTS.md, so the same content reaches GLM in both ZCode and Claude Code.

claim: Put a skill's trigger conditions in the first 250 characters of its description, and keep few skills enabled.
quote: Each turn injects the metadata of every enabled skill (name plus a description excerpt of up to 250 characters) into the model context; bodies are loaded on demand only when a skill is invoked.
source: Skill (ZCode docs)
detail: All skills share one metadata budget. Past it, 'the injection degrades to names only' and automatic triggering 'drop[s] sharply'. A description over 1024 characters drops the whole skill. A 'Vague description' is named as a reason a skill never triggers.

claim: Scope rules by path or topic and load them only when needed, rather than globally.
quote: If a rule can be loaded by path, do not load it globally; bring it into context only when needed.
source: Memory-mechanism (Z.ai Coding Plan docs)
detail: Z.ai recommends this, modelled on Claude Code's .claude/rules/. Its own ZCode harness does not support it: no path rules, no @import. The practice therefore holds only where the harness can scope rules. For portability across harnesses, the rules that matter must live in the root file.

claim: Z.ai says training on multi-day expert environments 'pushes the model toward taking ownership of substantial work end to end'. That describes what the lab intended in training, not a measured behaviour. Z.ai never advises against step-by-step instructions; its best-practice page still recommends Goal/Context/Constraints/Done-when and planning first for complex tasks.

claim:
Observed changes, from the lab's own releases:
- **Two-month cadence.** Flagships ship roughly every two months: GLM-4.5 in Jul 2025, 4.6 in Sep, 4.7 in Dec, 5 in Feb 2026, 5.1 in Apr, 5.2 in Jun, 5.3 in Aug. Speed and flash variants follow in between.
- **Target moved from chat to long-horizon work.** Each release pushes further: agentic, reasoning and coding in one model (4.5); 'agentic engineering' (5); 8-hour autonomous runs (5.1); a usable 1M context (5.2); RL on synthesised, verifier-checked environments shaped like multi-day expert work (5.3).
- **Reasoning became mandatory and effort-scaled.** It went from caller-toggled hybrid (4.5/4.6), to on by default with per-turn toggles and preserved reasoning across turns (4.7), to effort levels (5.2), to forced on with only low, high or max (5.3). Prompt-level thinking cues and thinking toggles are now obsolete; depth is a harness parameter.
- **Gains now come from post-training.** GLM-5.3 kept the 5.2 base. Z.ai explicitly trains the model to own the work end to end rather than rely on users to decompose tasks. The instruction style that fits is outcome, bounds and a verifiable done condition, not step lists.

The lab acknowledges costs of this approach:
- **Reward hacking.** It reports more of it in 5.2 than in 5.1, and now runs anti-hack guards during training and evaluation.
- **Token use.** Independent measurement shows it rising: Artificial Analysis measured GLM-5.2 at 43k tokens per task against 26k for 5.1, and calls GLM-5.3 (max) 'very verbose'. This conflicts with Z.ai's own efficiency claims.
- **Instruction decay.** An instruction-following benchmark co-authored by Zhipu (MTAC-IFBench) shows process-constraint compliance decaying over long sessions even for GLM-5.2, which misses about 20%. Constraints hold best when they sit in the repository policy file.

Harness positioning is dual:
- **Built and benchmarked inside Claude Code.** GLM is served through an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, maps Claude Code's effort vocabulary, and Z.ai runs its own benchmarks in Claude Code 2.1.x. It is therefore most tuned to Claude Code's system prompt and tool conventions.
- **Z.ai's own harness standardises on AGENTS.md.** ZCode, the 'Official Harness for GLM-5.3', reads only AGENTS.md: no CLAUDE.md, no @imports, no nested or path-scoped rules. It adds a /goal mode whose completion check counts only evidence, and SKILL.md skills with a 250-character trigger excerpt.
- **The lab's own guidance converges on OutcomeBound's shape.** It recommends Goal / Context / Constraints / Done-when, concrete checkable rules kept in a repository file, and reports of what was verified versus what is uncovered. That is close to OutcomeBound's Outcome / Context / Bounds / Completion bar.

Direction of travel:
- more autonomy per instruction
- effort set as a parameter
- verification by evidence
- multimodal self-verification (the 5.3-Flash line)
- AGENTS.md-first native tooling, while staying compatible with Claude Code

One caution on comparisons: Z.ai's latest published comparisons (Aug 2026) benchmark against Claude Fable 5, Opus 4.8, Mythos 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol, not the later frontier the maintainer lists.

FORECAST, none released:

- **GLM-6.0, 'Full Self-Training'.** Secondary reports say Tang Jie named GLM-6.0 at the 2026-08-31 H1 results briefing as the next base model, targeting 'full self-training', meaning recursive self-improvement across pre-, mid- and post-training. No release date was given. The Wukong meeting minutes (2026-08-31) record the direction as 'larger effective scale, longer native context, and unified native multimodal modeling'. They also say 'Training of the next-generation base model has already begun' and that the next flagship will be production-ready on day one.
- **Flash recipe at larger scale.** Z.ai's GLM-5.3-Flash blog says 'We are now scaling this recipe to larger models', using hybrid sparse and linear attention, and that the lessons are 'already shaping our next frontier model'.
- **Environment generation.** The GLM-5.3 blog names making environment generation and verification more autonomous as 'one of the next steps'.
- **Open Fable-class model.** Latent Space (2026-08-20) reports Prof. Jie Tang's belief that an open-weights Fable-class model will exist by end of 2026. That is the stated ambition, not a product commitment.
- **Instruction handling.** No announced change to how the model loads instructions. On current trajectory, expect effort-parameter control, reasoning that is always on, and AGENTS.md-first native tooling in ZCode to continue.

**Two routes into GLM.** GLM reaches coding agents in two ways. One is third-party harnesses through the GLM Coding Plan. The other is Z.ai's own ZCode. How instructions load depends entirely on the harness; the model itself loads nothing.

**1. Claude Code (Z.ai's primary third-party target).**
- **Setup.** Configured in ~/.claude/settings.json with these env values:
  - ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://api.z.ai/api/anthropic
  - ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set to the key
  - ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL, ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL and ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL mapped to glm-5.3[1m] or glm-5.3-flash[1m]
  - CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW=1000000
- **Instruction loading.** GLM then receives Claude Code's own system prompt, CLAUDE.md with @imports, rules, skills and memory exactly as Claude Code loads them.
- **Effort mapping.** /effort maps onto GLM effort. 'disabled' or 'none' becomes low; medium or high becomes high; xhigh, max or ultra becomes max. The default is max.
- **Evaluation harness.** Z.ai runs its GLM-5.x benchmarks in Claude Code 2.1.x: Terminal-Bench 3.0, ALE, CyberGym, ExploitGym, PostTrainBench and SWE-Marathon for 5.3. Z.ai's 'best reported harness' on Terminal-Bench for GLM-5.1 and 5.2 is Claude Code.
- **Measured compliance.** MTAC-IFBench measured higher GLM-5.2 compliance under Claude Code than under OpenCode.

**2. Other tools on the supported list.**
- **Coding agents:** ZCode, Claude Code, Claude for IDE, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Cursor, Cline, TRAE, Qoder, Droid, Kilo Code, Roo Code, Crush, Goose, Eigent.
- **General-purpose agents:** AutoClaw, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, SillyTavern.
- **Endpoints:**
  - Anthropic Messages: /api/anthropic
  - OpenAI Chat Completions: /api/coding/paas/v4
  - OpenAI Responses, for Codex through ~/.codex/models.json and config.toml: /api/v1
- **Instruction files.** Each tool loads instructions by its own conventions. Z.ai's Codex and Cline pages do not describe instruction-file handling.

**3. ZCode, 'Official Harness for GLM-5.3'.**
- **AGENTS.md sources.** At task start ZCode reads two files: ~/.zcode/AGENTS.md, then the workspace AGENTS.md. Global is appended first and the workspace file is the primary source.
- **What it does not load.** It does not merge nested AGENTS.md files, scan child directories, expand @import or @include, or pick rule files by task type. CLAUDE.md is only a one-time migration source.
- **Subagents.** They inject both AGENTS.md files by default since v3.7.1; injectAgentsMd:false opts out, and the built-in Explore subagent does not inject them.
- **Skills.** Each is a SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter, stored under ~/.zcode/skills/. Every turn injects the name plus the first 250 characters of the description. A description over 1024 characters drops the skill. A shared budget degrades injection to names only when too many skills are enabled.
- **Memory.** Optional and off by default. The MEMORY.md index lives under ~/.zcode/cli/memories/projects/<project>/memory/ and is loaded with a size cap.
- **/goal.** Runs a separate completion check each round that counts only evidence.

**4. Raw API and open weights.**
- **Thinking.** Thinking is forced on for 5.3 and 5.3-Flash; reasoning_effort takes low, high or max, default max.
- **Preserved thinking.** It requires returning reasoning_content unmodified. It is on by default on the Coding Plan endpoint and off on the standard API. The open-weights template defaults clear_thinking to false.
- **Tools and sampling.** tool_choice supports only 'auto'. Sampling defaults are temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95; tune one of them, not both.

**Implication for OutcomeBound.** A self-contained root AGENTS.md, with CLAUDE.md importing it, reaches GLM in both Claude Code and ZCode. Do not depend on @imports, nested files or path-scoped rules for anything that must load under ZCode. Put each skill's trigger condition in the first 250 characters of its description.

**Newer than the list, but variants rather than a new flagship.** These releases post-date glm-5.3 but none replaces it as the flagship:
- **GLM-5.3-Flash (2026-08-26).** A new base model: 320B-A18B, open weights, the first natively multimodal GLM-5 model, and the Coding Plan default in Z.ai's Claude Code guide.
- **GLM-5.3-FlashX (listed on OpenRouter 2026-09-18).** A roughly 200 tokens/s speed variant of 5.3-Flash.
- **GLM-5.3-Prime (listed on OpenRouter 2026-09-23).** GLM-5.3's own weights behind faster inference, at 1.5–2× throughput and $2.80 in / $8.80 out per million tokens. docs.z.ai has no page for it; docs.z.ai/guides/llm/glm-5.3-prime returned Page Not Found on 2026-09-25.

**Announced but not released: GLM-6.0.** It is named only in secondary reports of the 2026-08-31 H1 results call, not by a Z.ai page I could read. There is no date, card or weights. GLM-5.3 remains the flagship on docs.z.ai as of 2026-09-25.

**Release-date discrepancies across sources:**
- GLM-5.3: blog and Coding Plan 2026-08-14; API release note 2026-08-18; Hugging Face repo created 2026-08-25.
- GLM-5.2: Coding Plan 2026-06-13; weights and blog 2026-06-16. Interconnects says June 22.

source: Qwen Code docs: Agent Skills

source: Qwen Code docs: Common workflows, Enforce evidence-based conclusions

It also says '"back every claim with a query result" works better than "be careful"' and to keep the policy short. It matches OutcomeBound's PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED rule.

claim:
Observed changes, from primary sources, 2025-04 to 2026-09:

(1) Where thinking is controlled has moved from the prompt to the API and harness. Qwen3 had in-prompt /think and /no_think tags. Qwen3-2507 split into separate Instruct and Thinking models. From Qwen3.5 on, models think by default and the soft switch is gone. Qwen3.8 adds reasoning_effort tiers (xhigh default). In the open weights that tier is a natural-language line the chat template injects into the system message, and the open 2.4T Max cannot turn thinking off at all.

(2) Reasoning now persists across turns. The Qwen3/3.5 rule was 'no thinking content in history'. Qwen3.6 added preserve_thinking as an opt-in; 3.7 recommended it for agents; 3.8 made it the default. QwenCloud now says omitting reasoning_content from tool round-trips degrades accuracy.

(3) Specialist coding models have given way to general 'coding and cowork' flagships trained for long horizons. The line runs from Qwen3-Coder (non-thinking) and Coder-Next to 3.7-Max (35-hour runs) and 3.8-Max (10+ day runs, 'self-evolving' feedback loops). Qwen3.8 adds a universal reward system spanning execution checks, rubrics and agentic inspection, and Alibaba publicly claims progress on recursive self-improvement.

(4) Qwen is being trained to work in whichever harness it is dropped into. From 3.7 the lab runs cross-harness RL (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, Qwen Code, Hermes, QwenWork). Its APIs speak both the Anthropic and OpenAI Responses protocols, and its headline SWE numbers are measured in Claude Code. Qwen Code itself now reads AGENTS.md and pushes toward short resident context, path-gated rules, skills, hooks for hard gates, evidence policies, and bounded, verified subagents.

(5) Capability and verbosity rise together. On the same Artificial Analysis index (v4.3.2), tokens used went from 95M (Qwen3.5-397B) to 120M (3.7 Max) to 190M (3.8 Max 0902), while the score went from 18 to 29 to 45. Community reports of runaway thinking on the local 27B are common.

(6) Openness has swung. Max models were closed through 3.7-Max; 3.8 open-weighted a Max-class 2.4T model under a custom license, alongside Apache-2.0 27B and Flash-Next models.

Direction for OutcomeBound (inference): state outcomes, bounds and verifiers portably in AGENTS.md, and leave thinking depth, tool format and output budget to harness parameters. Keep always-loaded text short and put must-hold rules in deterministic checks. Expect a Qwen model to read the same kernel under Claude Code, Codex or Qwen Code. Lab-claimed harness invariance and multi-day autonomy are not independently verified. The independent measurements so far are Vals and Arena placements, Artificial Analysis scores and verbosity, and a small Kodesage test.

FORECAST, not a release.

Primary source: at Apsara on 2026-09-22, Alibaba stated 'Next-generation Qwen 4 Model in training' and announced a roadmap for 'Qwen 4.5 and Qwen 5 model series, projected to scale up to 5 to 10 trillion parameters'. No date, specs or pricing were given.

Architecture preview: per the lab, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (2026-08-27) previews Qwen4's architecture. It uses Gated DeltaNet plus Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA), Gated Residual, N-gram Embedding and the Muon optimizer, has 262K native context extensible to 1M, and costs far less to train and serve. Expect Qwen4 to keep the current API surface: thinking on by default, reasoning_effort tiers, preserve_thinking, and Anthropic and OpenAI-Responses compatibility. That continuity is my inference, not an Alibaba statement.

Secondary only, not in Alibaba's press release: OrcaRouter (2026-09-22) reports four tiers were previewed on stage, namely Qwen 4 Max, Plus, Flash and 27B open weights.

Alibaba also claims recursive self-improvement progress: Qwen3.8-Max ran 33 automated cycles and raised its Artificial Analysis score from 40 to 45, and Eddie Wu said the team 'plans to train a new model at the scale of 5 to 10 trillion-parameter'.

The maintainer expects Qwen 4.0 soon. Nothing in the primary sources dates it.

Qwen Code (QwenLM/qwen-code) was forked from Gemini CLI in July 2025; the current release is v0.24.5 (2026-09-24).

Context files:
- The default names are QWEN.md and AGENTS.md, both loaded, with QWEN.md first for /init. memory-constants.ts: 'It defaults to include both QWEN.md and AGENTS.md'. Override the names with the context.fileName setting (a string or an array).
- Discovery order:
  1. Global ~/.qwen/QWEN.md.
  2. For each file name, an upward scan from the CWD to the project root. The root is the nearest ancestor with a .git directory or a .git file, so git worktrees count. The scan runs only in trusted folders.
  3. Extension context files.
  4. A fixed-slot <projectRoot>/.qwen/QWEN.local.md, loaded last so it can 'supplement or override' the shared files. Users must gitignore it themselves.
- @path imports resolve relative to the importing file. /init generates a starter QWEN.md.
- Context files and baseline rules are resident on every request.

Rules, skills and memory:
- .qwen/rules/*.md files without paths: are baseline, part of the system prompt from the first request. Files with paths: globs are injected once, when a matching file is read or edited. Extension rules must be conditional.
- Skills live in ~/.qwen/skills and .qwen/skills as SKILL.md. Only name and description are listed until invoked. Skills can be paths-gated, can declare frontmatter hooks for hard gates, and can be turned off with skills.disabled or defaultDisabled.
- Auto-memory lives in ~/.qwen/projects/<project>/memory/ with a MEMORY.md index, one folder per worktree. Team memory in .qwen/team-memory/ is opt-in.
- /context detail reports the per-item resident cost.

Subagents: built-in subagents carry guardrails. They take bounded, independent work with disjoint write scopes, the parent reviews their claims, and fork agents do not commit unless asked.

Other harnesses: the lab also positions Qwen under Claude Code (Anthropic-compatible endpoint, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/apps/anthropic), Codex (OpenAI Responses via a model catalog), OpenClaw, Qoder, Hermes and QwenWork. Each harness's own context-file convention then applies; for example, Gloaguen et al. wrote the file to CLAUDE.md for Claude Code and to AGENTS.md for Codex and Qwen Code.

Model level (Qwen3.8 chat template): the system turn is built in this order:
1. The reasoning-effort sentence (xhigh or low; nothing for medium).
2. If tools are present, the '# Tools' block and the strict XML <tool_call><function=...><parameter=...> instructions.
3. The caller's system content, which is where a harness typically places AGENTS.md.
Thinking is wrapped in <think>. Historical thinking is kept unless preserve_thinking=false. Self-hosting needs the qwen3 reasoning parser and the qwen3_coder tool parser in vLLM or SGLang.

The maintainer's list ends at 'qwen-3.8-max'; the API id is qwen3.8-max, released 2026-08-03. These Qwen releases are newer, per primary sources:
- qwen3.8-max-0902 (alias qwen3.8-max-2026-09-02), a post-training snapshot released 2026-09-02. Per the Model Studio notice, the qwen3.8-max endpoint switched to it automatically on 2026-09-05 at 10:00 UTC+8, so 'qwen3.8-max' now means the 0902 weights.
- Open-weight Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B (about 2026-08-12/13, custom license) and Qwen3.8-27B (about 2026-08-13/14, Apache-2.0).
- qwen3.8-flash (API, 2026-08-26) and the open Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (blog 2026-08-27), explicitly 'an early preview of the architecture used in Qwen4'.
- qwen3.8-omni-flash (QwenCloud changelog 2026-09-18; blog 2026-09-20), built on the Flash-Next architecture.

No Qwen 4 model has been released as of 2026-09-25.

Quote is on the 2025-03-25 post, and the model id gemini-2.5-pro-exp-03-25 appears on it. The post says '2.5 models are thinking models'. 'On by default' is inferred, not stated. Google's first thinking model was 2.0 Flash Thinking.
quote: Going forward, we’re building these thinking capabilities directly into all of our models, so they can handle more complex problems and support even more capable, context-aware agents.

claim: Google calls it 'our first fully hybrid reasoning model', meaning Google's first, not the industry's. The 0–24576 range and gemini-2.5-flash-preview-04-17 are both on the page, which is dated April 17, 2025.

claim: The 2025-06-17 changelog entry says 'now with adaptive thinking' only for gemini-2.5-pro; gemini-2.5-flash is 'our first stable 2.5 Flash model'. The temperature point is not on the changelog. It comes from the Gemini 3 guide: 'previous models often benefited from tuning temperature'.

original_claim: Brought in thinking_level (low/high, default high) in place of thinking_budget, thought signatures and per-item media_resolution. Guidance: keep temperature at 1.0 because lower values can cause looping, drop chain-of-thought scaffolding, and write concise, direct prompts. Launched alongside Google Antigravity. Shut down 2026-03-09 and redirected to 3.1 Pro.

claim: Most of the row checks out on the 3.5 page: default medium (was high), improved low, thought preservation, sampling and thinking_budget 'no longer recommended'. The Antigravity CLI transition was announced at I/O on 2026-05-19. The Interactions API did not become the 'primary API' with 3.5 Flash. original_claim: Default effort changed from high to medium, and 'low' improved for short agentic tasks. The behaviour sentence states Google's own 'What's new' description as fact. It should say: Google says 3.6 Flash uses fewer reasoning steps, turns and tool calls, reduces unwanted file changes during diagnostic tasks, and runs diagnostic scripts before changes more often.

The model uses fewer tokens and turns, makes fewer unwanted edits during diagnostic tasks, and runs more upfront diagnostic scripts. Google says these API changes apply to 'all future Gemini model releases'.

claim: The quote is in Google's 2026-08-13 post, which also claims high adherence to reference designs. The model page says 'Supported (low, medium, high). Note: minimal is not supported and returns an error'. The Aug 2026 archive of the latest-model page gives medium as the default.

original_claim: The 'minimal' thinking level was removed (low/medium/high, default medium). Google says the model clarifies intent when needed, follows instructions more faithfully and is more diligent in planning and tool calls, and that it adheres better to reference designs.

model: Gemini 3.8 Flash (gemini-3.8-flash, GA) — current Gemini frontier text model
claim: GA on 2026-09-02. The latest-model page has the quote, the effort guidance, minimal returning an error, and the Antigravity agent default. 'Works harder' is from Google's blog ('3.8 Flash works harder'). The March 2026 partial cutoff is from the DeepMind model card, not this page: some domains are limited to January 2025.

original_claim: Google designed it to 'work harder': it takes smaller reasoning steps, calls tools iteratively and checks its own work, which costs more tokens. Effort level is the documented cost control, and 'minimal' returns an error. It is the default model for the Antigravity managed agent. Knowledge cutoff is March 2026, but only partial. Sampling parameters are ignored.

claim: Write short, direct instructions and drop elaborate prompt engineering carried over from older models
quote: Be concise. Gemini 3.x responds best to direct, clear instructions. Verbose or complex prompt engineering techniques designed for older models may cause the model to over-analyze.
source: What's new in Gemini 3.5 Flash (Gemini API docs)
detail: Stated for 'all Gemini 3.x models'. The same wording has appeared in Google's Gemini 3 guide since Nov 2025. For OutcomeBound this supports a small, plain kernel over long, heavily worded rule lists.

claim: The wording is also in the Nov 2025 archive of the Gemini 3 guide.
quote: If you were previously using complex prompt engineering (like chain of thought) to force Gemini 2.5 to reason, try Gemini 3 with thinking_level: "high" and simplified prompts.
source: Gemini 3 developer guide (now marked deprecated, superseded by the 3.5 guide)

claim: Applies from Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash-Lite onward, per the archived page. For earlier 3.x models Google says 'no longer recommended'.
quote: temperature, top_p, and top_k are deprecated and ignored. In future model generations, supplying these parameters returns an HTTP 400 error. Remove these parameters from all requests.
source: Using the latest Gemini models (3.6 Flash & 3.5 Flash-Lite guide, archived snapshot)
original_claim: Remove temperature/top_p/top_k from every request; sampling is no longer a control surface

The Antigravity managed agent already returns 400 for temperature, top_p, top_k, stop_sequences and max_output_tokens.

quote: To ensure determinism, we recommend defining a system instruction with explicit rules for your specific use case.
source: What's new in Gemini 3.5 Flash (Gemini API docs)

source: What's new in Gemini 3.8 Flash (Gemini API docs)
detail: Google's 3.8 launch post says '3.8 Flash works harder… executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively.' Inference, not stated by Google: prompts that demand repeated self-checks now duplicate trained-in behaviour and add cost. Checks sized to the risk are the better fit.

claim: This is AA's own measurement at high reasoning: $0.58 per task against $0.40 for 3.7 Flash, with per-token pricing unchanged.
quote: This is comparable to GPT-5.6 Terra (max, $0.53), but ~40% higher than its predecessor, driven by a 30% increase in average output tokens per task to 48k and increased turns on agentic evaluations
source: Artificial Analysis: Google has released Gemini 3.8 Flash
original_claim: Budget for rising per-task token use on the newest Flash; cost per task can grow even when the per-token price does not
detail: Independent measurement: Intelligence Index 59 at high effort, $0.58 per task, and 2.5 minutes per task, up from 2.2 on 3.7 Flash. At low effort it costs $0.24 per task and takes 0.8 minutes. The Register (2026-09-02) independently reported the same ~40% per-task increase. Earlier, 3.6 Flash had cut output tokens 17% compared with 3.5 Flash (Google citing AA).

quote: Higher thinking levels encourage the model to use more tools to explore and verify, so lowering the level can reduce tool calls.
source: What's new in Gemini 3.5 Flash (Gemini API docs)
detail: Google's example system instruction: 'You have a limited action budget of <n> tool calls. Use them efficiently.' Google also says to try lower levels or system instructions to reduce tool calls in agentic workflows.

claim: Separate prompt parts with one consistent format: either XML-style tags or Markdown headings, not both
quote: Employ clear delimiters to separate different parts of your prompt. XML-style tags (e.g., <context>, <task>) or Markdown headings are effective. Choose one format and use it consistently within a single prompt.
source: Prompt design strategies — Gemini 3 section (Gemini API docs)
detail: Same guidance for long contexts: supply all the data first, put the question at the very end, and bridge with a line like 'Based on the information above...'. Markdown-only AGENTS.md files already meet this.

claim: Put critical behavioural constraints, role and output-format requirements in the system instruction or at the very start of the prompt
quote: Place essential behavioral constraints, role definitions (persona), and output format requirements in the System Instruction or at the very beginning of the user prompt.
source: Prompt design strategies — Gemini 3 section (Gemini API docs)
detail: This favours an always-loaded kernel that is short and front-loaded with bounds and the reporting contract. Gemini CLI and Antigravity inject instruction files into the system-prompt region.

claim: State goals plainly; avoid persuasive or emphatic language
quote: Be precise and direct: State your goal clearly and concisely. Avoid unnecessary or overly persuasive language.
source: Prompt design strategies — Gemini 3 section (Gemini API docs)
detail: Google's practice is mixed. Its evaluated agentic template and the Gemini CLI system prompt (snippets.ts, 2026-09) still use MUST, ALWAYS and NEVER heavily. The written guidance favours plain wording, but that is not proven against emphatic phrasing for Gemini.

claim: Google lists these as behaviour dimensions 'you can steer' for agents. It is not a flat instruction.
quote: Ambiguity and permission handling: Defines when the model is permitted to make assumptions versus when it must pause execution to ask the user for clarification or permission.
source: Prompt design strategies — Agentic workflows (Gemini API docs)
original_claim: Tell agents explicitly how to treat risk (reads versus writes) and when to assume versus stop and ask for permission
detail: Google lists dimensions to steer: logical decomposition, problem diagnosis, how exhaustive to be, adaptability, persistence and recovery, risk assessment ('Explicitly distinguishes between low-risk exploratory actions (reads) and high-risk state changes (writes)'), verbosity, and precision. This lines up closely with OutcomeBound's Bounds, irreversible edges, and its rule to decide what can be decided and stop only at new authority.

claim: The text is from Google's example agentic system-instruction template, rule 8.2.
quote: On *other* errors, you must change your strategy or arguments, not repeat the same failed call.
source: Prompt design strategies — System instruction template (Gemini API docs)

detail: Google says researchers evaluated the template and it improved results on agentic rulebook-and-user benchmarks. That is Google's own claim, and it was written for Gemini 3 Pro. The template also has the model plan before every action and 'Inhibit your response' until reasoning is done. With 3.7/3.8's trained-in diligence, that part may now add tokens; this is an inference, not measured.

claim: Do not require structured text (XML/JSON/YAML status blocks) immediately before a tool call; use a dedicated update() tool call or Markdown headers, or drop the requirement
quote: If your prompt requires the model to output structured text (XML, YAML, JSON, etc.) (e.g., <UPDATE>...</UPDATE>) immediately before making a tool call, the tool call may occasionally fail with Malformed_Function_Call.
source: Function calling — Workarounds for pre-tool text requirements (Gemini API docs)
detail: Google's 3.8 Flash checklist and the Google Cloud 3.8 guide both repeat this. For OutcomeBound: do not mandate structured status or report blocks as a preamble to actions; ask for them at the handoff instead.

claim: Put extra instructions returned with tool output inside the function-response text, after two newlines, not as a separate part
quote: Instead, append any extra instructions to the end of the function response text separated by two newlines.
source: What's new in Gemini 3.5 Flash (Gemini API docs)
detail: Google warns that separate parts can cause 'thought leakage' and lower quality. The same applies to multimodal content, which belongs inside the function response. This matters for any engine whose check output goes back to the model through a tool.

claim: Stop prefilling the model turn to force formats or suppress preambles; use the system instruction or structured outputs
quote: If your application previously prefilled a model turn to suppress preambles or force JSON formatting, use system_instruction or Structured outputs instead.
source: Using the latest Gemini models (3.6 Flash guide, archived snapshot)
detail: Since 3.6 Flash and for 'all future Gemini model releases', a request whose last non-empty turn is a model turn returns HTTP 400.

claim: Google words this conditionally ('if ... the model ignores your custom tools in favor of bash'). It applies to gemini-3.1-pro-preview, and the changelog adds 'for users building with a mix of bash and tools'. Exposing helpers as shell commands is an inference, not Google advice.

The Antigravity 09-2026 agent also added built-in find_by_name and grep_search because earlier 'agents used shell commands'.

claim: Earlier versions' behaviour is only implied by 'reduces'. The diagnosis-only advice is an inference.

source: Using the latest Gemini models (3.6 Flash guide, archived snapshot)

The same page says 3.6 'prefers running diagnostic code scripts before making changes', which can add exploratory steps on simple work. Instructions that name what the agent owns and whether writes are in scope make the diagnose-versus-change line explicit.

claim: Confirmed: snippets.ts last changed 2026-09-08. The same file says GEMINI.md instructions 'take absolute precedence over the general workflows and tool defaults'. Note that Google moved consumer users from Gemini CLI to Antigravity CLI on 2026-06-18.

source: Gemini CLI system prompt source (packages/core/src/prompts/snippets.ts, main)

Precedence runs Sub-directories > Workspace Root > Extensions > Global. claim: This is AA's independent measurement: AA-Omniscience hallucination rate fell from 88% (3 Pro Preview) to 50% (3.1 Pro Preview).

source: Artificial Analysis: Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview — the new leader in AI

claim: This is not independent practitioner evidence. It is Zvi Mowshowitz's commentary on the same AA-Omniscience result (88% hallucination rate for Gemini 3 Pro), stated just before the quote. It restates the AA measurement rather than corroborating it.

source: Zvi Mowshowitz — Gemini 3 Pro Is a Vast Intelligence With No Spine

This covers Gemini 3 Pro; the 3.1 Pro measurement above shows improvement, and no comparable independent data was found for 3.5–3.8 Flash.

claim: The page also sets a 24 KB per-file truncation limit.
quote: If the total exceeds 20,000 tokens, Antigravity automatically demotes the largest rule files from inline text to lightweight pointers ( - <path>: <description> ), allowing the agent to read them on demand.
source: Rules | Google Antigravity Docs
original_claim: Keep always-on instruction files small; Antigravity caps them and demotes oversized rules to on-demand pointers
detail: Each rule file is capped at 24,000 bytes and truncated beyond that. AGENTS.md and GEMINI.md are always on for their directory scope and take no frontmatter. Files under .agents/rules/*.md need a valid trigger (always_on, model_decision, glob or manual), or they are silently discarded.

claim: Google gives these clauses only under 'Gemini 3 Flash strategies', with the cutoff clause fixed at 'January 2025'. They are not general guidance for all Gemini models. Gemini 3.8 Flash has a partial March 2026 cutoff.

source: Prompt design strategies — Gemini 3 Flash strategies (Gemini API docs)

claim: This is migration guidance for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, whose default is minimal: set thinking_level to medium or high for autonomous subagents so tool use does not stop too early. It is not stated for small or fast subagent models in general.

source: Using the latest Gemini models (3.5 Flash-Lite migration, archived snapshot)

claim: The quote is the 2026-07-21 changelog entry for 3.6 Flash. That default verbosity shifts between versions is an inference from it.
quote: Features improved token efficiency and code/agentic planning capabilities at a lower price point than 3.5 Flash, resolving developer feedback around output verbosity.
source: Gemini API release notes — July 21, 2026 (Gemini 3.6 Flash)
