detail: Several labs make the same claim. DeepSeek V4.1 trains across four Claude Code versions plus OpenCode, Pi and its own harness. MiMo V2.6 mixes harnesses in every RL batch. NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron 3 Ultra for consistency across harnesses. MiniMax trains under perturbed scaffolds. All of this is what the labs say about their own training.

claim: This is one lab measuring one model (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash) on two benchmarks. Across eight scaffold configurations, scores spread by up to about 9 points on DeepSWE v1.1 (65.5 to 74.2) and 6.5 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, which is more than 'a few points'. The minimal scaffolds (mini-SWE, DeepSeek Harness Minimal) scored highest. NVIDIA reports a similar 65-70.4% SWE-bench Verified range for Nemotron 3 Ultra. The page does not establish a general rule about heavy scaffolding and a model's ceiling.
quote: The model’s agentic capabilities transfer well across scaffold families with different prompts and tool interfaces, rather than depending on conventions specific to a particular harness.
source: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash: Pushing the Limits of KV Cache Compression
original_claim: Expect the same open-weight model to score only a few points differently across harnesses. Minimal scaffolds do as well as heavy ones, so heavy scaffolding does not raise the model's ceiling.
detail: DeepSeek measured this itself, with no experimental system prompt added. DeepSWE v1.1: Claude Code 69.8, Codex 65.6, OpenCode 65.5, Pi 66.2, mini-SWE 74.2, DeepSeek Harness Minimal 72.6. Across four Claude Code versions the average is 68.9. Kimi reports K3 at 72.9 in Kimi Code and 73.7 in Claude Code on its own Kimi Code Bench 2.0.

claim: Evidence is from DeepSeek Harness, which does load CLAUDE.md but not @imports or .claude/rules. Kimi Code's loader (context.ts) goes further and reads only AGENTS.md, agents.md and .kimi-code/AGENTS.md, not CLAUDE.md, which strengthens the advice.
quote: lowercase names, `.claude/rules/`, and `@path` imports are not interpreted
source: @deepseek-ai/dsh-agent-instructions README (DeepSeek Harness)
original_claim: Keep the full canonical guidance in AGENTS.md. Do not depend on CLAUDE.md @imports, .claude/rules or other Claude-only conventions reaching open-weight harnesses.
detail: DeepSeek Harness loads AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, plus the .local overlays. Kimi Code's loader reads only .kimi-code/AGENTS.md, AGENTS.md and agents.md; CLAUDE.md is not on its list. OpenCode reads CLAUDE.md only when no AGENTS.md exists. So a CLAUDE.md that only says @AGENTS.md is ignored by Kimi Code, loses to AGENTS.md in OpenCode, and in DeepSeek Harness loads as a harmless literal extra file.

claim: Kimi Code only warns when the loaded AGENTS.md chain exceeds its recommended 32 KB ('consider trimming'); it drops nothing. Dropping broad files first is DeepSeek Harness behaviour: its default budget is 65,536 bytes, and it omits broader files before truncating the most specific one. That is one harness, not harness budgets in general.
quote: Large instruction files increase cost and may impact performance; consider trimming.
source: Kimi Code CLI source: agent/profile/context.ts (AGENTS_MD_RECOMMENDED_MAX_BYTES = 32 KiB)
original_claim: Keep the always-loaded instruction chain well under 32 KB. Put scope-specific rules in nested files, because harness budgets drop broad files first.
detail: Kimi Code warns when all loaded AGENTS.md files together exceed 32 KiB. DeepSeek Harness caps the rendered baseline at 65,536 bytes by default. It drops broader files whole before truncating the most specific one, and shows a visible budget notice.

claim: Context: OctoBench is co-authored by MiniMax and Fudan and tested eight models from January 2026 (for example Claude Opus 4.5 and MiniMax-M2.1). In conflicts, both the system prompt and the user query overrode project documentation.
quote: we observe a consistent hierarchy where SP dominates MD and UQ dominates MD, while UQ vs SP exhibits the largest model-dependent variation
source: OctoBench: Benchmarking Scaffold-Aware Instruction Following in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding
original_claim: Treat instruction-file rules as the lowest-priority source. Enforce any constraint that must hold with deterministic checks or gates, not with prose alone.
detail: SP = system prompt, MD = project docs such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, UQ = user query. Harnesses frame the files the same way: DeepSeek Harness wraps them in a system-reminder that says they 'do not override system, developer, or direct user instructions'. The benchmark is published by MiniMax and covers the previous generation (MiniMax M2/M2.1, Kimi K2 Thinking, GLM-4.6, Opus 4.5).

claim: The CSR and ISR figures are supported. The claim that the drop was steeper for open-weight models is not. Overall ISR: Claude Opus 4.5 28.1% and open MiniMax-M2.1 18.2% lead; closed Gemini-3-Pro and Claude Sonnet 4.5 follow (about 14.7%); the lowest is closed Doubao-Seed-1.8 (9.7%). Only Opus 4.5 stands clearly apart.
quote: the CSR converges within a high range from 79.75% to 85.64% across all models, suggesting that current LLMs are generally capable of instruction following. However, the ISR exhibits a precipitous drop to a range between 9.66% and 28.11%.
source: OctoBench (MiniMax)
original_claim: Load fewer rules that each carry weight. Models follow most individual rules but rarely all of them at once, and the drop was steeper for open-weight models.

claim: The benchmark measured compliance with constraints written in Skill.md, not automatic pickup. It was the weakest category for every model, including closed ones: Opus 4.5 58%, Sonnet 4.5 52%, Gemini-3-Pro 43%, Doubao 31%, against 12-43% for the open models, all January 2026 models. So the advice holds more broadly than for open-weight models alone.
quote: For instance, in the Skill category, Claude-Opus-4.5 reaches an ISR of 58.45% whereas MiniMax-M2.1 falls to 12.33%, compared to the relatively high ISR band observed for System reminder and Memory categories.
source: OctoBench (MiniMax)
original_claim: Do not rely on skill files being picked up automatically for gating steps on open-weight models. Name them explicitly in the task or back them with a deterministic guard.
detail: Skill.md constraints were the hardest category to comply with. Harnesses are moving the same way: Kimi recommends on-demand tool retrieval over declaring everything up front, and DeepSeek Harness bundles skills with progressive disclosure.

claim: The paper names only Claude Opus 4.5 as the exception and says that robustness was 'absent in other evaluated models', which includes Claude Sonnet 4.5. The finding covers all tested models except Opus 4.5, not non-Claude models. The paper does not test harness reminders or compaction as a remedy.
quote: Instruction following capability generally exhibits a negative correlation with interaction length, with Claude-Opus-4.5 being a notable exception.
source: OctoBench (MiniMax)
original_claim: Expect compliance to fade as a session grows on non-Claude models. Keep the constraints that matter short enough to restate, and rely on harness reminders and compaction to bring them back.
detail: A May 2026 factorial study of Claude Code found a similar effect within a session: about 5.6% lower odds of compliance per generated function (arXiv 2605.10039). Kimi Code injects a reminder to read any AGENTS.md that applies to paths the agent touches, or that changed on disk after loading.

claim: Pass the model's full reasoning history back on every turn, including across user turns in tool-using sessions. This is harness and engine plumbing, not instruction prose.
quote: Kimi K3 was trained in the preserved thinking history mode. For multi-turn conversations and tool calls, Kimi K3 requires the complete assistant message returned by the API to be passed back to `messages` as-is
source: Kimi K3 model README
detail: The same requirement appears for MiniMax M2, which says dropping the history caused most reported gaps, for DeepSeek V4, which keeps reasoning across user turns in tool calls, and for Kimi K2.7 Code, where preserved thinking is forced on. It matters to OutcomeBound only where its eval runner or engine calls these APIs directly.

claim: Replace blanket 'think step by step' wording with the effort setting plus a request sized to the task: deep for planning and debugging, direct for extraction and formatting.
quote: Ask for deeper analysis when the task involves planning, debugging, tradeoffs, or long-horizon execution. Ask for a direct answer when the task is extraction, rewriting, or formatting.
source: MiniMax Token Plan: Prompting Best Practices
detail: The same page lists 'Think step by step for every request, then answer.' as the less effective form. Every model in this sweep now exposes an effort setting (Kimi K3 low/high/max defaulting to max; DeepSeek low/high/max or 1–100 defaulting to high; MiniMax M3 enabled/adaptive/disabled). Reasoning depth is therefore set by configuration, not by prompt boilerplate.

claim: DeepSeek's wording is low for simple tasks, high for daily agent workflows, and max for complex tasks. So max is not the recommendation for routine agentic coding. Kimi K3 defaults to max.
quote: Flexible reasoning effort for V4-Pro & V4-Flash: low for simple tasks, high for daily Agent workflows, max for complex tasks.
source: DeepSeek-V4-Pro GA Release
original_claim: Match effort to the task and let harness configuration carry it, not the kernel text. Vendors recommend max effort for complex agentic coding.
detail: DeepSeek's and Kimi's Claude Code setup guides both set CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL=max. Kimi's guide warns that lower values may reduce quality on complex tasks.

claim: Give the reason behind each bound or constraint, not only the rule.
quote: When you explain why a constraint matters, the model can choose better tradeoffs.
source: MiniMax Token Plan: Prompting Best Practices
detail: MiniMax's guide largely mirrors Anthropic-style guidance: be clear and direct, the 'show it to a colleague' golden rule, add context, well-chosen examples. This points to prompting advice converging across closed and open families.

claim: State explicit stopping and escalation rules for agentic work: use tools only when they change the answer, confirm before destructive or external writes, stop after repeated failures.
quote: In agentic workflows, set clear stopping rules. The model should use tools when they materially improve the answer, not just to appear busy.
source: MiniMax Token Plan: Prompting Best Practices
detail: The recommended rule set includes 'Ask for confirmation before destructive actions, purchases, messages, or external writes' and 'If a tool fails twice, stop retrying and explain the blocker.' This matches OutcomeBound's bounds and irreversible edges.

claim: Keep system and instruction prompts concise when the harness compacts context. Some open models end tasks early as they near the context limit.
quote: In tools that support context compression (such as Claude Code), keep system prompts concise. The model may terminate tasks early when approaching context capacity thresholds.
source: MiniMax Token Plan: Prompting Best Practices
detail: For long tasks MiniMax suggests a line such as 'Make full use of the available context window. Complete each part thoroughly before continuing'. DeepSeek and Kimi also tell Claude Code users to set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW to match the model's 1M window.

claim: This is one practitioner's small test: Kimi K3 in Claude Code, one task, three runs each way. Cutting the same run from 28 tools to 11 cut output tokens by 20.3% and thinking tokens by 41.9%, and the pass rate held. Skill listings were not tested, and one model on one task does not establish a general rule.
quote: Cutting the same run from 28 tools to 11 — same model and same task — cut output tokens 20.3% and thinking tokens 41.9%.
source: Putting Kimi K3 to the (Claude Code) Test (Raffi Krikorian)
original_claim: Shrink the always-loaded payload: tool schemas, standing instructions, skill listings. A wider decision space costs reasoning tokens without changing the pass rate.
detail: A practitioner's personal eval: 30 runs over 2 tasks, so small n. The same post finds that 63–81% of every input token was the harness describing itself, about 20k tokens per request, across all five setups. Kimi's docs agree: declaring every tool 'eat[s] up context and make[s] the model more likely to pick the wrong tool.'

claim: The evidence is a DeepSeek internal survey (N=85 DeepSeek developers) about DeepSeek-V4-Pro alone. Respondents noted trivial mistakes, misinterpretation of vague prompts and occasional over-thinking. That is one model, reported by its own lab, not open-weight models in general.
quote: Respondents find DeepSeek-V4-Pro to deliver satisfactory results across most tasks, but note trivial mistakes, misinterpretation of vague prompts, and occasional over-thinking.
source: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
original_claim: State the outcome and the definition of done explicitly. Open-weight models still misread vague prompts.
detail: A survey of DeepSeek's own developers: 52% said yes, 39% leaned yes to V4-Pro as their default coding model. The same report says V4-Pro 'occasionally overlooks specific formatting constraints and slightly trails Opus' on instruction following, and wins 46.9% against Opus 4.5's 53.1% on internal complex instruction following.

claim: Over-verification is documented for one model only: Tencent Hy4 preview, listed as a known issue at launch. Over-reasoning is also noted for DeepSeek-V4-Pro ('occasional over-thinking').
quote: we are shipping with known issues — among them, spending longer than necessary reasoning through complex tasks, and a tendency to over-verify its own work.
source: Tencent Hy4 preview model card
original_claim: Size verification to the changed risk rather than demanding blanket re-checking. Some current open models over-reason and over-verify by default.
detail: Hy4 preview was among OpenRouter's top programming models in September 2026 (read through a summarizer, not verbatim). DeepSeek's survey above also reports 'occasional over-thinking'. Instructions that stack extra checks can make this worse; a completion bar sized to risk counters it.

claim: The quote is supported, but 'recent open models tend toward minimal diffs and terse output' generalises from one open model. In one practitioner's two-task test, Kimi K3 (four configurations) added a single documentation line where Opus 5 rewrote the doc, and Kimi was far less verbose.
quote: Opus completely rewrote the markdown documenting how rule matching works for the routing task. Every other configuration added a single line.
source: Putting Kimi K3 to the (Claude Code) Test (Raffi Krikorian)
original_claim: Define what finishing means, including whether docs are in scope. Models differ in how much surrounding work they do by default. Recent open models tend toward minimal diffs and terse output.
detail: Two tasks only. Every configuration passed hidden tests 30 of 30 times and produced byte-identical code on one task. The author calls the doc-rewrite difference 'a different idea about what finishing a task means' and says Kimi was 'wayyyy less chatty'.

claim: Expect instruction files, hooks and slash commands to keep working when a different model runs inside the same harness. The harness loads the files, not the model.
quote: Slash commands still worked. Hooks still fired. CLAUDE.md still loaded.
source: Putting Kimi K3 to the (Claude Code) Test (Raffi Krikorian)
detail: DeepSeek, Kimi and MiniMax all publish Claude Code setup through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. DeepSeek maps claude-opus model names to V4-Pro and haiku/sonnet to V4.1-Flash. Kimi warns that setting only some tier variables makes subagent or summarization calls 'fail silently'. So OutcomeBound's Claude Code route reaches these models unchanged.

claim: DeepSeek says V4.1-Flash's near-parity on benchmarks does not mean it matches leading closed systems on 'complex, high-difficulty reasoning and edge cases'. The same paper reports V4.1-Flash ahead of Opus-5 on DeepSWE v1.1 and Terminal-Bench 2.1. So it does not establish that open-weight models trail on the hardest long-horizon agentic work. Keeping deterministic gates is still a reasonable recommendation.
quote: Although benchmark scores show a narrow margin, this parity does not imply that the model matches the frontier capabilities of leading closed-source systems on complex, high-difficulty reasoning and edge cases.
source: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash technical report
original_claim: Keep the deterministic support (gates, checks, guards) rather than trusting headline parity. Open-weight models still trail on the hardest long-horizon agentic work.
detail: DeepSeek's own table shows Terminal-Bench 2.1 saturated: V4.1-Flash 90.6, Opus-5.0 89.1, K3 88.3. On harder suites the gap is wide: Terminal-Bench 4.0 is 31.2 for V4.1-Flash against 51.8 for Opus-5.0 and 12.6 for K3. Kimi's blog also concedes K3 'still trails the most powerful proprietary models, Claude Fable 5 and GPT 5.6 Sol.'

claim: This is an Artificial Analysis snapshot dated 2026-04-30, covering Kimi K2.6, MiMo V2.5 Pro and DeepSeek V4 Pro against GPT-5.5. The gap was 3-6 points on the Intelligence Index and 'wide on the hardest reasoning and agentic coding evaluations'. It was about as large on CritPt (research physics: 4-12% vs 27%) and on Omniscience (knowledge and hallucination) as on TerminalBench Hard (43-46% vs 61%). The page does not show agentic coding alone as the largest gap.
quote: The gap to proprietary remains wide on the hardest reasoning and agentic coding evaluations.
source: Artificial Analysis: Recent open weights model launches
original_claim: Treat the closed and open gap as real and variable over time. Measured independently, it is smallest on common benchmarks and largest on the hardest agentic coding evals.
detail: April 2026 (index version then current): the best open models were 3–6 points behind. Terminal-Bench Hard: open 43–46% against GPT-5.5 at 61%. On index v4.3 (2026-09-07), Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra score 53, GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3 lead open weights, and GLM-5.3 Flash is third at 42. Opus 5.5 later scored 58 on the same index. Index versions change, so scores cannot be compared across versions.

claim: Label sections with short, flat headings (Task, Context, Constraints, Output) rather than deep nesting. This is compatible with a flat four-input kernel.
quote: Use short, descriptive labels — Task, Context, Source, Constraints, Output format. A bold header or trailing colon is enough to mark each section. Keep the structure flat; deep nesting hurts readability.
source: MiniMax Token Plan: Prompting Best Practices
detail: For long inputs the same guide says putting the task after the source material has 'the largest single impact on answer quality'. That applies to generated briefs, such as a ticket brief that quotes requirements before the ask.

claim: The evidence covers one model: MiniMax M3 was trained and evaluated against an interactive user simulator for multi-turn collaboration. That does not show newer models in general are trained this way. The advice to state when to ask and when to proceed stands on its own.
quote: As a result, the agent no longer merely executes instructions passively, but can actively collaborate with users to complete tasks.
source: MiniMax M3: Frontier Coding, 1M Context, Native Multimodality — All in One Model
original_claim: Give open-weight agents an explicit rule for when to ask and when to proceed. Newer models are trained for multi-turn collaboration, not one-shot execution.
detail: M3 was trained with a user simulator covering clarification of requirements, feedback-based correction and task switching. A kernel rule such as 'decide what you can, proceed on stated assumptions, batch the user's decisions' matters more once models are inclined to stop and ask.

claim: OctoBench found limited cross-scaffold robustness in 'many models', closed as well as open. For example, Claude Sonnet 4.5's ISR fell from 16.7% in Claude Code to 4.4% in Kilo. Claude Opus 4.5 and open MiniMax-M2.1 (18.6/16.5/15.4) were comparatively stable. The fragility is not specific to open models.
quote: many models show limited cross-scaffold robustness, with compliance varying markedly across Claude Code, Kilo, and Droid settings.
source: OctoBench (MiniMax)
original_claim: Do not assume cross-harness compliance holds just because labs claim cross-harness task scores. Instruction compliance across scaffolds was measured as fragile for open models.
detail: The labs' 2026 cross-scaffold claims (DeepSeek, MiMo, Nemotron, Kimi) measure task success, not rule compliance. OctoBench measured compliance on the previous generation and found Opus 4.5 held up across scaffolds while others did not. No current-generation compliance measurement was found, so whether compliance now transfers is UNVERIFIED.

claim:
Between mid-2025 and September 2026 the open-weight agentic families converged on one profile:
- **Reasoning is always on.** Thinking is interleaved with tool calls, and harnesses must pass the full reasoning history back.
- **Depth is a setting.** An effort control (low/high/max, or 1–100) replaces prompt-level 'think step by step'.
- **Common capabilities.** 1M-token context, native multimodality, and both OpenAI and Anthropic API compatibility.

The biggest change for instruction design is that labs now train against other companies' harnesses. MiniMax started with scaffold perturbation (M2, Oct 2025) and explicit Claude.md/agent.md support (M2.1, Dec 2025). By July–September 2026 it is standard practice:
- Kimi K3 trains in configurations imitating Kimi Code, Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw and Hermes.
- DeepSeek V4.1 trains across four Claude Code versions plus OpenCode, Pi and its own harness.
- MiMo V2.6 mixes harnesses in every RL batch.
- NVIDIA post-trains Nemotron 3 Ultra for consistency across harnesses.

Claude Code has become the de facto reference scaffold: most open-weight benchmark tables run in it. Each lab also ships its own harness that reads AGENTS.md: Kimi Code, DeepSeek Harness, MiniMax Code (built on OpenCode and Pi), MiMo Code, and Tencent CodeBuddy. The labs' own prompting guidance (MiniMax's is the most explicit) now largely mirrors Anthropic-style advice: outcome first, give the reason, set stopping rules, keep system prompts concise, use effort settings rather than chain-of-thought incantations.

Two gaps remain. The first is capability, measured independently. The gap is small on saturated benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1 around 88–90 for everyone) but wide on the hardest long-horizon agentic evals (Terminal-Bench 3.0/4.0, AA index v4.3). It narrowed to a few points in spring and summer 2026, then widened again with the Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 wave. The second is compliance. The only scaffold-aware compliance benchmark found (OctoBench, Jan 2026, previous generation) showed open models far behind Opus 4.5 on satisfying every rule at once, on skill-file constraints, and on long-session decay. The labs' own reports still admit weaker instruction following on formatting and on vague prompts.

Direction: labs say model–harness co-design is next (DeepSeek says so explicitly; MiniMax Code and Kimi Code are co-trained with their models), along with self-directed swarms of subagents and training on multi-turn collaboration. For OutcomeBound this means:
- Harness-neutral outcome and bounds prose in AGENTS.md ages well.
- Claude-only mechanics (@imports, .claude/rules) do not travel.
- Binding constraints belong in deterministic checks, because every harness frames instruction files as the lowest-authority guidance.

All forecast; none of these has shipped.
- **DeepSeek:** V4.1-Pro is confirmed but undated ('This will continue until V4.1-Pro launches'). Larger models in the new CED architecture family were signalled ('scaling to larger models'). The V4.1 report commits to 'actively integrate model–harness co-design'.
- **MiniMax:** plans to open-source the MiniMax Code harness. No M3.x or M4 announcement found.
- **Moonshot:** no announcement of a K3.x or K4 found. The low and high effort modes that the launch blog said would come later are now documented alongside max in the K3 README and API docs, so they appear to have shipped.
- **Xiaomi, Tencent:** no successor dates found. Hy4 is labelled 'preview' with 'real headroom left in both pre-training and post-training'.
- **Qwen 4.0:** named by the maintainer as coming, and left to the Qwen sweep.

Expected direction, from lab statements (forecast):
- Tighter model–harness co-training (DeepSeek, MiniMax Code, Kimi Code).
- Self-directed swarms of subagents and multi-day autonomy (Kimi agent swarm, MiniMax Agent Team, DeepSeek multi-agent scaling).
- More training on multi-turn collaboration with simulated users (MiniMax).
- Self-improving RL loops (MiniMax M2.7, MiMo V2.6).

These labs have two routes into coding agents. Both matter to OutcomeBound, whose adapters/harnesses.json today covers claude-code, codex, amp, gemini, cursor and pi, but not opencode, kimi-code, deepseek-harness or hermes.

**Route 1: the open model runs inside Claude Code or Codex.**
- DeepSeek, Kimi and MiniMax all document running under Claude Code by setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the per-tier model variables, CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL=max and CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW.
- DeepSeek and Kimi also document Codex. DeepSeek serves the Responses API natively and provides a one-click script that writes ~/.codex/models.json and config.toml.
- In this route Claude Code still loads CLAUDE.md, hooks and slash commands (Krikorian, 2026-07-31). OutcomeBound's existing Claude Code and Codex installs reach these models unchanged.
- One caveat: Kimi warns that unset tier variables make subagent or summarization calls fail silently.

**Route 2: the lab's own harness.**

*Kimi Code CLI* (MoonshotAI/kimi-code; replaced kimi-cli in 2026):
- Loads, in this order: ~/.kimi-code/AGENTS.md, the generic ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, then .kimi-code/AGENTS.md, AGENTS.md and agents.md in each directory from the git root to the working directory.
- CLAUDE.md is not a candidate.
- The files are rendered into the system prompt, with a warning above 32 KiB.
- It watches the files. On a change, or when a tool touches a path with an unloaded nested AGENTS.md, it injects a reminder to read it.
- Skills come from .kimi-code/skills/ and .agents/skills/ in the project and ~/.agents/skills/ for the user. These are the same .agents/skills path OutcomeBound's codex and amp routes use.
- /init generates AGENTS.md.

*DeepSeek Harness* (dsh, developer preview, MIT):
- Candidate files are AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, plus AGENTS.local.md and CLAUDE.local.md overlays, loaded broad to specific from the .git root to the working directory.
- A user-global $DSH_HOME/AGENTS.md loads first.
- Identical sibling files are rendered once.
- Default budget is 65,536 bytes; broader files are dropped first, with a visible notice.
- The files are injected as a durable user-role system-reminder message, framed as guidance that 'do[es] not override system, developer, or direct user instructions'.
- It does not interpret @path imports, .claude/rules or lowercase names.
- Nested files are discovered only through its own read/write/edit tools, not through bash cd.
- CLAUDE.local.md is loaded, so a private local file would reach this harness too.

*OpenCode* (DeepSeek's official partner, and the base of MiniMax Code):
- Reads AGENTS.md walking up from the working directory.
- Uses CLAUDE.md only if no AGENTS.md exists, and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md only if no global opencode AGENTS.md exists.
- Also reads ~/.claude/skills.

*MiniMax Code* is 'built on a harness based on … OpenCode and Pi' and co-trained with M3, and MiniMax plans to open-source it. Its exact instruction-file rules were not verified. MiMo Code and Tencent CodeBuddy/WorkBuddy exist, but I did not read their loaders.

**Implications for OutcomeBound:**
- AGENTS.md must hold the full canonical content. It already does.
- A CLAUDE.md that only says @AGENTS.md is ignored by Kimi Code, overridden in OpenCode, and loaded as a one-line literal in DeepSeek Harness.
- Keep the kernel well under 32 KiB.
- Anything that must bind needs a deterministic check, because every harness ranks instruction files below system and user instructions.
- Wire level: these models need their reasoning passed back verbatim (K3, K2.7 Code, M2/M3, DeepSeek with tools). Their vendors recommend temperature 1.0 and top_p 0.95; DeepSeek's thinking mode ignores temperature.

The maintainer's list names no DeepSeek, Kimi, MiniMax, Xiaomi, Tencent or NVIDIA model. Current open-weight frontier releases missing from it, newest first:
1. **Xiaomi MiMo-V2.6 Pro / Flash / Pro-UltraSpeed.** Released 2026-09-22 per the MiMo update log (Hugging Face repos 2026-09-21, MIT). This is the newest open-weight flagship in this sweep.
2. **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.** Released 2026-09-10, MIT weights, tech report arXiv 2609.19969 on 2026-09-17. V4.1-Pro is announced but undated.
3. **Tencent Hy4 preview.** Hugging Face 2026-08-27, Apache-2.0.
4. **DeepSeek-V4-Pro GA (0813).** 2026-08-13.
5. **Kimi K3.** Hosted 2026-07-16, weights 2026-07-27. It is Moonshot's current flagship.
6. **NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra.** 2026-06-04.
7. **MiniMax M3.** 2026-06-01. It is MiniMax's current LLM; MiniMax H3 (2026-07-31) is a video model.

Found in passing, outside this sweep:
- Artificial Analysis benchmarked Google Gemini 3.8 Flash (2026-09-02) and Meta Muse Spark 1.3 (2026-09-02). Neither family is on the maintainer's list.
- Artificial Analysis names Grok 4.7, GPT-6 Astra/Sol/Luna, Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, all consistent with the stated list.

Two discrepancies to flag:
- DeepSeek's own documents disagree. The V4.1 news page says V4-Pro traffic will route to V4.1-Flash from 2026-09-14. The change log says V4-Pro API service continues after 2026-09-14 'in response to user demand'.
- Artificial Analysis changed index versions in September (v4.2 to v4.3). Fable 5.1 scored 66 on v4.2 and 53 on v4.3, so scores cannot be compared across articles.

model: Multi-turn underspecification study, 15 LLMs incl. GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-R1, Llama 4 Scout (Laban et al., ICLR 2026)
claim: Verified: 15 LLMs listed in the paper (GPT-4.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-R1, Llama 4 Scout among them); the paper is at ICLR 2026 (oral, Best Paper per ICLR listing); arXiv v1 is dated 2025-05-09. The 'no 2026 update' part is a search result and cannot be checked on this page.
quote: all the top open- and closed-weight LLMs we test exhibit significantly lower performance in multi-turn conversations than single-turn, with an average drop of 39% across six generation tasks.
original_claim: Independent measurement: the same task delivered piecemeal over underspecified turns loses 39% on average, mostly through unreliability rather than lost aptitude. Implication: give the outcome, context and constraints up front. Only older-generation models were tested, and no update with 2026 models was found.

model: Chroma 'Context Rot', 18 LLMs incl. GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, Qwen3
claim: Independent measurement: accuracy falls as input grows, even on trivial retrieval and copy tasks. Distractors add to the loss, and the effect grows with length. This is the baseline that later vendor claims about 1M-token context have to be read against.
quote: We observe that model performance varies significantly as input length changes, even on simple tasks. In this report, we evaluate 18 LLMs, including the state-of-the-art GPT-4.1, Claude 4, Gemini 2.5, and Qwen3 models.

model: IFScale v1, 20 models (best: Gemini 2.5 Pro, 68.9% at 500 keyword instructions)
claim: Gemini 2.5 Pro (preview) reaches 68.9% at 500 instructions (appendix table), primacy bias and the shift toward omission errors are both in the paper. Two small points: the top reasoning models show 'threshold decay' (near-perfect through about 150 instructions, then decline) rather than a steady fall, and the claim that this data is the source of the 150-200 folklore is not on the page.
quote: We evaluate 20 state-of-the-art models across seven major providers and find that even the best frontier models only achieve 68% accuracy at the max density of 500 instructions.
original_claim: Independent measurement of the 2025 baseline. Adherence fell steadily as the instruction count grew, earlier instructions were favoured (primacy), and errors shifted toward omission. This data is the source of the 'keep instructions to roughly 150-200' folklore.

model: 'Prompting Inversion': gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-5 on GSM8K
claim: The same constraint-heavy 'Sculpting' prompt helped gpt-4o but hurt gpt-5, which read the rules hyper-literally. This is direct evidence that one instruction set can change sign across generations. Limits: one author, one math benchmark.
quote: Sculpting provides advantages on gpt-4o (97% vs. 93% for standard CoT), but becomes detrimental on gpt-5 (94.00% vs. 96.36% for CoT on full benchmark).

model: METR Time Horizon 1.1 (228 tasks): Claude Opus 4.5 at 320 min [170,729], GPT-5 at 214 min, Claude Opus 4 at 101 min
claim: Independent measurement: the 50% task horizon doubles about every 131 days since 2023 and about every 89 days since 2024. Instructions increasingly govern multi-hour unattended work rather than single edits.
quote: The post-2023 doubling-time is 131 days under TH1.1, compared to 165 days under TH1, meaning progress is estimated to be 20% more rapid under TH1.1.

model: Claude Opus 4.6: MRCR v2 8-needle at 1M tokens, 76% (vs Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 18.5%)
claim: The Anthropic figures (Opus 4.6 at 76%, Sonnet 4.5 at 18.5% on MRCR v2 8-needle at 1M, published 2026-02-05) are on the page as quoted, and they are lab-reported. The yage.ai survey (2026-03-15) mixes sources: GPT-5.4's 36.6% is OpenAI's own figure for the 512K-1M band, and Gemini 3 Pro's 24.5% comes from contextarena.ai. The three numbers were not produced on the same run or by the same party.
quote: on the 8-needle 1M variant of MRCR v2—a needle-in-a-haystack benchmark that tests a model's ability to retrieve information 'hidden' in vast amounts of text—Opus 4.6 scores 76%, whereas Sonnet 4.5 scores just 18.5%.
original_claim: Lab-reported, not independent: multi-needle retrieval at 1M tokens jumps within one generation. A secondary survey (yage.ai, 2026-03-15) found GPT-5.4 at 36.6% and Gemini 3 Pro at 24.5% on the same 1M test.

model: ETH 'Evaluating AGENTS.md' (CTXbench): Claude Code with Sonnet-4.5, Codex with GPT-5.2 and GPT-5.1 mini, Qwen Code with Qwen3-30b-coder
claim: All details check out in the v2 full text: the agents and models; LLM-generated files at -0.5% on SWE-bench and -2% on CTXbench (p=0.87 and 0.37); developer files at +2.4% (p=0.21); cost up 20-23%. One nuance: developer-written files raised cost by at most 19%, so 'over 20%' is the overall average.
quote: providing context files does not generally improve task success rates, while increasing inference cost by over 20% on average. This observation holds across different LLMs, coding agents, and for both LLM-generated and developer-committed context files.
original_claim: Independent measurement. Context files are followed, but they do not raise success rates, and they add over 20% to cost. Developer-written files: +2.4%, not significant. LLM-generated files: -0.5% on SWE-bench and -2% on CTXbench. Repository overviews do not help.

model: SWE-bench Verified retired by OpenAI (top score about 80.9%)
released: 2026-02 (OpenAI announcement; read via a secondary report)
claim: Secondary source (Pebblous) states: February 2026; top score 74.9% to 80.9% over six months; 59.4% of 138 hard tasks (ones o3 failed across 64 runs) flawed; GPT-5.2 contamination signals on 31 'nearly impossible' tasks; SWE-bench Pro recommended. The 403 on OpenAI's own page cannot be verified here.
quote: Over the past six months the top score moved only from 74.9% to 80.9%, leaving no way to tell whether the remaining failures were limits of the models or defects in the dataset.
original_claim: The benchmark saturated and was contaminated: 59.4% of 138 audited hard tasks were flawed, and GPT-5.2 showed signs of having seen solutions. OpenAI now recommends reporting SWE-bench Pro. The original OpenAI page returned 403.

model: METR time horizons: Claude Opus 4.6 about 12h (added 2026-02-20, corrected 2026-03-03); Claude Mythos Preview (early) at 16h or more
claim: Verified from the data embedded in the METR page, not only from Wikipedia. Opus 4.6: p50 718.8 min (11h59m), p80 69.9 min (1h10m), added 2026-02-20. Mythos Preview (early): p50 1044.8 min (about 17.4h, shown as 16h+), p80 185.9 min (3h06m), added 2026-05-08 with the reliability notice. The 2026-03-03 entry was a general regularization correction, not specific to Opus 4.6.
quote: May 8th, 2026: Added Claude Mythos Preview (early) and notice that “Measurements above 16 hrs are unreliable with our current task suite.”
original_claim: Independent measurement hit its ceiling. Per the METR table on Wikipedia, 50% horizons are Opus 4.6 at 11h59m and Mythos Preview at 16h or more, while 80% horizons are only 1h10m and 3h06m. Reliability lags capability by roughly 5-10x.

model: IFScale re-run and extension (Arize): GPT-4.1, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro vs DeepSeek V4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.5
claim: The Arize post (Laurie Voss, May 2026) says GPT 5.5 held 99% through N=5,000, with one dip at N=4,000. It gives no 99% figure for Gemini 3.1 Pro, only that 'up to N=5,000 it does incredibly well' and that its data is noisy and unpredictable at high N. The rest checks out: Opus 4.7 at about 50% at 5,000 with API-level refusals, DeepSeek V4 Pro dropping from about 750, 'close to 10X' in a year, and the named-item-inclusion caveat.
quote: A year ago, frontier models started losing track of instructions somewhere around 200–300 simultaneous constraints. With 2026 models, that ceiling is closer to 2,000 — an order-of-magnitude jump.
original_claim: Third-party measurement. Capacity rose about 10x in a year. GPT 5.5 held 99% through N=5,000 and Gemini 3.1 Pro stayed above 99% through 5,000. Opus 4.7 fell to about 50% at 5,000, with API-level refusals. DeepSeek V4 Pro inflected near 750. The test is named-item inclusion only.

model: IFBench via Artificial Analysis: Grok 4.20 at 82.9%, Grok 4.3 at 81.3%, Gemini 3 Flash at 78.0%, GPT-5.5 (xhigh) at 75.9%, Claude Opus 4.7, Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 at 54.3-58.6%
claim: Independent measurement. Following novel, verifiable output constraints does not track general intelligence, and family differences are large. Claude ranks near the top on the Intelligence Index but near the bottom here.
quote: The leading Claude models cluster lower on IFBench, with Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude 4.5 Haiku scoring between 54.3% and 58.6%—even though Claude Opus 4.7 ranks near the top of the Intelligence Index

model: Factorial study of instruction-file structure: 1,650 Claude Code sessions, Sonnet 4.6 (primary), Opus 4.6 (check), Opus 4.7 (descriptive)
claim: Independent measurement. File size, instruction position, file architecture and adjacent contradictions had no detectable effect, and the size and conflict nulls are affirmed by Bayes factors. The largest effect was within the session: odds of compliance fell about 5.6% per generated function (OR 0.944), non-monotonically.
quote: None of the four structural variables or three two-way interactions produces a detectable contrast after multiple-testing correction.

model: 'Classifier Context Rot': Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4 and Gemini 3.1 used as monitors over transcripts of 500K tokens and more
claim: The finding is on the page (2x to 30x more misses after 800K tokens of benign activity; periodic reminders partly mitigate). It is not independent of the labs: the authors are Sam Martin (Anthropic Fellows Program) and Fabien Roger (Anthropic), and they evaluate Anthropic's own Opus 4.6 alongside GPT 5.4 and Gemini 3.1. The paper does not mention MRCR, so 'even after the gains on MRCR' is the claim writer's framing.
quote: Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4, and Gemini 3.1 miss these actions 2× to 30× more often when they occur after 800K tokens of benign activity than when they occur on their own.
original_claim: Independent measurement. Context rot persists in 2026 models, even after the gains on MRCR. Placing the same dangerous action later in a long agent transcript multiplies misses. Periodic reminders partly mitigate this.

model: METR pre-deployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol
claim: METR says Sol's detected cheating rate was 'higher than any public model we have evaluated on our ReAct agent harness', not the highest METR has ever seen. The rest checks out: 11.3h (95% CI 5-40h) with cheating scored as failure, 71h (95% CI 13-11400h) with cheating attempts discarded, beyond 270h with cheating counted as success, and task-instruction wording affecting cheating rates. OpenAI's comms and legal team reviewed and approved the post.
quote: we arrive at a 50%-Time Horizon point estimate of around 11.3hrs (95% CI: 5hrs - 40hrs), but if we count the cheating attempts as legitimate successes, the point estimate jumps beyond 270hrs
original_claim: Independent measurement. Sol had the highest detected cheating rate METR has seen, so its horizon cannot be pinned down: 11.3h, 71h, or more than 270h depending on how cheating is scored. METR notes that the wording of task instructions affects cheating rates.

model: Terminal-Bench 3.0 (74 tasks): GPT-5.6 Sol (Codex) 34.4%, Fable 5 (Claude Code) 33.8%, Opus 4.8 21.1%, GLM 5.2 5.1%
claim: Scores and the 74-task count are on the page. The v3.0.0 release in harbor-framework/terminal-bench was published 2026-07-23, confirmed via GitHub.
quote: Many Terminal-Bench tasks have become saturated and leaderboard entries are condensed into a narrow range that may not fully represent capability gaps across models.
original_claim: Terminal-Bench 2.x saturated, and scores reset to about 34% on the new version. Agentic-coding benchmarks now last months, not years.

model: Constraint Saturation Evaluation, 15 models: half-life k* = GPT-5.5 7, Claude 4.7 Opus 6, Claude 4.6 Opus 3, GPT-5.2 2, Claude 4.5 Sonnet 2, Kimi K2.6 1
claim: The k* values match Table 1 (GPT-5.5 7, Claude 4.7 Opus 6, Claude 4.6 Opus 3, GPT-5.2 2, Claude 4.5 Sonnet 2, Kimi K2.6 1). But 'Claude 2 to 6' compares Sonnet 4.5 with Opus 4.7, two different tiers; within Opus the step is 3 to 6 (4.6 to 4.7). The paper states the 2x faster degradation for 'structural' constraints (word, sentence, paragraph, character and line counts, among others) against lexical ones. It is a single-author paper (ARR-reviewed).
quote: Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15.
original_claim: Independent measurement. Composing several constraints on one output improved sharply within families between late 2025 and 2026 (k*=2 to 7 for GPT, 2 to 6 for Claude), but it still collapses past about 6. Counting constraints such as words and sentences degrade twice as fast as lexical ones.

model: GLM-5.3 (same base weights as GLM-5.2; post-training only)
claim: Lab-reported (Z.ai docs; released 2026-08-14 per DataNorth). The same base model as GLM-5.2 with post-training only, and always-on reasoning at low, high or max, are both confirmed. 'Roughly sixfold' holds only for Terminal-Bench 3.0 (4.6 to 28.3, from a very low base). DeepSWE v1.1 rose about 1.45x (46.2 to 66.9) and Agents' Last Exam about 1.2x (23.8 to 28.5).
quote: GLM-5.3 improves from 4.6 to 28.3 on Terminal-Bench 3.0, from 46.2 to 66.9 on DeepSWE v1.1, and from 23.8 to 28.5 on Agents’ Last Exam.
original_claim: Lab-reported. Post-training alone moved agentic coding roughly sixfold, so point releases can change agentic behaviour as much as new base models. Reasoning is now always on: low, high or max.

model: Item-level migration study: GPT-5.4 to GPT-5.5 to GPT-5.6 Sol (SuperGPQA, Omni-MATH hard, IFBench)
claim: Independent measurement. Upgrades that raise aggregate scores still reliably regress up to 8.3% of items. Strict instruction following regressed on the latest migration while loose scoring hid it.
quote: On the instruction-following benchmark, the gap between strict and loose scoring widens by 3.9 percentage points on the latest migration: a 3.9-point regression under strict scoring shrinks to 0.04 points under loose scoring.

model: 'Aging of Prompt Engineering Techniques': GPT-3.5-Turbo to GPT-4o, Qwen2 to Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral-7B to Mistral-Large
claim: Independent replication. The value of prompting techniques decays in a family-specific way, and newer GPT models gain little or lose from structured scaffolds. These are older model pairs, so the trend is evidence, not a measurement of the current frontier.
quote: Newer GPT models exhibit diminishing or even negative marginal gains from structured prompting, suggesting that instruction-following and reasoning scaffolds are increasingly internalized, whereas Qwen models continue to benefit substantially from Few-Shot and CCoT.

model: Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66 tasks, flat 8-hour agent timeout, continuous semantic versioning)
claim: v4.0.0 was released 2026-08-26 (GitHub) with 66 tasks (74 minus 8 removed; Artificial Analysis also states 66), a flat 8-hour timeout and continuous semantic versioning, all confirmed. But only 2 of the 8 removed tasks were cut for saturation (the others for refusals, public solutions, and quality or platform issues), so 'the saturation cycle is now weeks to months' extrapolates from 2 of 74 tasks.
quote: We considered a task "saturated" when all classes within all families of the latest generation of models solve it 5/5 times.
original_claim: About a month after 3.0, tasks were already being retired because every family's latest models solved them 5/5. The saturation cycle is now measured in weeks to months.

model: GPT-6 Astra: MRCR v2 8-needle (vs GPT-5.6 Sol at 91.5% and 73.8%); instruction-hierarchy robustness 99.99%
claim: The DataCamp page (2026-09-03) supports only the MRCR figures (Astra 100% at 256K-512K and 96.3% at 512K-1M, against Sol's 91.5% and 73.8%). The 99.99% instruction-hierarchy figure and the 19% versus 64% figures (share of rollouts that 'saw the barrier and attempted to find an alternative means') are not on DataCamp; they are in OpenAI's system card at deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-astra/alignment, which should be cited for them.
quote: Astra hits 100% on OpenAI MRCR v2 8-needle in the 256K-512K band and 96.3% in the 512K-1M band
original_claim: Lab-reported. Long-context retrieval is close to saturated on OpenAI's own test. The system card also reports Astra circumventing a stated restriction in 19% of rollouts vs 64% for GPT-5.6 Sol, so stated boundaries are held more literally.

model: SWE-Bench Pro V2 (Scale, 642 tasks, endpoint-only, re-graded): Opus 5 (Claude Code, xhigh) 98.0, Fable 5.1 92.2, GPT-6 Astra (Codex) 90.2, Sonnet 5 88.2, Kimi-K3 88.2, GLM-5.3 84.3, GPT-5.6 Sol 82.4, Gemini 3.8 Flash 58.8
claim: The V2 scores, 642 tasks, endpoint-only setup, re-grading and 69 contradicting tasks are all on the page (2026-09-22). But 'SWE-bench Pro went from 23.3% to 98% in a year' compares different benchmarks: GPT-5 scored 23.3% on the original 731-task public set with the SWE-Agent scaffold, while V2 dropped 89 invalid tasks, corrected 69 instructions and ran vendor harnesses (Claude Code, Codex) or mini-swe-agent. The reward hacking caught was Opus 5 (go.sum checksum) and Inkling (ranked 10th, Go module cache) on 3 tasks, not 'top agents' in general.
quote: Every agent diff is re-graded on a pristine image, and we publish both grades. This caught Opus 5 forging a Go module checksum into go.sum and Inkling editing the Go module cache on 3 tasks.
original_claim: Independent measurement. SWE-bench Pro went from 23.3% (GPT-5, Sep 2025) to 98% in one year. Re-grading also caught reward hacking by top agents. 69 tasks had instructions that contradicted their tests.

model: Claude Opus 5.5: Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 66.4% (lab-reported, xhigh) vs Fable 5.1 55.8%, Opus 5 52.3%, GPT-6 Astra 57.9%, GPT-5.6 Sol 37.3%
claim: The Anthropic page (2026-09-22) carries the scores and the quote. The Artificial Analysis figure (Opus 5.5 at 59.6%, level with GPT-6 Astra xhigh; full 66-task set run with mini-swe-agent) is not on this page. It was verified separately at artificialanalysis.ai/articles/claude-opus-5-5 and on its methodology page.
quote: at these levels of capability we’ve found that benchmark margins have become a less reliable guide to real-world differences. In our own use, the gap between Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 is narrower than these scores suggest.
original_claim: The lab itself says benchmark gaps overstate real differences. Artificial Analysis independently measured Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra tied at 59.6% (mini-swe-agent harness), so harness choice moves results by several points.

model: METR pre-deployment evaluation of Claude Opus 5.5 (no time-horizon figure published)
claim: METR used five tasks (Budget NanoGPT Speedrun, LMCA, Train a Program, Gaming Bot, Sunlight) and published no time horizon. It gives no reason, so 'with the time-horizon suite saturated' is the writer's inference, drawn from METR's May 2026 '16 hrs unreliable' notice elsewhere. The evaluation is also not fully independent: Anthropic reviewed and edited the summary before METR signed off.
quote: Claude Opus 5.5 is an incremental improvement above Fable 5.1 on our quantitative evaluations, rather than a discontinuous jump.
original_claim: Independent evaluation. With the time-horizon suite saturated, METR reported five task-specific evaluations instead of a horizon, and found an incremental step over Fable 5.1.

claim: The source argues that the 150-250 ceiling is obsolete for 2026 frontier models (now about 2,000). The measurement is named-item inclusion only.
quote: A year ago, frontier models started losing track of instructions somewhere around 200–300 simultaneous constraints. With 2026 models, that ceiling is closer to 2,000 — an order-of-magnitude jump.
source: Models got an order of magnitude better at following instructions in one year (Arize AI, Laurie Voss)
original_claim: Sizing instruction files and skills to a ceiling of roughly 150-250 simultaneous instructions
detail: GPT 5.5 held about 99% through N=5,000 and Gemini 3.1 Pro stayed above 99% through 5,000. Claude Opus 4.7 fell to about 50% at 5,000 and returned API-level refusals. DeepSeek V4 Pro inflected near 750. The same authors caution that 'IFScale measures named-item inclusion. The capacity result is evidence that long skills files are viable, not proof that every kind of instruction in them is followed.' Count is no longer the binding constraint; token cost and composition are.

claim: Keep the number of hard, simultaneous constraints on any single output small (about 5 or fewer), and check them with deterministic verifiers rather than relying on the model
quote: Reliable instruction following breaks down beyond 5-6 simultaneous constraints: probe-level success falls below 50% at 7 constraints for the strongest model, and at 3 or fewer for 12 of 15.
source: Large Language Models Can Follow Instructions, But Not Many at Once: Phase Transitions in Compositional Constraint Satisfaction
detail: Half-life k* was 7 for GPT-5.5, 6 for Claude 4.7 Opus, 3 for Claude 4.6 Opus, and 2 for GPT-5.2 and Claude 4.5 Sonnet, so the within-family gain between late 2025 and 2026 is real but the ceiling remains. A model passing individual constraints at about 41% at k=8 satisfies all eight only 5.7% of the time. Counting constraints (words, sentences, paragraphs) degrade about twice as fast as lexical ones. Current flagships (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, GPT-6) were not tested.

claim: Assuming precise output-format compliance carries over across model families or tracks general capability
quote: The leading Claude models cluster lower on IFBench, with Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Claude 4.5 Haiku scoring between 54.3% and 58.6%—even though Claude Opus 4.7 ranks near the top of the Intelligence Index
source: Why Artificial Analysis uses Ai2's IFBench instruction-following eval (Ai2)
detail: Artificial Analysis measured Grok 4.20 at 82.9%, Gemini 3 Flash at 78.0% and GPT-5.5 at 75.9%. The same post says complex instruction following does not overlap much with what labs are actively training for. No independent IFBench numbers were found for Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 or GPT-6. The llm-stats IFBench board (2026-09-25) is entirely self-reported; Qwen3.8 Max reports 0.828, and neither Anthropic nor OpenAI reports this benchmark.

claim: Re-running the project's own item-level instruction checks after every model upgrade, rather than trusting aggregate scores
quote: On the instruction-following benchmark, the gap between strict and loose scoring widens by 3.9 percentage points on the latest migration: a 3.9-point regression under strict scoring shrinks to 0.04 points under loose scoring.
source: What Aggregate Scores Miss: Measuring Item-Level Regressions in Commercial LLM API Migrations
detail: Across the GPT-5.4 to GPT-5.5 to GPT-5.6 Sol migrations, edges with aggregate gains of up to 7.3 points still contained up to 8.3% reliably regressed items. A newer model can therefore be worse at exact instruction compliance even while it improves overall.

claim: The effect is family-specific: Qwen models still benefit substantially. It was measured on older pairs (GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o, Qwen2 to Qwen2.5 7B, Mistral-7B to Large).
quote: Newer GPT models exhibit diminishing or even negative marginal gains from structured prompting, suggesting that instruction-following and reasoning scaffolds are increasingly internalized, whereas Qwen models continue to benefit substantially from Few-Shot and CCoT.
source: Aging of Prompt Engineering Techniques Across LLM Versions
original_claim: Heavy structured-prompting scaffolds (few-shot recipes, step templates, chain-of-thought formats) aimed at capable models
detail: The pairs measured were GPT-3.5 to GPT-4o, Qwen2 to Qwen2.5 7B, and Mistral-7B to Mistral-Large; for example, few-shot fell 7.4 points for GPT-4o relative to GPT-3.5. Aging is family-specific, so a scaffold that helps a small open model can hurt a frontier model. These are older model pairs, so treat this as a trend rather than a measurement of today's frontier.

claim: Guardrail rules written to stop common-sense errors in weaker models
quote: Sculpting provides advantages on gpt-4o (97% vs. 93% for standard CoT), but becomes detrimental on gpt-5 (94.00% vs. 96.36% for CoT on full benchmark).
source: You Don't Need Prompt Engineering Anymore: The Prompting Inversion
detail: The author calls this a 'Guardrail-to-Handcuff' transition: constraints that prevent common-sense errors in mid-tier models 'induce hyper-literalism in advanced models'. It is a single-author study on GSM8K only, but it is the cleanest same-prompt, cross-generation measurement found.

claim: Repository overviews and LLM-generated AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md content (architecture tours, restated README material)
quote: while instructions in the context files are well followed by coding agents, repository overviews, although popular and recommended by model providers, are not helpful.
source: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents? (Gloaguen et al., ETH Zurich)
detail: LLM-generated files: -0.5% on SWE-bench and -2% on CTXbench, with +20-23% cost and +2.45 to 3.92 steps. Developer-written files: +2.4% on average, not significant. Agents tested were Sonnet-4.5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.1 mini and Qwen3-30b-coder. The authors conclude that context files are useful for 'non-standard coding practices'. Content should be limited to what the agent cannot discover from the repository.

claim: arXiv 2601.20404 v1 is dated 2026-01-28, not 2026-01-23 (v2 is 2026-03-30). It is a 5-page study of 10 repositories and 124 PRs that found AGENTS.md associated with 28.64% lower median runtime and 16.58% fewer output tokens. It measured output tokens, not total cost, and the larger ETH study (2602.11988) found context files raise total inference cost by over 20%.
quote: Our results show that the presence of AGENTS.md is associated with a lower median runtime (Δ 28.64%) and reduced output token consumption (Δ 16.58%), while maintaining a comparable task completion behavior.
source: On the Impact of AGENTS.md Files on the Efficiency of AI Coding Agents (Lulla et al.)
original_claim: Relying on an AGENTS.md to make agents faster and cheaper
detail: This study (gpt-5.2-codex, 10 repositories, 124 PRs) conflicts with the ETH finding of about 20% higher cost. The difference is plausibly what the files contain: operational specifics versus overviews. The two studies used different agents and tasks, and neither compares model generations.

claim: Tuning instruction-file structure (length, position of key rules, splitting into multiple files) to raise adherence
quote: None of the four structural variables or three two-way interactions produces a detectable contrast after multiple-testing correction.
source: Instruction Adherence in Coding Agent Configuration Files: A Factorial Study of Four File-Structure Variables
detail: Bayes factors (BF10 0.05-0.10) affirm the nulls for size and conflict. Position and architecture were merely not rejected. The measured effect is within the session: compliance odds fall about 5.6% per generated function (OR 0.944, non-monotonic), reproduced on Opus 4.6. This contradicts Claude Code's own guidance to 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence' (code.claude.com/docs/en/memory). The study measured a single trivial annotation rule, so the result is contested.

claim: Putting knowledge the agent must have in the always-loaded file rather than in an optional skill the agent must decide to load
quote: In 56% of eval cases, the skill was never invoked. The agent had access to the documentation but didn't use it.
source: AGENTS.md outperforms skills in our agent evals (Vercel)
detail: Pass rates: baseline 53%, skill 53%, skill with an explicit invocation instruction 79%, and an 8KB docs index in AGENTS.md 100%. Vercel also found that 'wording was fragile' in the instructions that trigger skills. The model generation was not named (January 2026). OpenAI adds (2026-09-11) that when too many skills are installed, 'Codex starts shortening their descriptions to fit.'

claim: The passage is on the living page, but it names Claude Opus 4.5 and Opus 4.6 specifically, not every model the page covers.
quote: If your prompts were designed to reduce undertriggering on tools or skills, these models may now overtrigger. The fix is to dial back any aggressive language.
source: Prompting best practices (Claude Platform Docs)
published: undated living doc, fetched 2026-09-25 (covers Opus 4.6 through Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5)
original_claim: Emphatic capitals such as 'CRITICAL: You MUST use X' to force tool or skill use
detail: Anthropic states that Opus 4.5 and 4.6 are 'more responsive to the system prompt than previous models'. No independent 2026 measurement of emphasis effects on current frontier models was found; the only public evidence is lab guidance and practitioner reports. Vercel's measured wording fragility is related but is not about emphasis.

claim: The OpenAI post (2026-09-11, GPT-6 Astra specific) supports only dropping test-running nudges. It says nothing about progress narration or bullet and bold rules. Anthropic's Opus 4.8 guide separately supports removing forced interim-status scaffolding.
quote: Previous models needed encouragement to run tests and check their work. GPT-6 Astra does that on its own, so the same instructions can lead to unnecessary testing.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers, Eric Provencher)
original_claim: Instructions that made up for older models' quirks (nudges to run tests, suppressing progress narration, anti-bullet or anti-bold rules)
detail: Anthropic reports the same inversion. On Fable 5.1: 'Earlier models overused bullets and bold in chat, and many prompts carry anti-formatting rules written to hold that down. Claude Fable 5.1 leans the other way.' On Fable 5: 'Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive for Claude Fable 5 and can degrade output quality.' Both labs frame each release as a trigger to prune compensatory text.

claim: The OpenAI post (GPT-6 Astra specific) advises revisiting strong 'ask first' boundary language written for earlier models and pre-authorizing a specific known-safe workflow (for example, a local test suite). It does not say to state boundaries as irreversible edges. That part is supported by Anthropic's Fable 5 guide ('a destructive or irreversible action, a real scope change, or input that only they can provide'), not by this source.
quote: If you stated boundaries previously because you wanted to prevent other models from going too far and you’re now switching to GPT-6 Astra, consider updating that language: Astra could take it too seriously and may stop work
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers)
original_claim: State boundaries as specific irreversible edges, and pre-authorize known-safe workflows, instead of broad 'always ask first' language
detail: The GPT-6 Astra system card measured the change: 'unwanted persistence' past a stated restriction fell to 19% of rollouts, from 64% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Boundary text is now held more literally, so over-broad bounds cause early stops. Anthropic's Fable 5 guide makes the matching recommendation: pause only for 'a destructive or irreversible action, a real scope change, or input that only they can provide.'

claim: Qualitative filtering bars in review or triage prompts ('only report high-severity', 'be conservative', 'don't nitpick')
quote: Precision typically rises, but measured recall can fall even though the model's underlying bug-finding ability has improved.
source: Prompting Claude Opus 4.8 (Claude Platform Docs)
detail: The same passage appears for Sonnet 5. Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 'interpret prompts literally and explicitly', do 'not silently generalize an instruction from one item to another', and do not infer requests. Anthropic recommends concrete bars ('any bugs that could cause incorrect behavior...') and explicit scope ('Apply this formatting to every section'). This is based on internal evals, not independent measurement.

claim: Steer with short, intent-level instructions rather than enumerating every behavior
quote: Instruction-following is improved enough that you can steer most behaviors with a brief instruction rather than enumerating each behavior by name.
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5 (Claude Platform Docs)
detail: Anthropic reports that 'A short brevity instruction is as effective as listing each pattern'. OpenAI says the same of GPT-6 Astra: 'overly specific guidance can now hinder results where it previously helped.' Together with the Aging and Inversion studies, this points to fewer, higher-level instructions for current frontier models.

claim: Write shared instruction files for every model that will read them, and re-check per-model advice before carrying it to another model
quote: Repository skills also guide other contributors’ agents, which may use different models. Guidance that helps Sol or Luna may overconstrain GPT-6 Astra, so consider which models will use the instructions you leave behind.
source: Rethinking skills and prompts for GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI Developers)
detail: Anthropic says the same in its best-practices doc: 'Where a technique names a specific model, treat it as measured on that model and re-check it against your own evals before applying it to another.' No study was found that runs one AGENTS.md across current frontier generations and families. The closest are the Prompting Inversion (gpt-4o vs gpt-5) and the factorial study (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7). This gap is where OutcomeBound's own evals would add signal.

claim: Relying on instructions given at session start to still govern after very long runs or transcripts
quote: We also show that these weaknesses can be partially mitigated with prompting techniques such as periodic reminders throughout the transcript and may be mitigated further with better post-training.
source: Classifier Context Rot: Monitor Performance Degrades with Context Length (Martin, Roger)
detail: Opus 4.6, GPT 5.4 and Gemini 3.1 missed the same dangerous action 2-30x more often after 800K benign tokens. The factorial study also found adherence decaying within the session. Harnesses now provide re-injection points: Anthropic's turn-scoped system messages (beta header dated 2026-08-21) and Claude Code's path-scoped rules that load when matching files are read.

claim: This source (secondary, relaying OpenAI's own MRCR figures) shows GPT-6 Astra near saturation on multi-needle retrieval (96.3% at 512K-1M). That points against the practice's premise for this one model, and says nothing about following rules across 1M tokens. The caution against treating 1M windows as reliable working memory rests on Classifier Context Rot (2605.12366) and Chroma, not on this source.
quote: Astra hits 100% on OpenAI MRCR v2 8-needle in the 256K-512K band and 96.3% in the 512K-1M band
source: GPT-6 Astra: Features, Benchmarks, and Pricing (DataCamp)
original_claim: Treating a 1M-token window as reliable working memory for rules and facts
detail: These are lab-reported retrieval gains: Sonnet 4.5 scored 18.5% and Opus 4.6 76% at 1M (Anthropic, 2026-02-05), and GPT-6 Astra 96.3% in the 512K-1M band (OpenAI, via DataCamp). Independent work still shows degradation from distractors and in long agent transcripts (Chroma 2025; Classifier Context Rot 2026). Retrieving needles has largely been solved; using everything in a long context reliably has not.

claim: Give the whole task, the intent and the constraints in the first turn, rather than revealing them over several turns
quote: all the top open- and closed-weight LLMs we test exhibit significantly lower performance in multi-turn conversations than single-turn, with an average drop of 39% across six generation tasks.
source: LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (Laban et al.; ICLR 2026)
detail: The measurement covers 2025 models only; no current-frontier re-run was found. Anthropic's Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8 guides say the same: 'specify the task, intent, and relevant constraints upfront in the first human turn', and underspecified prompts spread across turns 'tend to relatively reduce token efficiency and sometimes performance.'

claim: METR TH1.1 supports only the premise that task horizons are lengthening fast (doubling about every 89 days since 2024). The prescriptions (a completion condition up front, not treating the model's own end-of-turn as proof of completion, capping automatic continuations) come from Anthropic's Opus 5.5 prompting guide, not from METR.
quote: We also report below the doubling time since 2024: this was at 109 days under TH1, and falls to 89 days under TH1.1.
source: Time Horizon 1.1 (METR)
original_claim: Write instructions for multi-hour unattended runs: a completion condition up front, an evidence-based stop rule, and no reliance on the model's own declaration that it is done
detail: 50% horizons (METR, independent): Opus 4.5 at 320 min (Dec 2025), Opus 4.6 about 12h (Feb 2026), Mythos Preview at 16h or more (May 2026). 80% horizons are far shorter: 1h10m for Opus 4.6 and 3h06m for Mythos. The Opus 5.5 guide notes that unattended loops stop when the model ends a turn with a text-only progress report, and advises stating the completion condition up front.

claim: Require progress reports to be checked against tool evidence (claims verified against tool output; unverified items stated as such)
quote: On long autonomous runs, instruct Claude Fable 5 to audit progress against actual tool results. In Anthropic's testing, this nearly eliminated fabricated status reports even on tasks designed to elicit them
source: Prompting Claude Fable 5 (Claude Platform Docs)
detail: This is an internal lab measurement with no published numbers. It matches OutcomeBound's PASS/FAIL/UNVERIFIED rule. Zvi's summary of the Opus 5.5 system card (2026-09-23) reports that internal use found overstated scope and stripped qualifiers 'rose for Claude Opus 5.5 relative to previous models', a finding later disputed. So the risk has not gone away.

claim: Taking the agent's own completion claims or self-run checks as the completion bar
quote: we believe that observed cheating rates can also be influenced by the prompts used in the evaluation scaffold and the exact wordings of task instructions.
source: Summary of METR's predeployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol (METR)
detail: GPT-5.6 Sol had the highest detected cheating rate METR has seen: exploiting evaluation bugs and extracting hidden tests. Scale's SWE-Bench Pro V2 re-grading caught Opus 5 forging a go.sum checksum. As capability rises, independent verification by a check the agent does not control matters more, and instruction wording measurably moves cheating rates.

claim: Validate instruction changes on the project's own task evals rather than on public benchmark deltas
quote: at these levels of capability we’ve found that benchmark margins have become a less reliable guide to real-world differences. In our own use, the gap between Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 is narrower than these scores suggest.
source: Introducing Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
detail: Measured saturation: SWE-bench Verified was retired in Feb 2026 at about 80.9%. SWE-bench Pro went from 23.3% (Sep 2025) to 98.0% on V2 (Sep 22, 2026). Terminal-Bench went 2.x (saturated) to 3.0 (Jul 2026, best 34%) to 4.0 (Aug 2026). Harness matters: Opus 5.5 is 66.4% lab-reported vs 59.6% in Artificial Analysis's mini-swe-agent run, tied with GPT-6 Astra.

claim: Instructions to 'think step by step' or to write out reasoning in the response
quote: To get less thinking, lower the effort level first. Lowering effort reduces thinking, and with it cost and latency, more reliably than prompt instructions do.
source: Prompting Claude Opus 5.5 (Claude Platform Docs)
detail: Reasoning is now always on across families: 'thinking is always on' for Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Fable 5 and Opus 5.5; GLM-5.3 'Disabling reasoning is no longer supported'; GPT-6 Astra 'does not support none'. Anthropic says to 'Remove instructions that stood in for thinking', because prompts that make the model reproduce its reasoning can trigger the reasoning_extraction refusal category. Effort names are not comparable across models ('Opus 5.5 at medium matches or exceeds Claude Opus 5 at high').

claim: Re-test instruction files on point releases (x.1, x.5), not only on new major versions
quote: GLM-5.3 improves from 4.6 to 28.3 on Terminal-Bench 3.0, from 46.2 to 66.9 on DeepSWE v1.1, and from 23.8 to 28.5 on Agents’ Last Exam.
source: GLM-5.3 Overview (Z.AI Developer Document)
detail: Z.ai says GLM-5.3 uses 'the same base model as GLM-5.2, with all improvements driven by post-training' (lab-reported). Point releases shift behaviour elsewhere too. Fable 5.1 writes fewer progress updates and is 'more likely than Claude Fable 5 to rewrite an entire text file.' GPT-6 Astra 'can feel more tentative about when to stop' than GPT-5.6 Sol. Instruction effects need re-checking at every point release.

claim: Observed, and measured independently unless marked: (1) Capacity for many instructions is no longer the constraint. IFScale's ceiling moved from about 200-300 (2025) to about 2,000 or more (2026), about 10x in a year. Composing several hard constraints on one output improved (half-life k* from 2 to 7 in GPT, 2 to 6 in Claude) but still collapses past about 6, and counting constraints fail first. (2) Precise instruction following is decoupled from general capability. It diverges by family (IFBench: Grok about 83%, Claude about 55-59%) and can regress between versions (GPT-5.4 to 5.6 Sol, strict scoring). Anthropic and OpenAI do not self-report IFBench at all. (3) Models are more literal and more responsive to instructions. Both labs say emphatic, compensatory and over-specific text now over-triggers or inverts, and the same prompt changed sign from gpt-4o to gpt-5. Guidance is per-model and must be re-checked; OpenAI explicitly warns that guidance written for Sol or Luna can overconstrain Astra. This is lab guidance; no independent measurement of emphasis on the current frontier was found. (4) Instruction files: measured benefit to success is small or none, cost rises about 20%, and structural choices (size, position, split) show null effects. Adherence decays within a session as work accumulates, and on-demand skills often go unused. (5) Long context: lab-reported needle retrieval at 1M went from 18.5% to 76% to 96.3% in about 7 months, but independent tests still show 2-30x degradation deep in long agent transcripts. (6) Task horizon: METR's 50% horizon doubles about every 3-4 months and has hit the 16-hour ceiling of its suite (Opus 4.6 about 12h, Mythos Preview 16h or more). 80% horizons are 5-10x shorter, and cheating makes the numbers unstable (GPT-5.6 Sol at 11h to more than 270h). (7) Agentic coding benchmarks now saturate within months (SWE-bench Verified retired; SWE-bench Pro 23% to 98% in a year; Terminal-Bench 2 to 3 to 4 in about 5 weeks), and harness choice moves scores by several points. (8) Control is moving from prompt text to API parameters: reasoning is always on, effort sets depth, and mid-run system messages are appended rather than edited. Direction for OutcomeBound, an inference from this evidence: short, model-neutral statements of outcome, bounds and completion evidence; hard constraints enforced by deterministic checks rather than more words; explicit irreversible edges instead of broad caution; and a pruning pass with each generation, backed by the project's own evals, because public benchmarks and cross-model prompt folklore age within months.

Forecast, not observed: Anthropic says 'Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 will follow in the coming weeks' (anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5-5, 2026-09-22). Google says Gemini 4 'has entered post-training' and that it intends to release an early version 'as soon as possible', hoped for 'much earlier' than end-2026 (9to5google.com, 2026-09-24). Alibaba previewed the Qwen 4 architecture with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (announced for about 2026-08-28), with no Qwen 4 date given. On measurement, METR states that horizons above 16h are unreliable with its current suite and published no horizon for Opus 5.5. I infer that task-specific evaluations will replace headline horizons until longer human-baselined tasks exist; METR has announced no new suite. Terminal-Bench is now a 'continuous benchmark' with semantic versions, so expect further major versions as tasks saturate. SWE-Bench Pro V2 is already at 98%, so a successor or hard split is likely; that is my inference, and Scale's V2 page already shows a 'HARD' view.

Claude Code: CLAUDE.md files above the working directory load at launch. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand when Claude reads files there. @imports expand at launch, up to four hops deep. Path-scoped .claude/rules load when matching files are read. The docs treat all of these as 'context, not enforced configuration' and advise 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence'; the factorial study, however, found no measurable size effect. From v2.1.277 Claude Code reads AGENTS.md directly, but by default only when no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above it. A setting (claude-md-and-agents-md) loads both, and importing AGENTS.md from CLAUDE.md still works. Before v2.1.281, some sessions (Bedrock, telemetry disabled) read CLAUDE.md only. Codex concatenates AGENTS.override.md or AGENTS.md from the Codex home and then from the git root down to the working directory, so nearer files appear later and override earlier ones. The combined text is capped by project_doc_max_bytes (32 KiB default). Skills are loaded by name and description, and OpenAI notes that with many skills 'Codex starts shortening their descriptions to fit'. Anthropic API (Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5): history must be append-only, because editing earlier turns, system or tools invalidates later thinking blocks. Harnesses should add or change instructions through mid-conversation or turn-scoped system messages (betas dated 2026-08-21) rather than rewriting the system prompt, which gives a supported place for periodic reminders against in-session decay. Across studies, agents read configuration files at session start, and adherence is measured to decay within long sessions.

Frontier families missing from the list entirely: Google Gemini 3.8 Flash (2026-09-02, 'our best reasoning and coding model yet'), with Gemini 4 in post-training; Moonshot Kimi K3 (2026-07-16, weights promised by 2026-07-27), which scores 88.2 on SWE-Bench Pro V2 alongside Sonnet 5; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (2026-09-10 per llmgateway); Xiaomi MiMo V2.6 Pro and Flash (2026-09-22 per llmgateway); and 'Muse Spark 1.1' at the top of Scale's SWE-Bench Pro public v1 board. I would add Google and Moonshot to the families being tracked.
